World.title: Banning the hijab
World.content:
France’s far-right National Rally party, led by presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, has renewed calls to ban the hijab in public spaces—an unprecedented stance globally that has drawn fierce backlash across the French political spectrum, including right-wing and center-right factions alongside the left.

Enforcing such a measure remains highly impractical even if the National Rally secures power.

Beyond its feasibility, critics argue the proposal reflects a fundamental misunderstanding of French secularism (Laïcité), conflating state neutrality in public institutions with an infringement on personal liberty and the basic right to choose one’s attire.

In recent years, French authorities have adopted increasingly hardline stances on practices widely accepted across other European nations.

Pausing football matches for a single minute to allow fasting players to break their Ramadan fast was framed as an infraction against secularism, despite being a standardized, routine accommodation across major European leagues.

In another instance, state pressure forced a fast-food chain to abandon a halal menu  targeted at areas with large Arab-French populations.

Similarly, the government banned the hijab in sports competitions citing threats to state secularism.

The move was accompanied by a controversial public statement from the Interior Minister, who declared: “Long live sports, down with the veil.”

Building on this momentum, the far-right has pushed for a total public ban on the headscarf, underscoring a growing mainstream consensus around these proposals—and explaining why prominent political figures continue to champion them.

The fundamental question is how a global powerhouse like France—whose international stature and prestige draw heavily from the brilliance of its cultural identity, the vitality of its political framework, and a history of integrating diverse ethnicities and producing creative pioneers across every field—could reach this critical crossroad.

Despite hosting vibrant democratic debates across diverse ideological spectrums, the country now finds itself in a paradoxical position.

Leading presidential contenders in opinion polls—notwithstanding the rise of left-wing figures like Jean-Luc Mélenchon—are openly calling for a ban on the Islamic headscarf in public spaces.

Such proposed restrictions stand in sharp contrast to the reality of a nation that welcomes 70 million international tourists annually, all displaying a diverse mosaic of cultural attire and head coverings on French streets.

While acknowledging the unique structure of the French secular model—rooted in the historic 1905 law separating church and state—critics caution that expanding restrictions into the public sphere represents a dangerous escalation.

Unlike its European neighbors, France enforces a strict secularism that bars visible religious symbols from public institutions, including the removal of crucifixes from classrooms and the two-decade-old prohibition of the Islamic headscarf in public schools.

However, extending these prohibitions to public streets marks a severe departure from established precedent.

Expanding restrictions beyond state institutions constitutes a direct violation of explicit constitutional guarantees protecting freedom of belief and fundamental personal liberties.

Author’s biography

Amr al-Shobaki is an Egyptian writer, political analyst and managing-editor of Ahwal Masria magazine.

He holds a Bachelor’s degree in Political Science from Cairo University (1983), a Master’s degree in Political Science from the Institute of Political Studies in France (1993), and a PhD in Political Science from the Sorbonne University in France (2002).

World.title: Leaked tapes reveal Muslim Brotherhood plotting new Egyptian revolution and government-in-exile
World.content:
Egyptian media host Amr Adib and writer Abdel-Rahim Ali broadcasted audio recordings of Muslim Brotherhood leaders during Sunday’s episode of the “al-Hekaya” (The Story) show on MBC Egypt.

The recordings allegedly reveal plans for a new revolution and the formation of a government in exile, RT reported on Sunday.

According to Ali – a writer and researcher specializing in Islamist groups – the leaks document meetings between leaders and members of the Muslim Brotherhood and Egyptian opposition forces abroad.

These meetings reportedly included discussions about instigating political change in Egypt and preparing for what they called a new “revolution,” followed by an agreement on the form of the constitution and the political system of the country.

Ali explained that the obtained recordings total around 30 hours, but could not be broadcast in their entirety for security reasons.

He indicated that these meetings raised the idea of ​​a “civil state” as a formula to avoid early clashes with state institutions and religious movements.

Ali pointed out that the discussions were not limited to preparing a political project.

According to the recordings he presented, they also included discussions about forming a political entity abroad and a government-in-exile that could manage the transitional period should a change occur within Egypt.

According to Ali, these recordings are part of what views to be organized moves to reorganize the ranks of the Muslim Brotherhood and its allies abroad, and to prepare political alternatives that can be used in the event of unrest or a change in the internal Egyptian scene.

World.title: Tomb dating back to late Fifth Dynasty uncovered north of Saqqara
World.content:
The joint Egyptian-Spanish archaeological mission has uncovered a tomb dating back to the late Fifth Dynasty in the Mariette Necropolis north of Saqqara, the Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities announced on Monday.

The tomb, dating back to the reign of King Djedkare Isesi, contains funerary chapels belonging to two high-ranking officials.

The tomb features exceptionally well-preserved scenes and colorful reliefs depicting agricultural activities and processions carrying offerings, many of which still retain their original colors.

The discovery provides valuable new insights into the architecture, art, and administrative life of ancient Egypt during the late Fifth Dynasty.

The tomb consists of a medium-sized platform containing two funerary chapels.

One of them belongs to a person named “Younmin”, who held a number of high positions, including judge, court director, and chief clerk responsible for reviewing petitions and complaints.

The second chamber belongs to his father “Ity”, who held clerical positions related to the management of agricultural lands and offerings.

The mission is working under a joint scientific project between the Autonomous University of Barcelona in Spain and the Supreme Council of Antiquities, continuing excavation and archaeological research in the area north of Saqqara.

The Secretary-General of the Supreme Council of Antiquities, Hisham al-Leithy, emphasized the importance of this discovery, stating that it adds new archaeological information about the Saqqara necropolis during the late Fifth Dynasty.

He said that the discovery also sheds further light on the nature of these tombs, their architectural and artistic styles, and the administrative positions held by high-ranking state officials during this era of ancient Egyptian history.

World.title: Liberia: Cassell Kouh Faces US$50,000 Debt Claim After Alleged Failure to Honor Court Payment Deal
World.content:
Monrovia-Businessman Cassell Anthony Kuoh is facing a US$50,000 action of debt before the Debt Court for Montserrado County after allegedly failing to honor a payment arrangement he entered into with businessman Atef Aidebi in July 2026.

By: Willie N. Tokpah

Court documents reviewed by FrontPageAfrica show that the dispute stems from an alleged US$70,000 loan Aidebi says he extended to Kuoh in 2024.

According to the complaint filed before the Debt Court, Kuoh repaid US$20,000, leaving an alleged outstanding balance of US$50,000.

The case took a more formal turn on July 13, when Kuoh and Aidebi entered into a written payment stipulation at the Debt Court.

Under that arrangement, Kuoh proposed paying 25 percent of the US$50,000 balance, US$12,500, by July 31, 2026, followed by two installments of US$18,750 each on August 31 and September 30, 2026.

The stipulation contained a serious default clause.

It stated that if Kuoh defaulted on the agreed payments, the entire balance would immediately become due and payable, with the Debt Court empowered to proceed against him until the debt was fully settled.

However, Aidebi’s subsequent complaint alleges that Kuoh failed and refused to comply with the payment stipulation, prompting the creditor to return to court seeking recovery of the US$50,000.

The plaintiff’s complaint, filed in the Debt Court’s September 2026 term before Judge James E. Jones, asks the court to hold Kuoh liable for the full US$50,000, in addition to applicable statutory interest, costs, attorney’s fees and other relief the court may deem appropriate.

Aidebi’s lawyers also say they are prepared, if required during trial, to produce WhatsApp exchanges between the parties which they contend document repeated efforts to secure repayment.

Kuoh Acknowledges Debt Dispute

The case has also drawn attention because Kuoh has addressed the matter publicly on social media report.

In his response, Kuoh acknowledged that the allegation before the court concerns him, while arguing that owing money is not necessarily evidence of wrongdoing by a businessperson.

His position, in substance, is that any businessperson can become indebted, a response that places the dispute in the context of business obligations rather than an outright denial that the debt relationship existed.

That response is key, because the court record contains a document bearing Kuoh’s name in which he agreed to a specific repayment schedule for the outstanding US$50,000.

The central issue before the Debt Court, therefore, is not simply whether Kuoh and Aidebi had a financial relationship, but whether Kuoh failed to honor the repayment commitment he made in the July payment stipulation and whether the creditor is consequently entitled to recover the full amount claimed.

From US$70,000 Loan to US$50,000 Court Battle

The complaint paints a picture of a financial obligation that has remained unresolved since 2024.

Aidebi alleged that Kuoh borrowed US$70,000 and repaid only US$20,000.

After unsuccessful attempts to secure the remaining US$50,000, the parties apparently sought an amicable solution through the July payment agreement.

That arrangement, however, allegedly did not resolve the dispute.

Instead, the creditor has now asked the Debt Court to enforce the alleged obligation and impose costs associated with the litigation.

While Kuoh’s social-media response portrays indebtedness as something that can happen to businesspeople, the court documents raise a more pointed question: why was a formal payment agreement entered into if the outstanding obligation was not subsequently honored

The Debt Court will ultimately have to determine the legal validity of the creditor’s claims and whether Kuoh remains liable for the amount sought.

Until then, the US$50,000 claim remains an allegation before the court, and Kuoh is entitled to present his defense.

But with a written payment stipulation now forming part of the court record, and with Kuoh publicly acknowledging the underlying dispute, the case has moved beyond a private disagreement and into the formal judicial process.

World.title: When Girls Are Not Taught: Why Menstrual Health Education Must Become a National Priority
World.content:
Every girl deserves to understand her body

Across many African communities, from bustling cities to small townships like New Kru Town in Liberia — menstruation remains wrapped in silence, myths, and misinformation. It is spoken of in whispers, if at all, leaving generation after generation of girls to face one of the most formative phases of growing up without proper guidance, accurate information about the reproductive process of the female body, or dignity.

By Jamesetta Pinky Gibson

In many communities, this silence is not accidental, it is inherited. This practice, which has been passed through generations, treats menstruation as a private matter rather than a health issue. Cultural discomfort discussing the body across generations, and a lack of trained educators, combine to keep accurate information out of reach, even in homes where parents and teachers genuinely want to help.

I saw this reality firsthand in Fundaye, New Kru Town, Monrovia, where I conducted an empirical study for my undergraduate thesis that examined knowledge gaps and hygiene practices about menstruation among young women aged 18–25. Fundaye is a densely populated, low-income semi-urban community where limited access to clean water, sanitation, and hygiene facilities creates additional challenges for young women managing their menstrual health.

What stayed with me most was not simply the statistics I collected, but the conversations behind them.

One finding stood out more than any other.

Nearly nine out of every ten respondents (89.6%) reported that they had never received menstrual hygiene education in their community, while 91.7% believed that the education available in their community was inadequate.

These figures are more than numbers.

They point to a serious gap in the information young women need to make informed decisions about their health.

We cannot expect informed health decisions from people who have never been given informed health education.

My research also found that although 93.8% of respondents understood that poor menstrual hygiene could contribute to reproductive tract infections, only 31.3% correctly identified the recommended frequency for changing menstrual materials. This difference is important. Awareness of a health risk does not necessarily mean a person has the practical knowledge needed to prevent it. Where information had reached respondents at all, it came primarily from parents and guardians (28.1%) and schools (25%), while trained health workers accounted for less than one in five sources (19.8%), suggesting the health sector itself remains underused in providing education on this issue for locals.

When girls are not properly taught about menstruation, they may become susceptible to myths, misinformation, fear, embarrassment, or advice that may not always be accurate. The consequences can extend beyond menstrual hygiene to health-seeking behavior, confidence, and school participation. This is why menstrual health education should not be treated as an optional addition to healthcare. Instead, it should form part of preventive education about the reproductive process of the female body.

But my research also revealed something encouraging: young women are willing to learn.

Many of the women I engaged with were willing to ask questions, share their experiences, and better understand their bodies. Their curiosity reminded me that the challenge is not that young women do not care about their health. In many cases, they have simply not been given enough opportunities to access accurate, practical information.

Much of what we know about menstrual hygiene in this region comes from schools. Awareness campaigns, health talks, and research studies are overwhelmingly built around classrooms, reaching girls who are enrolled, attending, and easy to find in one place. But not every girl is in school. Some have dropped out. Some are working. Some never enrolled at all. My research in Fundaye deliberately looked beyond the classroom, into the community itself, and what it found is that the gap outside school walls may be even wider than the one inside them. If menstrual health education continues to live mainly in classrooms, we risk leaving behind exactly the girls who need it most.

And Liberia is not alone.

A multi-country analysis using household survey data across Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda, and Ghana, among six Sub-Saharan African countries studied — found that younger women consistently faced a higher unmet need for menstrual hygiene management than women aged 35 and older (Akoth et al., 2024). The pattern mirrors what I observed among the 18–25 age group in Fundaye: the youngest women, the ones with the most reproductive years ahead of them, are also the ones least served by existing menstrual health systems.

This means the conversation must move beyond telling girls to “practice good hygiene.” We must also ask whether they have been taught enough to do so.

The solution begins with education, but it cannot rest on one group alone.

Addressing this challenge requires collective action.

First, parents and guardians must be encouraged and supported to create safe, open conversations about menstruation at home, rather than leaving daughters to learn informally or not at all.

Second, schools and universities should provide age-appropriate menstrual and reproductive health education so that young people receive accurate information before misconceptions take root.

Third, healthcare workers should take a more active role than they currently do, incorporating menstrual health education into routine reproductive health services rather than leaving the subject to informal sources.

Fourth, faith leaders and community leaders can help break the inherited silence surrounding menstruation, replacing it with dignity, understanding, and respect.

Fifth, the media has a responsibility to take menstrual health conversations out of the shadows — using newspapers, radio, television, and digital platforms to replace myths with facts.

In addition, government institutions — including the Ministries of Health, Education, and Gender — together with county health teams, civil society organizations, and development partners, all have a role to play in ensuring that every girl, regardless of where she lives, has access to accurate menstrual health education.

This is not simply a women’s issue.

It is a public health issue.

It is an education issue.

It is a human dignity issue.

Most importantly, it is a shared responsibility.

This is why this agenda also connects directly to the Sustainable Development Goals. Improving menstrual health education contributes to SDG 3: Good Health and Well-being, by supporting prevention over treatment. It advances SDG 4: Quality Education, because girls need accurate health information to participate fully in school. And it supports SDG 5: Gender Equality, because menstrual stigma and unequal access to information limit young women’s opportunities.

For Liberia, this is therefore more than a conversation about menstruation. It is a conversation about health, education, and dignity.

Research should never end when a thesis is defended or remain confined to library shelves. Its greatest value is realized when evidence informs conversations, influences policy, strengthens programs, and improves lives.

My research in Fundaye provides a localized picture of a challenge that deserves wider attention. It is not the final word, but it is a call to listen, learn, and act.

As a young researcher and advocate, I believe that collaboration is our greatest opportunity. By bringing together educators, health professionals, policymakers, community leaders, development partners, civil society organizations, researchers, and young people themselves, we can create practical, community-driven solutions that ensure every girl has the knowledge she needs to manage her menstrual health with confidence and dignity.

The evidence is before us.

Now is the time to act.

Because when we educate girls, we do more than improve menstrual health — we empower healthier families, stronger communities, and a more informed nation.

Research should inspire action, influence policy, and improve lives.

Note on sources

Statistics attributed to “my research” are drawn from the author’s undergraduate thesis, Menstrual Hygiene Practices and Their Association with Reproductive Tract Infections Among Young Women Aged 18–25 Years in Fundaye, New Kru Town, Liberia (Gibson, 2026, African Methodist Episcopal University). The regional comparison is drawn from: Akoth, C., Wambiya, E. O., Kibe, P. M., Mbuthia, G. W., Ng’ang’a, L., Otieno, P., & Oguta, J. O. (2024). Prevalence and factors associated with unmet need for menstrual hygiene management in six countries in Sub-Saharan Africa: A multilevel analysis. BMC Women’s Health, 24(1), 473.

World.title: Breaking: Former Police Crime Commissioner Johnny Dean Charged Over Alleged US$10,000 Bribe
World.content:
Monrovia-Former Liberia National Police Commissioner for Crime Services Johnny Bolar Dean has been forwarded to court and charged with criminal conspiracy, bribery, tampering with a criminal investigation and obstruction of government functions by a public servant, in a case emerging from Liberia’s massive illicit drug investigation.

By Willie N. Tokpah

A police charge sheet dated September 1 accuses Dean of accepting US$10,000 from Stephanie Fefe Mensah while police were investigating individuals identified in the case as Edison Brown and Alpha Bah in connection with the alleged US$317 million cocaine trafficking operation.

Police alleged that Dean, then serving as one of the country’s senior crime-fighting officials, used his position to interfere with the investigation, disclose confidential information and frustrate efforts to investigate individuals connected to the drug case.

The allegations place a former senior police commander at the center of one of Liberia’s most consequential narcotics investigations and raise questions about whether the country’s own law-enforcement apparatus was compromised from within.

US$10,000 Question

According to the charge sheet, Dean admitted receiving the US$10,000, but rejected the investigators’ characterization of the payment.

Police say Dean told investigators that Mensah gave him the money for safekeeping and that he described Mensah as his lover.

Investigators, however, alleged that the payment was connected to the criminal investigation and was intended to influence or compromise the handling of the case.

Police later recovered the money from Dean.

The central question now before the court will be whether the US$10,000 represented an innocent transaction between two individuals, as Dean reportedly maintains, or an improper payment connected to an active criminal investigation, as police allege.

From Professional Standard To Court

The criminal charges followed an administrative inquiry by the Professional Standards Division of the Liberia National Police.

Dean and Mensah were reportedly turned over to the Crime Services Department on August 18, following that administrative investigation.

A Special Investigative Team headed by Assistant Commissioner of Police Harold T. Jones subsequently conducted the criminal investigation.

The investigation ultimately resulted in Dean being charged and forwarded to court for judicial determination.

The case is particularly important because of Dean’s former position.

As Commissioner of Crime Services, he occupied a senior role within the police structure responsible for investigating serious crimes.

Police now allege that the same authority was used to interfere with an investigation rather than advance it.

DEAN’S Defense: ‘I am not connected to any drug cartel

Dean has publicly rejected allegations linking him to the drug-trafficking operation.

In statements circulated on social media, the former police commissioner denied being connected to any drug cartel and pushed back against claims that he participated in criminal activity.

Dean has maintained that allegations should not be treated as facts and has indicated that he is prepared to allow the evidence and the legal process to determine the matter.

His position is particularly relevant to the US$10,000 allegation because the police charge sheet itself records his explanation that the money was given to him for safekeeping rather than as a bribe.

Dean’s defense therefore presents a fundamentally different interpretation of the same transaction: police characterize the money as part of an alleged effort to compromise an investigation, while Dean’s account is that he merely received and held the money for Mensah.

That dispute is now likely to become a central issue in the court proceedings.

Deeper Problem For Liberia’s Drug Investigation

The charges against Dean come as Liberia continues to grapple with the fallout from a cocaine investigation involving a shipment authorities have valued at approximately US$317 million.

The investigation has generated scrutiny not only of suspected traffickers but also of individuals within Liberia’s security and law-enforcement institutions.

The emergence of allegations against a former Crime Services Commissioner adds another layer to the controversy: whether the country’s institutions tasked with fighting organized crime were themselves vulnerable to influence from the criminal networks they were investigating.

The Dean case could have implications beyond the former commissioner’s personal legal battle.

If prosecutors establish that a senior police official accepted money and used confidential information or his authority to frustrate an active investigation, it could expose serious weaknesses in the internal controls of Liberia’s security institutions.

But if Dean’s explanation is ultimately accepted by the court, the case could raise equally important questions about the evidentiary basis for prosecuting senior security officials based on disputed financial transactions.

Dean has now been forwarded to court, where the prosecution will be required to prove its allegations through evidence.

The proceedings are expected to focus on the origin and purpose of the US$10,000, Dean’s communications and interactions with Mensah, the status of the investigation involving Brown and Bah, and whether Dean disclosed confidential information or otherwise interfered with police work.

For Dean, the case represents a dramatic turn for a former senior police commander now facing criminal prosecution over conduct allegedly committed while exercising the powers of his office.

For Liberia, the case borders on how far the alleged drug network penetrated the country’s security system, and whether officials entrusted to investigate the operation instead helped protect those under investigation.

For now, the allegations contained in the police charge sheet remain unproven accusations.

Dean is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty by a court of competent jurisdiction.

World.title: Liberia’s Opposition Tries Unity Again
World.content:
Three years out from a vote nobody has scheduled yet, Liberia’s opposition parties gathered under George Weah’s roof to try, for a third time this decade, to do what has never once held: stay together. The 2016 Ganta accord fizzled before it was ever tested at the polls. The 2019 Collaborating Political Parties won Senate seats before a fight over its own governing document tore it apart from the inside. This time, organizers say, they’re doing it in a different order — settling how they’ll govern themselves before anyone fights over who leads — betting that the sequence, not the sentiment, was what was missing all along.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

The venue was the Jamaica Resort in Thinker’s Village, Paynesville, and the guest list read like a reunion. Alexander Cummings of the Alternative National Congress. Benoni Urey’s All Liberian Party, represented. Musa Hassan Bility, now leading the Citizens Movement for Change, after first declining the invitation and then showing up anyway. Simeon Freeman of the Movement for Progressive Change. D. Maxwell Kemayah of the Movement for Economic Empowerment. Former House Speakers J. Alex Tyler and Bhofal Chambers, representing the host party. Presiding over all of it, in a role that would have seemed unlikely a decade ago, was former President George Weah — the man whose 2017 election victory the last generation of these same opposition figures spent years trying to prevent, and whose own single term as president these same figures spent years trying to end.

On Sunday, they agreed to form a steering committee — two representatives per party — tasked with drafting a framework document for what organizers are careful to call political cooperation, not an electoral alliance. Not a joint 2029 ticket. Not, yet, anything that requires anyone to answer the question that has broken every previous version of this project: who leads it.

That carefulness is not incidental. It is, this paper’s reporting suggests, the entire lesson of what came before.

A PATTERN WITH A BODY COUNT

This is not Liberia’s opposition’s first attempt at unity, and it is worth being precise about how the earlier ones died, because the specifics matter more than the general sense that opposition coalitions in Liberia tend not to last.

In 2016, opposition leaders met in Ganta, Nimba County, and signed what became known as the Ganta accord, aimed at coordinating their approach to the 2017 election. It produced meetings, statements of intent, and ultimately no lasting structure. By the time the 2017 race arrived, Weah’s own Coalition for Democratic Change — built with the National Patriotic Party and the Liberty Party for Democratic Progress — was the alliance that held together and won, while the broader opposition coordination effort that Ganta represented had already come apart.

The bigger, more instructive collapse came next. In February 2019, the Unity Party, the Alternative National Congress, the All-Liberian Party and the Liberty Party signed a memorandum of understanding forming the Collaborating Political Parties, certified by the National Elections Commission that August. For a while, it worked: CPP candidate Abraham Darius Dillon won a 2019 Montserrado County Senate by-election, and the alliance took six Senate seats in the 2020 election — more than any single party managed. Then, in September 2021, it broke. ALP leader Benoni Urey accused ANC leader Alexander Cummings of tampering with the coalition’s framework document ahead of CPP’s internal primaries, alleging that party leaders had been given photocopies while an original circulated with signatures added later. The legal complaint went nowhere — it was later dropped for insufficient evidence — but the damage was already done. ALP walked out in December 2021. Unity Party followed in February 2022. The Liberty Party split the following month, with a Senate-led faction leaving while its chairman stayed. What remained regrouped around Cummings as standard-bearer with Charlyne Brumskine as his running mate — and won 1.61 percent of the presidential vote in 2023, with no Senate seats to show for an alliance that had held six of them three years earlier. The CPP held a dissolution ceremony in April 2024, closing out five years that had started with real electoral wins.

THE RECORD, BY THE NUMBERS

2016 — Ganta accord signed ahead of the 2017 election. No lasting alliance followed.

2019 — CPP formed by UP, ANC, ALP and Liberty Party; NEC-certified that August.

2020 — CPP wins 6 Senate seats, more than any other single party.

Sept. 2021 — Framework-document dispute between Urey and Cummings triggers the split.

Dec. 2021–Mar. 2022 — ALP, then UP, then a Liberty Party faction all withdraw.

2023 — Remaining CPP ticket (Cummings-Brumskine) wins 1.61% of the presidential vote; zero Senate seats.

April 2024 — CPP formally dissolves.

Notice what killed the CPP. It wasn’t the voters, and it wasn’t the government. It was a dispute over the document meant to govern how the alliance itself made decisions — a fight over the rules before the rules were ever tested by an election.

WHAT WEAH IS ACCUSING BOAKAI OF, AND WHY IT’S DRIVING THIS

The immediate backdrop to Sunday’s roundtable is a months-long campaign by Weah accusing President Joseph Boakai’s Unity Party government of authoritarian drift. “Despite a peaceful democratic transition, President Boakai seeks to rule as a tyrant,” Weah said in August, pointing to what he called “the continuous use of extrajudicial powers” to “trample upon the constitutional rights of Liberians who hold opposing views.” He has cited the detention of former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor — intercepted, her lawyers say, en route to meet her own counsel — and accused the government of pursuing a narcotics investigation selectively, going after opposition figures while, he claims without offering documentation, treating implicated security officials more leniently. He has separately criticized Boakai’s replacement of Justice Minister N. Oswald Tweh and Solicitor General Augustine Fayiah as evidence of interference in ongoing prosecutions.

“The rule of law is being tampered with,” Weah said this month. “It is wrong, tampering with justice.”

None of those allegations have been independently substantiated in the reporting available for this piece, and Weah himself has acknowledged offering no documentary evidence for the claim of political targeting. The government has not been quoted here disputing the specific characterizations, and this paper takes no position on whether the underlying prosecutions are legitimate or politically motivated. What is not in dispute is that this rhetoric — building since at least June, when Weah, Cummings and other opposition leaders first rallied publicly around the idea of unity ahead of 2029 — is the organizing energy behind Sunday’s gathering. An opposition that agrees on little else has found, in accusations of democratic backsliding, a shared grievance broad enough to sit everyone at the same table.

A CASE THAT’S DIVIDING AS MUCH AS IT’S UNITING

Three days before the roundtable, Weah went to see Howard-Taylor himself. He arrived at Monrovia Central Prison flanked by CDC chairman Janga Kowo and former House Speaker Bhofal Chambers, with hundreds of supporters gathered outside under heavy police guard, having already called the charges against her “bogus.” It was, in effect, the same argument he would later make publicly about Boakai and the rule of law — except this version wasn’t rhetoric aimed at a press conference or a complaint to the UN. It was Weah, in person, standing by the woman who served as his own vice president for six of the last eight years.

That personal stake is exactly what has made the case as divisive inside the opposition as it is useful to Weah’s argument outside it. Howard-Taylor’s own party, the National Patriotic Party — the CDC’s governing partner for the entirety of Weah’s presidency — did not send an institutional delegation to Sunday’s roundtable. NPP Chairman George Mulbah said the party was never properly invited and complained of being treated like an “auxiliary” rather than an equal partner. CDC Secretary-General Jefferson Koijee countered that only individual NPP members, not the party’s leadership, had ever been asked — and then went further, faulting the NPP for what he called “one of the weakest responses in the history of a party once renowned for its fighting spirit” to Howard-Taylor’s prosecution.

There’s an irony sitting inside that fight. By most accounts, it was the NPP’s quieter, more measured approach — not CDC’s public solidarity campaign — that is credited with helping secure Howard-Taylor’s actual compassionate release from Central Prison. Loud advocacy and practical results pulled in different directions here, and the party that got results is the one being accused of not caring enough. A handful of self-described “Concerned NPP Partisans,” along with at least one sitting senator, broke with their own party leadership to publicly back the unity effort anyway — a fracture inside a fracture.

None of that makes the underlying prosecution political theater or proves that it isn’t. The case traces back to a cocaine seizure that had nothing to do with any opposition figure to begin with — nearly four tons, valued at roughly $317 million, which also implicated senior police and intelligence officials — a harder thing to wave away as manufactured than a single, conveniently timed indictment would be. But it does mean the drug probe is doing double duty in this story. It is simultaneously the grievance Weah cites to justify uniting the opposition against what he calls creeping authoritarianism, and a live fault line splitting the opposition’s own ranks over how loudly, and by whom, that grievance should be pressed. A coalition that cannot agree on how to handle the case of its own most prominent example may struggle to present a united front on anything larger.

THE FEAR ANIMATING THE ROOM

Underneath both the drug case and the wider run of corruption dockets sits a broader anxiety inside CDC and allied circles: that Boakai’s Unity Party is using law enforcement to do to the last government what an election alone might not — weaken its most viable 2029 figures one prosecution at a time. Boakai has publicly rejected that reading. “There will be no selective justice, political protection, sacred cows,” he pledged after July’s cocaine seizure, and his government has cast each case, Howard-Taylor’s included, as ordinary law enforcement rather than retaliation.

The pattern critics point to, though, keeps recurring. Former Finance Minister Samuel Tweah, who served under Weah for the CDC’s full six years in office, was acquitted on all counts in a corruption trial in May — only for the Asset Recovery and Property Retrieval Task Force to summon him again five days later a fresh matter. CDC went further, accusing the Boakai administration of funneling $275,000 through the head of the state petroleum refining corporation to bribe jurors in the case, and casting the new summons as retaliation for the jury’s refusal. None of that has been independently verified in reporting available for this piece, and the government has not been quoted here disputing the specifics. But paired with Howard-Taylor’s prosecution, it is the concrete evidence CDC points to when it argues the pattern runs bigger than any single case.

Critics have also noted the asymmetry runs the other direction, too: allegations connected to people in Boakai’s own circle — including, according to civil society groups, his own son — have so far produced denials rather than arrests, investigations or independent review, even as more than a dozen security-agency officials have been dismissed and both Howard-Taylor and Tweah have faced criminal process. Whether that gap reflects selective enforcement or simply how far each investigation happens to have gotten is not something this paper can settle. What does seem clear is that the fear itself — that accountability is being applied unevenly, aimed disproportionately at the people best positioned to lead an opposition ticket in 2029 — is doing real work inside the coalition Weah convened Sunday. It may be, as much as any shared vision of what comes after Boakai, the glue holding a historically fractious opposition at the same table this time.

THE SEQUENCING BET

What’s different this time is not the cast — Cummings and Urey were both there for the CPP’s rise and its unraveling — but the order of operations.

The CPP put the destination first: a joint political party, a shared platform, a path to a single 2023 presidential ticket, all committed to in a signed, NEC-certified document before the coalition had ever been tested by an internal disagreement. When that first real disagreement came, over the document itself, there was no established process to resolve it that didn’t feel to at least one party like betrayal. Sunday’s organizers appear to be betting that skipping straight to a governing structure is what broke the last attempt, and that a longer runway spent agreeing on how disputes get handled might survive contact with the next one. That is the entire logic of a steering committee whose sole job, for now, is drafting a framework document — not endorsing a candidate, not even declaring the coalition an electoral vehicle. Cummings framed the ambition modestly: “They are in power, and they are managing our resources. We will unite and be the voice of the Liberian people in holding the government accountable,” he said, explicitly not a positioning statement about 2029.

The other structural change is who is doing the convening. Unity Party — the party that anchored the last coalition — is now the government the coalition exists to oppose, not a member of it. And the host this time is Weah’s CDC, a party that spent the CPP era as its target rather than its member, now lending its convening power and Weah’s personal standing to an effort that includes newer, smaller vehicles like Bility’s CMC, Freeman’s MPC and Kemayah’s MOVEE alongside CPP veterans. Whether a coalition organized around one dominant party’s former president can avoid the leadership friction that sank a coalition organized around no single dominant figure is, itself, an open question — arguably just a different version of the same problem CPP had, rather than a solution to it.

WHAT’S NEXT

MPC’s Simeon Freeman said the group plans to reconvene within two weeks at another venue to continue the process. The steering committee’s framework document — its actual content still unwritten — is where this effort will be tested for real, since it is exactly this kind of document, and exactly this kind of internal disagreement over its terms, that ended the CPP. Bility, for his part, framed the stakes in plainer terms than the diplomatic language of “cooperation” and “framework” being used around him: “We are happy that we are able to come together,” he said. “It is about the Liberian people, united under one voice to advocate for them and to rescue them from the so-called rescuers.”

Cummings called the current process “still in its early stages” but said he is confident it can succeed “if the parties remain focused on their broader objective.” That is what everyone said about the CPP in February 2019, three years and a dissolution ceremony before it mattered. What is different this time is not the confidence. It’s whether the document the steering committee produces answers the question that keeps recurring: not whether Liberia’s opposition wants to unite, which it clearly does, again, but whether it can survive agreeing on who’s in charge once unity starts costing something.

World.title: Liberia: Why EX-VP Howard-Taylor Abandoned Preliminary Evidence Hearing—and What It Means for Her Drug Case
World.content:
Monrovia – The criminal case against former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor has taken another major turn, with her lawyers abandoning a preliminary examination of the evidence after the court declined to grant the defense access to materials it said were necessary to meaningfully challenge the State’s case.

By Willie N. Tokpah, [email protected]

The decision, taken Monday at the Monrovia City Court, clears the way for prosecutors to pursue the next stage of the proceedings, including a possible grand jury indictment.

Magistrate L. Ben Barco granted the defense request to withdraw the preliminary examination and instructed the Clerk of Court to communicate the development to the appropriate criminal court.

But the decision has also opened a new legal and political question: why would Taylor’s lawyers abandon a proceeding they had initially requested to test the State’s evidence?

The answer, according to a statement issued Monday by Taylor’s family and legal support team, is that the defense no longer wanted the preliminary stage to proceed without access to the evidence it considered necessary to challenge the prosecution.

The defense maintains that Taylor has never been served with a formal indictment setting out the specific facts and allegations against her and says its original request for a preliminary examination was intended to scrutinize the evidence used to justify what it described as her “unprecedented arrest and incarceration.”

The legal team said the prosecution objected to the defense request for disclosure and that the court sustained the objection.

“Rather than allow the preliminary stage to become a platform for unproven theories without the safeguard of full discovery,” the family and legal team said, “we have chosen to proceed directly to trial, where pretrial discovery is guaranteed.”

The statement also sought to draw a sharp distinction between the Government’s criminal complaint and an indictment.

“As of this statement, Madam Howard-Taylor has not been indicted by a grand jury,” the statement said, stressing that a complaint is not an indictment and that an indictment, if returned, would not amount to a conviction.

That distinction is at the center of the defense’s public response to the case.

Taylor’s lawyers say the former Vice President remains innocent and accuse government officials and some media reports of creating the impression that she has already been indicted or found guilty.

The Government, meanwhile, has accused Taylor of involvement in an alleged transnational narcotics network and related financial crimes.

The allegations include controlled-drug offenses, illicit trafficking, criminal facilitation, criminal solicitation, criminal conspiracy, money laundering and aiding the consummation of crime. Taylor has denied the allegations.

Three Weeks of Legal Drama

The case has unfolded rapidly since Taylor was stopped at Roberts International Airport on August 19, while preparing to leave Liberia.

Her detention triggered an extraordinary sequence of events involving police custody, medical concerns, court proceedings, imprisonment, compassionate release and a contentious preliminary examination.

Following her detention, Taylor was taken to Liberia National Police headquarters for questioning and investigative procedures. The following day, August 20, concerns over her health became a major issue.

FrontPageAfrica observed medical personnel being taken into the LNP withholding facility as reports emerged that Taylor was experiencing dangerously high blood pressure.

She was subsequently taken for medical treatment after reportedly becoming ill while in police custody. Her lawyers later relied on her medical condition in seeking relief from continued detention, arguing that she required continued medical attention.

From Police Custody To South Beach

Despite the health concerns, Taylor was eventually brought before the Monrovia City Court.

On August 25, the court rejected her lawyers’ request to allow her to remain at a medical facility and ordered her committed to the Monrovia Central Prison, commonly known as South Beach.

The decision placed the former Vice President behind bars while her lawyers continued challenging her detention and raising concerns about her health.

A major shift came on September 4, when Criminal Court “C” Judge Ousman F. Feika granted Taylor compassionate release on medical grounds. The release came with conditions, including the surrender of her travel documents and restrictions concerning visitors and her movement.

The order, however, did not end the criminal case. Taylor was released from custodial detention to receive medical care while the prosecution continued pursuing its allegations.

Preliminary Examination Battle

The preliminary examination became the next major battleground. Taylor’s lawyers had invoked Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law to seek an examination of the evidence being relied upon by the State.

The purpose of such a proceeding was to test whether the prosecution had established sufficient probable cause for the case to proceed. When the proceedings began on September 4, however, the defense sought access to evidence it said was necessary to prepare for the examination.

The court rejected that requst.

The ruling became important, becascrutinisefense had wanted to scrutinize the State’s evidence and question prosecution witnesses in a proceeding it viewed as an important safeguard against an unsupported criminal case.

The prosecution subsequently presented Liberia National Police Crimes Services Commissioner Raphael Wilson as its first witness. Wilson testified about an alleged narcotics operation and claimed Taylor had been approached over a proposed protection arrangement.

His testimony also touched on alleged meetings involving Liberians and foreign nationals in Dubai and Liberia, as well as an alleged political plot involving the administration of former President George Manneh Weah. Those allegations remain contested and have not been established as facts by a court.

The Disputed Audio Recording

The proceedings took another contentious turn when prosecutors introduced an audio recording through Wilson. The recording quickly became one of the most disputed pieces of evidence in the preliminary proceedings. Taylor’s defense objected to its admission and challenged the State’s reliance on the recording as it attempted to establish its case.

The dispute raises questions about the evidentiary foundation for recorded conversations, including what prosecutors must establish concerning authenticity, relevance and admissibility before such material can be relied upon in criminal proceedings. But the recording was never tested to a conclusion at the preliminary stage.

Instead, the defense has now withdrawn from the proceeding altogether.

Why Walk Away?

The defense’s decision appears to have been driven less by an abandonment of its challenge to the allegations than by a disagreement over the procedural environment in which that challenge would take place.

The family and legal team say the defense sought the preliminary examination precisely because Taylor had not received a formal indictment detailing the specific allegations against her.

But after the court denied access to evidence the defense considered necessary, continuing the examination could have left lawyers challenging the State’s witnesses without what they regardefenceequate disclosure. The defense has therefore chosen a different route.

Rather than continue the preliminary examination, it says it will proceed directly toward trial, where it expects broader pretrial discovery protections.

That strategy carries an important consequence, the defense gives up the opportunity to continue contesting probable cause at the preliminary-examination stage, while the prosecution gains a clearer path toward seeking a grand jury indictment.

The move does not mean Taylor has been indicted, it does not m,ean the allegations have been proven and it does not amount to an admission of guilt.

Defense’s Warning

In its statement, Taylor’s family and legal support team appealed to the Government, public officials, the media, civil society, religious leaders and human-rights advocates to maintain what it called the principles of due process.

The family specifically urged the Government to distinguish between allegations, an indictment and a conviction.

It also called on public officials to refrain from what it described as prejudicial pronouncements while the matter remains before the courts.

The defense further urged the media to verify the procedural status of the case rather than present allegations as established facts.

“Madam Howard-Taylor asks for no special treatment,” the statement said, “only the constitutional protections owed to every Liberian.”

The statement concluded with the family and legal team expressing confidence that a fair hearing on the full record would vindicate the former Vice President.

Tear Gas Adds To Courtroom Drama

Monday’s legal development unfolded against the backdrop of another unusual incident at the Monrovia City Court.

As police officers stood in formation awaiting Taylor’s expected arrival, one Liberia National Police officer discharged a canister of tear gas inside the court’s compound.

The incident briefly caused fear and confusion among journalists, lawyers, security personnel and members of the public.

Liberian journalist Saah Augustine Mbayoh was nearly struck by the tear gas, while a FrontPageAfrica Judicial Reporter was also in the immediate vicinity.

The officer responsible had not been publicly identified as of Monday.

FrontPageAfrica observed that, shortly before the incident, the officer had dropped his baton and face shield twice while standing in the police formation.

It remains unclear whether he was experiencing a medical problem, disorientation or another difficulty.

The LNP had not publicly explained the circumstances surrounding the discharge as of Monday.

There is also no indication that the tear-gas incident was connected to Taylor or the crimina l allegations against her.

What Happens Next?

The immediate consequence of the defense withdrawal is that the preliminary examination will no longer serve as the forum for testing the State’s evidence. The matter can now proceed toward the indictment stage. But an indictment is not automatic. The prosecution must still pursue the applicable legal process, and any grand jury action would determine whether Taylor is formally indicted.

If an indictment is returned, the case would then move deeper into the criminal court process, where the prosecution would have to prove its allegations beyond the applicable legal standards at trial.

For Taylor, the case has already produced three weeks of extraordinary legal turbulence, an airport arrest, police detention, a reported health crisis, medical treatment, imprisonment at South Beach, compassionate release and a preliminary examination that ended almost as quickly as it began.

For the prosecution, Monday’s withdrawal removes the immediate preliminary-examination hurdle.

For the defense, it represents a strategic decision to bypass a proceeding it says became unfairly constrained by the denial of access to evidence and instead confront the allegations at trial, where it expects fuller discovery rights.

The disputed audio recording, the alleged financial transactions, the narcotics allegations and the Government’s claims concerning Taylor’s alleged connections to an international network are likely to remain central to the case.

But for now, Jewel Howard-Taylor has not been convicted, and according to her legal team, she had not been indicted by a grand jury as of September 7.

The next major test will be whether the Government obtains a formal indictment and, if it does, how prosecutors and the defense ultimately litigate the evidence before a criminal court.

World.title: Put Liberia Before Self
World.content:
Two opposition alliances in a decade have collapsed for the same reason: leaders who agreed on what they were against, but not on who among them mattered less. A third attempt is now underway. Liberia cannot afford a third failure.

WE WANT TO BELIEVE IN SUNDAY’S ROUNDTABLE. Liberia’s opposition parties, gathered under George Weah’s roof at the Jamaica Resort, agreed to build a steering committee and, eventually, a framework for working together ahead of 2029. On paper, it is a modest, careful step. It should be judged as one. But this newspaper has watched this movie before and so has every Liberian old enough to remember 2016 and 2019, so we are going to say plainly what optimism alone will not fix: this effort will fail exactly like the last two did, unless the people in that room are honest about why the last two failed.

THEY DID NOT FAIL BECAUSE LIBERIANS stopped wanting an alternative to the party in power. They failed because the leaders building the alternative could not stop competing long enough to build it. The 2016 Ganta accord produced statements and handshakes and nothing that survived contact with an actual election. The 2019 Collaborating Political Parties did better — it won Senate seats; it built real infrastructure — right up until a dispute over its own governing document turned ally against ally. Within six months, three of its four founding parties had walked out. What remained managed less than two percent of the presidential vote in 2023 and formally dissolved in 2024. Both collapses trace back to the same root: coalition-building in Liberia keeps getting treated as a contest over whose turn it is to lead, rather than a project bigger than any one leader’s ambition.

WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY BE DIFFERENT

A STEERING COMMITTEE IS NOT a guarantee of anything. It is a tool, and it will do exactly as much good as the people using it are willing to let it do. If this attempt is going to end differently than the last two, three things need to happen that did not happen before.

FIRST, THE FRAMEWORK DOCUMENT the committee is now drafting needs to settle, in writing and in advance, how internal disputes get resolved — before there is a dispute to resolve. The CPP did not die because its members disagreed. Alliances always disagree. It died because when the disagreement came, over the framework document itself, there was no trusted process to settle it, so the fastest way out was to walk. A framework agreed to under pressure, after a fight has already started, is not a framework. It is a ceasefire, and ceasefires break.

SECOND, THE LEADERSHIP QUESTION must be answered honestly at some point, and burying it indefinitely is not the same as solving it. Organizers are right to avoid rushing into a 2029 ticket the way CPP did. But if this coalition survives long enough to matter, someone will eventually have to stand at the top of it, and everyone else will have to accept not being that person. That is the moment that broke the last alliance. Pretending the moment will not come again is not strategy. It is postponement.

Every one of these men has led a party, and most have wanted to lead a country. That is not disqualifying. But it is exactly the instinct that has killed this project twice, and nothing about human nature suggests it will behave differently a third time without real safeguards.

THIRD, AND HARDEST: every leader at that roundtable needs to ask honestly whether they are in the room to hold a government accountable, or to position themselves for 2029. Both motives can coexist in the same person. But a coalition built mostly on the second motive, dressed in the language of the first, will not survive its own founders’ ambitions any better than the CPP did. Liberians can tell the difference, eventually, even when it takes a while.

A SMALLER PATTERN INSIDE A LARGER ONE

IT IS WORTH NAMING what this really is. Liberia is Africa’s oldest republic, and for most of its nearly two centuries it has cycled through the same failure in different costumes: leaders who treat public office and political movements alike as instruments of personal advancement rather than public trust, and a governing class that reorganizes itself every few years without ever quite reforming itself. Opposition alliances collapsing over who leads them is not a separate problem from the corruption dockets sitting untried in Margibi, or from a $317 million cocaine seizure implicating the country’s own security officials, or from a government pledging “no sacred cows” while critics count the cows it has left standing. They are the same disease. It is the habit of putting the individual before the institution, term after term, government after government, opposition and incumbent alike, and it is the reason a country with Liberia’s history, resources and resilience keeps having to rebuild the same trust from the same low starting point.

NONE OF THAT is an argument against this week’s effort. It is the argument for taking it seriously enough to get right. Liberians did not gather in Ganta in 2016, or sign the CPP charter in 2019, because they lacked appetite for a credible alternative. They gathered because they wanted one, twice, and watched it dissolve into the same rivalries it was built to overcome. A third attempt that repeats that pattern will not just cost the men in that room a coalition. It will cost the country another cycle of cynicism about whether unity, accountability and reform are things Liberia’s political class is even capable of delivering to itself, let alone to the people it asks to vote for it.

THE STEERING COMMITTEE reconvenes within two weeks. What it produces will say more about whether this country’s opposition has learned anything than any speech delivered at the Jamaica Resort. We hope, genuinely, that it has. Liberia does not need another alliance built to serve the ambitions of the people inside it. It needs one built to outlast them — because the country, not any one of its would-be leaders, is the only party in this story that cannot afford to lose again.

World.title: Liberia Inducted Into African Petroleum Regulators Forum
World.content:
Monrovia — Liberia has secured a seat at the continental petroleum regulatory table following the induction of the Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority into the African Petroleum Regulators Forum (AFRIPERF), strengthening the country’s efforts to build regulatory capacity as its oil and gas program expands.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The membership brings Liberia into a continental network of petroleum regulators working to promote safe, efficient, equitable and sustainable development of Africa’s petroleum resources.

For the LPRA, the move is expected to provide greater access to regulatory expertise, technical training and knowledge-sharing while helping Liberia align its petroleum governance framework with emerging continental standards.

AFRIPERF was established in Accra, Ghana, on September 18, 2025, following a meeting of petroleum regulators from 16 African countries. Eight countries — Nigeria, Ghana, Somalia, The Gambia, Madagascar, Sudan, Guinea and Togo — initially signed the Forum’s Charter.

The Forum seeks to bridge gaps in petroleum regulatory capacity across Africa by harmonizing regulatory standards, promoting knowledge and technology transfer, strengthening institutional capacity and coordinating African regulators on global energy policy.

As a member, the LPRA will participate in technical working groups, training programs and regulatory experience-sharing platforms. The Authority says the knowledge gained will be applied to Liberia’s oversight of its growing hydrocarbon sector, particularly in the areas of safety, environmental protection and transparency.

Liberia’s induction comes as the LPRA oversees eight active Production Sharing Contracts (PSCs) and prepares for its 2026 Direct Negotiation Petroleum Licensing Round, scheduled to launch in the fourth quarter of 2026.

“Regulating an active offshore program is a technical business, and the fastest way to build that competence is to sit in the room with regulators who have already done it,” LPRA Director General Marilyn Logan said.

Logan said the induction is part of the Authority’s broader strategy of developing bilateral and multilateral partnerships to strengthen its technical capacity and improve Liberia’s ability to manage an expanding petroleum portfolio.

The LPRA is also expected to use its AFRIPERF membership to strengthen Liberia’s regulatory environment ahead of the upcoming licensing round, with the goal of providing greater predictability for investors while essuring that petroleum activities meet appropriate safety and environmental standards.

The Authority’s participation comes at a potentially important stage in Liberia’s emerging petroleum industry, as the government seeks to attract new investment while strengthening oversight of the country’s offshore resources.

Through AFRIPERF, Liberia will now have a platform to engage directly with regulators from across the continent, share lessons from its own petroleum experience and draw on countries with more established oil and gas industries.

The LPRA says it remains committed to the responsible development, regulation and management of Liberia’s petroleum resources for the benefit of all Liberians.

World.title: World Bank: Liberia Can Unlock 5.3% of GDP in Fiscal Space by 2030
World.content:
Monrovia — Liberia could unlock additional annual fiscal space equivalent to between 3.9% and 5.3% of GDP by 2030 if it implements reforms aimed at increasing domestic revenue, improving natural resource management and making public spending more efficient, the World Bank says.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The assessment was contained in the World Bank’s “Liberia Public Finance Review 2026: From Stabilization to Fiscal Transformation,” launched Monday in Monrovia.

Speaking at the launch, Georgia Wallen, World Bank Group Country Manager for Liberia, said the country’s public finances have reached a critical turning point following improvements in economic and fiscal management.

“Economic growth has strengthened, the fiscal deficit has narrowed significantly, and public debt has declined,” Wallen said, attributing the progress to what she described as “proactive policy choices and sustained commitment.”

She said the next challenge is to build on those gains by mobilizing more public resources while ensuring that existing resources are spent more effectively.

The $8.4 Billion Challenge

Wallen said Liberia’s Vision 2030 and the government’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development will require approximately $8.4 billion over five years to finance priorities including infrastructure, human capital development, economic transformation, governance and social inclusion.

The World Bank’s review, she said, seeks to address a central question: How can Liberia create sustainable fiscal space to finance its development ambitions without undermining recent gains in fiscal stability?

The report identifies four major opportunities.

The review estimates Liberia’s tax gap at approximately 3% of GDP, indicating significant room to increase revenue without necessarily raising tax rates.

The World Bank recommends stronger tax compliance and enforcement, alongside greater use of technology and improved implementation of Liberia’s Revenue Code and Medium-Term Revenue Strategy.

Getting More From Natural Resources

Mining revenues have increased nearly fivefold over the past decade, rising from approximately $27 million in 2016 to $141 million in 2025, according to the review.

The World Bank says Liberia could increase the contribution of the sector further through better information-sharing, stronger revenue administration and improved coordination among government institutions responsible for managing natural resource revenues.

Making Every Dollar Count

With significant progress made in fiscal consolidation, Wallen said Liberia must now focus on ensuring that public spending produces greater results.

The review recommends improvements in project preparation, procurement and payroll management, as well as closer coordination between domestically financed projects and investments supported by external partners.

Protecting Fiscal Gains

The World Bank also calls for stronger oversight of state-owned enterprises, more prudent debt management and better integration of climate and commodity-price risks into fiscal planning.

Such measures, the report says, would help protect Liberia from future economic and fiscal shocks.

Building on Existing Reforms

Wallen stressed that the Public Finance Review is not intended to create another lengthy reform agenda for the government.

“The PFR doesn’t seek to add another list of reforms simply,” she said. “Rather, it seeks to help policymakers prioritize, sequence, and accelerate actions for the greatest impact.”

She said the World Bank views the report as the beginning of deeper engagement with the Liberian government, development partners and the private sector to translate the recommendations into concrete reforms.

Wallen said expanding fiscal space would ultimately have a direct impact on the lives of ordinary Liberians by helping finance roads, electricity, healthcare, education and climate resilience.

The ultimate objective, she said, is job creation and an improved quality of life for Liberians

World.title: Govt. encourages inclusive investment in mining sector
World.content:
Government says it is creating opportunities for both local and foreign investors, while ensuring increased participation of local enterprises and small-scale miners in Zambia’s mining sector.

Acting Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Permanent Secretary Tobias Musonda says the government has invested heavily in understanding the country’s mineral potential to support targeted exploration and attract investment into new mining projects.

Mr Musonda says the opportunities extend across the mineral value chain, including upstream activities, mining and downstream processing.

He said the government is committed to providing a stable policy environment and security of tenure for license holders to encourage long-term investment in the sector.

“We are trying, as a government, to ensure that there is stability in the policy environment vis-à-vis the mining sector transition, but also ensuring security of tenure for license holders,” Mr Musonda said.

Mr Musonda noted that the government is also implementing local content measures to ensure mining companies support local enterprises and strengthen linkages between the mining sector and the wider economy.

He said job creation and Corporate Social Responsibility are also critical components of the government’s investment agenda.

Mr Musonda also said the government has continued to improve the efficiency of the mining licensing regime, noting that processing a licence previously took about 200 days.

He further added that the reforms are aimed at creating an open, transparent and investor-friendly mining environment while ensuring that investment translates into jobs, local business opportunities and broader economic benefits.

And speaking in a separate interview with the media, Association of Zambia Women in Mining President Namakau Kaingu has welcomed the government’s efforts to strengthen the small-scale mining sector, saying the initiative will empower women economically and increase their contribution to national development.

Ms Kaingu says the government’s engagement with large-scale mining companies to create opportunities for small-scale miners will enable women to access mining areas, equipment and markets.

She said the initiative is timely as Zambia works towards increasing copper production to three million tonnes annually.

Ms Kaingu said some large-scale mining companies have already set aside portions of their mining areas for women miners and are willing to support small-scale operators with equipment and markets for their minerals.

She cited mining companies working with women miners, saying such partnerships have the potential to accelerate growth in the sector.

“For us, we are happy because it is going to empower us economically and also increase our contribution to the economy through sales and taxes,” Ms Kaingu said.

Ms Kaingu further commended the government for introducing reforms in the mining sector, saying the changes have created greater opportunities for small-scale miners.

She said the ongoing training of small-scale miners will equip them with the skills required to participate meaningfully in the industry.

World.title: President Hichilema’s second term opportunity for prosperity-Economist
World.content:
Renowned business expert, Paul Chisunka, says President Hakainde Hichilema’s second term of office is a pivotal opportunity for Zambia to transition from macroeconomic stabilisation to sustained, inclusive and shared prosperity.

Commenting on the President’s inauguration speech, Mr Chisunka said the renewed mandate must be leveraged to implement disciplined, long-horizon decisions in debt management, energy, industry, skills development, infrastructure, taxation, and local content.

The seasoned Economist emphasised the urgent need for predictable, investor-friendly policies, enhanced accountability in public financial management and credible, transparent national budgets.

He has since called for timely and accurate reporting on national productive capacities, exports, and job creation to enable the government to measure progress and recalibrate strategies where necessary.

“We have an opportunity to build on economic stabilisation, but project outward into the ambitious growth agenda that the President has clearly articulated, so that we can create a more productive, resilient and inclusive Zambia,” Mr Chisunka said.

Mr Chisunka further called for accelerating reforms in clearing verified Value Added Tax (VAT) refunds, publishing aging data on outstanding refunds, reviewing tax expenditures, and strengthening procurement, cash management and internal controls.

He also advocated for a meritocratic, world-class public service which is driven by expertise, professionalism and experience, adding that Zambia must reposition itself as a competitive, export-oriented economy with robust local procurement frameworks.

Mr Chisunka identified the country’s vast and strategic natural assets, copper, cobalt, manganese, gold, gemstones, forests, farmland, hydro and solar as critical drivers that must generate greater shared value for communities.

“Our natural resources must be managed as national assets that can generate greater shared value for the entire country through enhanced livelihoods, increased incomes and dignified jobs,” he said.

The business expert also stressed the need for expanded and innovative micro, small and medium enterprises (MSME) financing, describing small businesses as the backbone of the Zambian economy.

He proposed non-traditional financing models such as blended finance, impact financing, and patient capital, with reduced reliance on collateral and greater focus on verifiable cash flows.

Mr Chisunka further suggested that the government should provide strategic guarantees in priority sectors such as energy and agriculture to spur productivity and crowd-in private investment.

“We need to ensure that supply and development initiatives are well integrated into local content commitments so that we build a cadre of Zambian suppliers and co-mining contractors that can compete at an international level,” he said.

Mr Chisunka also called for targeted economic opportunities for youth and women in mining and other sectors, backed by strong environmental and social safeguards.

He urged the government to broaden the tax base, formalise the informal sector, and bring order to artisanal mining.

He further advocated for the mobilisation of domestic capital from pension institutions and insurance funds, and diaspora investment, alongside prioritising concessional development financing and green, social and sustainability-linked bonds.

Mr Chisunka stated that with a young, agile and trainable population, and a presidency that articulates a clear development agenda, Zambia is well positioned to emerge as a leading economy in Southern Africa.

World.title: Free education gives vulnerable learners a second chance
World.content:
A school headteacher at Mumbolo Secondary School in Mwansabombwe District has commended the United Party for National Development (UPND) administration for introducing free education.

Mumbolo Secondary School headteacher Ireen Mpundu told ZANIS in an interview that her school has 22 former dropouts who have since returned to class because of the free education policy.

Ms Mpundu said the introduction of free education, which is now law, has given hope to many vulnerable children in the community to attain an education.

Ms Mpundu disclosed that Mumbolo Secondary School has a total enrolment of 318 learners, of whom 22 are those who returned because of the free education policy.

“Our school runs from form one to form five. We have a total number of 318 learners. 22 of these learners are the ones who just returned because of free education,” she said.

She added that the free education policy has helped address the issue of school dropouts, as even the less privileged in the community are now able to attend school.

Meanwhile, Ms Mpundu appealed to the relevant authorities to consider constructing additional classroom blocks at the school to accommodate the growing number of learners.

She also requested for the construction of staff houses, saying that currently all teachers travel long distances from Kazembe and other surrounding areas to get to the school.

“Accommodation is the biggest challenge here. There is not even a single house for teachers at this school. We stay from different locations, others from Kazembe and we travel on a daily basis using motorbikes which is not safe for us,” she requested.

And a former school dropout who returned to school because of the free education policy has thanked the government for actualising the initiative and signing it into law.

Emmanuel Chimuka said he had stopped school because he had no one to support him with the required school materials, but that the introduction of free education has enabled him to return to class.

Another school dropout, Ezborn Chunga, said he stopped school because his parents could not afford to buy him school uniforms or pay tuition fees, but the free education policy has enabled him to return to class.

Meanwhile, Esnart Mwanza said both her parents are dead, and her grandmother whom she had been living with also passed away, leaving her with no one to support her education.

“I used to stay with my parents but after they died, I started staying with my grandmother. Unfortunately, she also died. So, I had no option but to stop school. Now that there is free education my dream will be realised,” she said.

She said the introduction of free education has given her another opportunity to get back to school so that she can get her desired education.
