World.title: Poland’s oldest operating electric train, 63-year-old “Granny”, returns to the tracks after a refurb
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s oldest operational multiple-unit electric train, a 63-year-old vehicle nicknamed Babcia (meaning “Granny”), is returning to service after refurbishment. The train, whose official name is EN57-038, rolled off the production lines on 9 May 1963 at a factory in the city of Wrocław belonging to Pafawag, a state locomotive manufacturer. For decades, it served in the southern Małopolska province, transporting passengers in cities including Kraków, Tarnów, Nowy Sącz and Sucha Beskidzka. In 2003, it was transferred to Masovia, the province around Poland’s capital, Warsaw, where it has operated ever since. “Masovian Railways continually invests in modern rolling stock, making our fleet among the most modern in Poland,” said Czesław Sulima, the operations director for the regional rail operator. “However, we fully understand the importance of tradition and sentiment.” “Babcia has become a permanent fixture in Polish railway history,” he added. “We are delighted that after a major overhaul, this unique vehicle will once again serve passengers and delight lovers of old-time travel, combining history with modernity.” Babcia has previously undergone periodic modernisation and maintenance, most recently in 2022, when she regained her original yellow and blue livery associated with the historic Pafawag factory. The latest work included upgrades to the train’s monitoring system and toilet, which now operates in “closed circulation” (a polite way of saying that waste is no longer dropped directly onto the track). State rail operator PKP has for years been promising to phase out the few remaining old “open” toilets. Now that Babcia has been refurbished, she will return to service early on Saturday morning, running a 10 km route on weekends between the town of Tłuszcz and village of Mostówka, just northeast of Warsaw. Babcia is one of the EN57 class of electric multiple unit trains produced by Pafawag between 1961 and 1993. A total of 1,429 were manufactured, with many still in use – though none as old as EN57-038. The history of the Wrocław factory itself dates back to the 1830s (when the city was part of Germany and called Breslau), making it one of the oldest manufacturers of rolling stock in Europe. After World War Two, when Wrocław became part of Poland following border changes, the factory came under the ownership of the new communist state. In the 1990s, after the fall of communism, it was privatised, being acquired in 1997 by German company ADtranz, which was in 2001 itself taken over by Canada’s Bombardier Transportation, which was then acquired in 2021 by France’s Alstom. Train travel has been booming in Poland in recent years. In the first half of 2026, a record 44.7 million passengers travelled with PKP Intercity, the main long-distance operator, more than 10% up on the previous year’s record and some 45% higher than three years earlier. While the country is seeking to expand its high-speed rail network and increase train speeds up to 320 km/h (199mph), there has also been a growing interest in older trains. That prompted PKP to launch a special “unhurried” service earlier this year, allowing passengers to travel along scenic routes in restored 1980s trains. World.title: Poland to begin using sewage water to cool power plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland will begin using reclaimed sewage water to cool power plants from the start of next year. The measures are intended to reduce the use of fresh water and make the power system more resilient to increasingly frequent droughts. The change comes after some of Poland’s power plants were partially shut down this summer amid a series of heatwaves and lack of rain that led to record-low water levels in many rivers. 💧⚡ Otwieramy sektor energetyczny na wodę odzyskaną. Od 1 stycznia 2027 r. polskie elektrownie i elektrociepłownie będą mogły wykorzystywać wodę odzyskaną ze ścieków komunalnych w systemach chłodzenia. Nowe rozwiązania przedstawiliśmy dziś wspólnie z ministrem energii… pic.twitter.com/qRDOgjcDwb — Dariusz Klimczak (@DariuszKlimczak) September 3, 2026 “This may seem to many like a minor change, but it is of fundamental importance for many power-generating units in Poland,” said energy minister Miłosz Motyka. “Thanks to this, we will be even more resilient and even better prepared for crises of all kinds.” The legislation was first proposed by a group of MPs from The Left (Lewica) and the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), two members of the current ruling coalition, in May, and was then approved by parliament in July. Last week, President Karol Nawrocki signed it into law. The law, which will come into force at the start of 2027, introduces a definition of water recovered from municipal sewage, which, in turn, will allow its use in the cooling circuits of power stations and combined heat and power plants. Power stations require large amounts of water to help cool and condense steam, which drives the turbines, back into liquid form so that it can be reheated into steam once more. Orlen Termika, a subsidiary of state energy giant Orlen, has announced that it plans to invest more than 1 billion zloty (€230 million) over the next four years to maximise the benefits of the change by connecting sewage treatment plants with three of its power and heat plants around Warsaw. According to Andrzej Gajewski, the CEO of Orlen Termika, one of the plants, Żeran, will be able to save up to 80% of previous water use. Another, Siekierki, will save up to 20%. The company also plans to install heat pumps to extract heat from sewage, which can then be used to help supply heat to residents of Warsaw before the water is then used to cool down the plants. Sewage is relatively warm, typically between 10°C and 20°C, making it a good source of recoverable heat. “From the point of view of security of supply for Warsaw’s residents and from the point of view of efficiency – that is, the price of heating – this is the best and most advantageous solution,” emphasised Gajewski. Poland’s power grid operator has, for the second time in three days and third time this summer, invoked emergency measures to ensure supply amid a heatwave. Before this summer, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced https://t.co/fIDR4SimgG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 6, 2026 Poland has experienced increasingly hot temperatures in recent years. This summer, the country broke its all-time record, as temperatures reached more than 40°C. That, along with low amounts of rainfall, has seen rivers reach record lows. As a result, Poland’s power grid operator has this summer been forced three times to invoke emergency measures to ensure supply. Previously, it had only done so twice in the eight years since such powers were introduced. Last month, state power supplier Enea announced that it had reduced operations at two of its coal-fired plants due to the low level of water in the Vistula. Around 1.1 gigawatts (GW) of capacity, just over 1% of Poland’s total, was taken offline. World.title: Prime minister’s “right-hand man” elected as Polish constitutional court judge
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has succeeded in having Maciej Berek, whom he recently described as his “right-hand man”, elected by parliament as a Constitutional Tribunal (TK) judge, staving off a rebellion from some members of his own coalition. Critics argued that the nomination violated the government’s pledge to “depoliticise” the TK, including by banning recently active politicians from sitting on it. Berek served as a government minister from 2023, when Tusk came to power, until last month, when he stepped down in order to run for the TK. However, it is far from clear what will happen next. Opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has this year refused to swear in four TK judges chosen by parliament, and he has made clear that he also opposes Berek’s candidacy. ✅Sejm dokonał wyboru Macieja Berka na stanowisko sędziego Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. pic.twitter.com/ek0ak9C33v — Sejm RP🇵🇱 (@KancelariaSejmu) September 4, 2026 In mid-August, Berek announced that he was leaving the government, where he had served as minister in charge of overseeing the implementation of policy. Shortly afterwards, Tusk confirmed that Berek would be nominated to fill an upcoming vacancy on the TK. The prime minister argued that, during his time in government, Berek had undertaken a technocratic role that was “apolitical and nonpartisan”. He said that Berek’s extensive experience in constitutional law and the legislative process made him an ideal candidate. However, some MPs from Tusk’s junior coalition partners publicly opposed the nomination. They noted that the government’s parliamentary majority had, in 2024, approved a law banning anyone who had served as a politician in the last four years from becoming a TK judge. The law never went into force as it was effectively blocked by a combination of then-President Andrzej Duda and the TK itself, which were both aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party from 2015 to 2023 and now the largest opposition group. Polish NGOs have urged Tusk's "right-hand man" to withdraw his Constitutional Tribunal candidacy, warning his political ties could undermine efforts to restore the court’s independence. The nomination has also exposed tensions within the ruling coalitionhttps://t.co/jQn0MyuS7G — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 21, 2026 Ahead of today’s vote in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, it remained unclear if Berek’s candidacy would be approved. In the end, he obtained the necessary majority, receiving the support of 226 MPs among the 437 who voted in the 460-seat chamber. Within the ruling coalition, only four MPs voted against Berek’s candidacy, including one from Tusk’s own centrist Civic Coalition (KO), Klaudia Jachira. Another opponent was Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left (Lewica), one of Tusk’s junior coalition partners, and the speaker of the Sejm. Eleven MPs from the ruling coalition did not take part in the vote. The entire right-wing and far-right opposition voted against Berek’s candidacy. Berek is now meant to join the TK after the next vacancy on its 15-person bench opens up on 18 September, when the nine-year term of an existing judge, Justyn Piskorski, ends. However, under Polish law, a new TK judge must first swear an oath “before the president”. Nawrocki has used this requirement to refuse to swear in four of the judges chosen by the ruling majority in the Sejm this year. He has, however, sworn in three others. Nawrocki argued that there were legal doubts over the appointment of the quartet whose oaths he refused to receive. However, the government says that the president does not have the right to assess their candidacies and that the swearing-in is merely a formality. The crisis around Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has deepened further after the tribunal ruled that the president is not obliged to swear in new TK judges appointed by parliament. President Nawrocki last month refused to swear in four new judges https://t.co/ycnweW9pSR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 13, 2026 The four judges instead organised their own swearing-in ceremony in the Sejm before a notary, after which they forwarded their oaths to the president and attempted to take their seats on the TK. However, the tribunal’s chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, refused to allow them to serve, citing their failure to swear an oath before the president. Święczkowski previously served as a deputy justice minister in the former PiS government and is still seen as loyal to the party. In May, the European Court of Human Rights issued an interim order requiring that the four judges be allowed to take up their positions. However, Święczkowski has ignored it, arguing that the ECHR does not have the authority to make such a decision. The European Court of Human Rights has ordered Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) to accept four judges whom opposition-aligned President Nawrocki refused to swear in. The decision was welcomed by the government but rejected by the TK itself https://t.co/9NxInPdYk9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 6, 2026 It appears likely that Nawrocki will refuse to swear in Berek. “I think the last thing the TK needs is another politician, especially a politician who is a close collaborator of Prime Minister Donald Tusk,” said Nawrocki on Thursday. On Friday morning, ahead of the Sejm vote, the president’s chief of staff, Zbigniew Bogucki, addressed the chamber to outline the president’s opposition to Berek’s candidacy. He said that, as well as Berek’s political association with the government, there are doubts over whether he even meets the formal requirements to sit on the tribunal, in particular the need to have practised the law for at least 10 years. Berek says he does meet that requirement. Adding to the confusion is the fact that Tusk’s government does not regard the current TK as legitimate because of the presence of judges, including Piskorski, who were unlawfully appointed when PiS and Duda were in office. It ignores all TK rulings. Tusk has emphasised that one of the reasons he wants to appoint Berek to the TK is to help “fix” the tribunal. Berek’s nomination means that there are now eight TK judges chosen by the ruling coalition, giving them a majority on the court. However, with Nawrocki and Święczkowski refusing to accept four of them, and likely to reject Berek too, some kind of drastic action would be required to allow them to begin to serve. The proportion of Poles who negatively assess the justice system has increased under the current government, despite its promises to restore the rule of law. State pollster @CBOS_Info found 61% now hold a negative view, up from 55% in 2022 and 51% in 2017 https://t.co/P3fbTTbS5C — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: AIGEL to Celebrate 10th Anniversary with Prague Concert
World.content:
On October 21, electronic duo AIGEL will perform at Futurum Music Bar in Prague as part of a special concert marking the band’s 10th anniversary.

AIGEL was formed by Tatar poet and singer Aigel Gaisina and St. Petersburg producer Ilya Baramiya. Over the past decade, the duo has developed a distinctive sound combining electronic music, trip-hop and psychedelic influences.

Get your ticket here

Their music crosses linguistic and cultural boundaries, with songs performed in Russian, Tatar, English and German.

AIGEL gained international attention with the viral tracks “Tatarin” and “Pyyala.” The latter topped streaming charts in 25 countries and reached No. 1 on the global Shazam chart.

Over 10 years, the duo has released five albums and dozens of singles. They have also received a Cannes Lion for the music video “You’re Born” and toured extensively across Europe and beyond.

Now based in Europe, AIGEL is preparing a special anniversary show in Prague, combining the duo’s electronic sound with Gaisina’s distinctive and expressive vocals.

The concert will take place on October 21 at Futurum Music Bar.

World.title: Prague to Add 51 New Trams Next Year as Network Expands
World.content:
Prague is set to receive 51 new trams next year as the city expands its tram network and begins replacing some of its oldest vehicles.

The Prague Public Transport Company (DPP) has ordered another 25 Škoda 52T trams under an existing framework agreement with Škoda Transportation.

Each tram costs CZK 82.5 million, including CZK 40 million in European subsidies. Prague has now committed to buying 71 of the new vehicles in three separate orders.



The first 20 Škoda 52T trams entered regular service in Prague last year. Another batch is being delivered this year, while the latest orders will continue into 2027.

The newest order for 25 additional trams is due to be completed by December 3 next year.

The new vehicles are needed not only because Prague is building new tram lines but also because the existing fleet needs to be renewed. Some of the oldest trams still in operation are the T3M models, while a large part of the fleet consists of reconstructed T3R.P and T3R.PV vehicles and their derivatives.

Replacing older models with a smaller number of standardised tram types should also reduce maintenance and servicing costs, according to the deputy mayor. The new trams are expected to remain in service for around 20 to 30 years, compared with approximately 15 years for buses.

The Škoda 52T is 32 metres long and 2.5 metres wide and can carry up to 243 passengers. Of these, 173 can travel standing. The tram therefore offers almost 16 percent more capacity than Prague’s Škoda 15T trams.

The maximum operating speed is 70 kilometres per hour.

The 52T was designed specifically for Prague’s tram network, including sections with narrow and sharply curved tracks. This allows the vehicles to operate on existing routes without requiring major changes to the infrastructure.

World.title: Prague Castle to Celebrate Václav Havel With Four-Month Festival
World.content:
Prague Castle will host a four-month festival celebrating the legacy of Václav Havel, with theatre, film, music, design and public debates taking place from October through January.

The Havel ALIVE festival will mark what would have been Havel’s 90th birthday and explore the continued relevance of his ideas. Most events will be free.

One of the main highlights will be the Czech premiere of The Warning, an unfinished Havel play that remained hidden for almost 40 years. The manuscript was discovered by David Dušek among the papers of writer Zdeněk Urbánek.



The production has been prepared by Jiří Havelka, artistic director of Dejvické Theatre, and will feature actors Martin Myšička and Ivan Trojan. The theatre will also present We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here at Prague Castle’s Riding Hall.

The festival will also focus on Havel’s influence on Czech design. In cooperation with Designblok, Prague Castle will present Design for Václav Havel, featuring objects connected with his presidency, including Bořek Šípek’s Olga chair, original glass pieces and Castle Guard uniforms designed by Theodor Pištěk.

For the first time, the exhibition will also show the entire presidential office, including Havel’s library. It will open during Designblok on October 7 and remain at the Riding Hall from October 21 to January 17.

Music and dance will feature prominently as well. On November 18, students and teachers from the Academy of Performing Arts in Prague will present a gala evening directed by Magdalena Švecová. Other performances will draw on Havel’s writings, his Anticodes poetry collection, his relationship with the underground music scene and the events of November 1989.

The programme will also include screenings of Citizen Havel and Leaving, a musical evening led by Pavel Klusák, and discussions about art, architecture, freedom and democracy.

Selected festival events

October 4 — Guided tours of Lány Chateau and Prague Castle focused on Havel’s presidency. Free.

October 7 — Opening of Design for Václav Havel at the Prague Castle Riding Hall.

October 8 — Pavel Klusák’s All the President’s Rockers: Václav Havel & Music. Free.

October 14 — Citizen Havel screening followed by a discussion. Free.

October 22 — Thinking Havel Live: Democracy and the Future of Europe. Free.

November 4 — Dejvické Theatre presents We’ll Start It Tomorrow, or Who’s the Gentleman Here. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 5–6 — Czech premieres of Havel’s The Warning. Tickets CZK 390–490.

November 12 — Thinking Havel: Between the Individual and the System. Free.

November 18 — Havel: Inspiration for a New Generation, a gala evening at the Prague Castle Riding Hall from 7 p.m. Tickets CZK 250.

November 26 — Lecture on Havel’s designer and architect Bořek Šípek at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 3 — Thinking Havel: Politics and Spiritual Values, a debate with Alice Koubová, Milena Bartlová and Petr Kratochvíl at the Riding Hall from 6 p.m. Free.

December 8 — Literature at the Castle: Writing Havel, a lecture at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 5 p.m. Free.

December 15 — Screening of Leaving, followed by a discussion with Dagmar Havlová and other guests at the Supreme Burgrave’s Office from 6 p.m. Free.

January 14 — Ceremonial presentation of the Jindřich Chalupecký Award 2027 at Prague Castle.

World.title: Prague Airport to Expand Border Control at Terminal 1
World.content:
Prague Airport is expanding and modernising the border control area for arriving passengers at Terminal 1 to increase capacity and reduce waiting times.

The project will add five new passport control desks and four EasyGoGate (EGG) self-service gates for eligible European passport holders.

The work is scheduled to begin in September 2026 and is expected to be completed by the end of April 2027.



The expansion comes as Prague Airport faces increased pressure at border control, particularly during peak hours. The introduction of the European Entry/Exit System (EES) in October 2025 has added to the workload at the airport.

The project will also enlarge the waiting area before passport control and upgrade the ventilation system throughout the border control area.

The total investment is estimated at CZK 290 million, including construction, design and engineering work, technical supervision and safety coordination. The new passport control equipment will be supplied and installed by the Police of the Czech Republic.

Police representatives said the changes are also intended to strengthen security at the Schengen Area’s external border while ensuring the new facilities meet current security and legal requirements.

Some queues and restrictions are expected

The renovation will take place in stages to limit disruption to airport operations. However, passengers may encounter temporary restrictions at passport control and longer queues during some phases of the work.

At one stage, three passport control desks will be temporarily closed. This phase will be scheduled during a period of lower passenger traffic.

EU citizens will continue to be able to use the passport control desks and EGG self-service gates designated for European passport holders. They are not required to register through the EES.

During the other stages of construction, restrictions will mainly affect the area immediately before passport control. Passenger routes will be adjusted around the construction zones, while the overall flow through border control will remain unchanged.

World.title: Prague Bids to Host 2029 European Figure Skating Championships
World.content:
Prague is preparing a bid to host the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships, with the O2 Arena expected to serve as the main venue if the Czech capital wins the right to stage the competition.

Prague City Council approved the candidacy on Monday following an approach from the Czech Figure Skating Union.

The proposal comes several months after Prague hosted the 2026 World Figure Skating Championships in March.



City councilor for education and sports Antonín Klecanda (STAN) said the success of that event helped encourage the city to pursue another major international competition.

“The response was very positive, and other countries asked whether another event of this kind could be held in Prague,” Klecanda said on Monday. “We reached an agreement, and today we approved our candidacy to host the European Figure Skating Championship in 2029.”

The 2026 World Championships attracted a record number of spectators for a figure skating world championship, according to Klecanda. He also said international visitors had responded positively to Prague’s role as host city.

The city has not yet determined when the 2029 championship would take place. The date will be discussed at a later stage, while Prague currently expects the competitions to be staged at the O2 Arena.

The financial impact of hosting the championships has not yet been calculated. The city would have to cover not only the direct costs of organizing the competition but also additional expenses linked to public services, including increased public transport capacity, emergency services and police deployment.

Klecanda said these costs could reach tens of millions of Czech crowns. He argued, however, that part of the expenditure could be offset by additional tax revenue generated by the event, while the championship would also strengthen Prague’s international profile.

The final decision on the host city for the 2029 European Figure Skating Championships has yet to be made.

World.title: Pickles Prague Festival: A Celebration of Pickled and Fermented Vegetables
World.content:
The Pickles Prague Festival will take place on September 19-20 at the Prague Exhibition Grounds, bringing together producers, food enthusiasts and visitors interested in pickled and fermented vegetables.

The festival will run from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. and will focus on the wide variety of vegetables preserved through pickling and fermentation.

More info here.

Visitors can expect everything from traditional pickled cucumbers, peppers and beets to less familiar varieties from the Czech Republic and abroad.

Alongside tastings and opportunities to buy pickled products, the programme will include workshops and educational talks covering pickling techniques, fermentation, the nutritional aspects of fermented vegetables and the role of preserved foods in different culinary traditions.



The event will also feature live music throughout the day, while a dedicated children’s area will offer activities for younger visitors, making the festival suitable for families as well.

Admission to the Pickles Prague Festival is free.

World.title: Czech Politicians Divided Over AfD Victory in Saxony-Anhalt
World.content:
The Alternative for Germany (AfD) has secured a major victory in the Saxony-Anhalt state election, prompting different reactions from Czech politicians.

While some have congratulated the party and called for dialogue with its leaders, others have warned that the result reflects the growing strength of political extremism.

The result has also renewed debate in the Czech Republic over migration, security and how mainstream parties should respond to the AfD.



Martin Kupka, chairman of the Civic Democratic Party (ODS), described the result as a warning for Europe. He said democratic parties could not counter extremist movements simply by labeling them or ignoring issues that concern voters.

“Democratic parties must offer clear solutions: a tough migration policy, security, less regulation and no populist waste of public money,” Kupka said.

He added that the Czech Republic should avoid following the same political path.

Vít Rakušan, leader of the Mayors and Independents (STAN), similarly said the election should serve as a lesson for Czech politicians.

According to Rakušan, mainstream democratic parties risk losing voters when they leave issues such as migration and social problems to populist movements.

Rather than focusing solely on the AfD’s success, he said, democratic parties should develop practical and sustainable responses to issues that voters consider important.

Former Prime Minister Petr Fiala offered one of the strongest warnings. In a post on social media, the ODS politician called the result a “political earthquake” and said the AfD’s success could not be explained solely by the failure of mainstream democratic parties to address voters’ concerns.

Fiala argued that the reasons were more complex than economic dissatisfaction alone. “The causes are deeper and far from just economic,” he wrote.

The response from the Czech government’s current Foreign Minister Petr Macinka was more cautious. Macinka said the next steps by the AfD and Germany’s Christian Democratic Union (CDU) would be particularly significant.

He said it would be important to see how the winning party uses its strong mandate and how the CDU responds to the result.

Tomio Okamura, chairman of the Freedom and Direct Democracy (SPD) party and speaker of the Czech Chamber of Deputies, took a more positive view of the AfD’s performance.

He congratulated the party and said the election showed that voters were dissatisfied with the policies of Germany’s established parties, particularly the CDU.

“The people of the former East Germany have made it clear that they no longer want this policy to continue,” Okamura said in an interview with Czech Television.

Okamura also rejected criticism based on the AfD’s classification as a far-right party. He questioned the credibility of reports concerning extremism and pointed to similar accusations involving his own SPD.

Radek Vondráček of the ANO movement also called for a different approach to the AfD. Speaking to Czech Television, the chairman of the Chamber of Deputies’ foreign affairs committee said the election had given the party a clear mandate and expressed hope that it would be able to form a stable government.

“I hope that the time for dialogue is coming, when citizens will receive some appropriate result for what they have chosen,” Vondráček said.

World.title: Boris Brejcha Brings his High-Tech Minimal Show to Prague in October
World.content:
One of the world’s most sought-after producers and the king of the high-tech minimal genre, German DJ Boris Brejcha, is returning to the Czech Republic.

As part of his Reflections world tour, he will perform at Prague’s O2 Arena on Friday, October 2, 2026. For electronic music fans, one of the highlights of the season.

Boris Brejcha, whose identity is inextricably linked to a mysterious Venetian mask, promises a show full of spectacular lighting and a breathtaking visual spectacle.

He is recognized worldwide as a creator and pioneer of the “high-tech minimal” genre. The concert will be the artist’s only performance in the Czech Republic.

Official ticket sales have already begun. Tickets are available exclusively through the official Ticketmaster and Ticketportal sales networks.

Where did the iconic mask come from?

At the age of six, Brejcha suffered serious injuries in a plane crash. He sustained severe burns to his face and body. Music became his escape, and he began producing it on his own at the age of twelve.

He launched his official career in 2006. He made his debut at the Universo Paralello festival in Brazil, where he was inspired by the local carnival and chose his iconic Joker mask, which has become an integral part of his image.

Brejcha is best known as a creator and pioneer of high-tech minimal—a musical genre that combines electronic music with elements of techno, house, and trance, featuring distinctive melodies. He plays exclusively his own original music.

“Hello, Prague! Returning to your beautiful city is always a special experience for me. This time, I’m bringing the ‘Reflections’ show to the O2 Arena, which will feature a unique visual stage and my exclusive extended set. I’m already looking forward to the amazing atmosphere we’ll create together in the arena. It’ll be a night we’ll never forget. See you there,” says Boris Brejcha.

The unique atmosphere will be further enhanced by artistic support from Brejcha’s own label, FCKNG SERIOUS.

World.title: “Debt slavery is coming”: Viktor Orbán sounds alarms and attacks Tisza government
World.content:
Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán has returned to the political spotlight after several weeks away on holiday, launching a sharp attack on the Tisza government over fuel prices, the budget deficit and rising public debt.

“This was not a day for the Hungarians…”

Orbán summarised his criticism in a short Facebook post, warning that “debt slavery” could once again be on the horizon.

“Fuel prices are sky-high! The budget deficit has run wild! Debt slavery is on the horizon again! This was not a day for the Hungarians…”

As Index writes, the former prime minister had spent several weeks on holiday, first in Serbia and later in Croatia.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Fidesz attacks government’s economic record

Orbán’s remarks came alongside criticism from the Fidesz parliamentary group, which accused the Tisza government of delivering a poor economic performance since taking office. According to Fidesz, Hungarian families are currently facing the highest fuel prices seen so far this year, placing additional pressure on household budgets.

The parliamentary group also pointed to what it described as a rapidly worsening budget deficit and growing public debt, arguing that the combination of higher fuel costs and deteriorating fiscal indicators represents a serious burden for the population.

Stay up-to-date: Russian senator claims Hungary was forced to “prove its loyalty” to Brussels

Warning over public debt

Fidesz claimed that the government’s economic management had been characterised by a series of negative records, with both household costs and key macroeconomic indicators moving in an unfavourable direction. The opposition party argued that rising public debt and a larger state budget deficit could threaten Hungary’s economic stability over the longer term.

Orbán’s brief intervention echoed those concerns, framing the economic situation as a return to the threat of “debt slavery” — a phrase frequently used in Hungarian political discourse to describe excessive public indebtedness and dependence on external financing.

The former prime minister did not provide further details or figures in his post, instead delivering a concise political message focused on the three issues he presented as the main economic problems facing Hungarians: fuel prices, the budget deficit and public debt.

World.title: Russian Embassy says Hungary’s pledge of dialogue ‘worth nothing’ after expulsion of 10 diplomats
World.content:
Russia has sharply condemned Hungary’s decision to expel 10 employees of the Russian Embassy in Budapest, describing the move as an unprecedented and unjustified escalation and warning that it would trigger a response.

Moscow accuses Hungary of anti-Russian rhetoric

The criticism came after Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced on Tuesday that Hungary had ordered 10 members of the Russian diplomatic mission to leave the country because, according to the Hungarian authorities, they had engaged in activities incompatible with diplomatic status under the Vienna Convention.

Russian Ambassador to Hungary Evgeny Stanislavov said in a statement published by the embassy in Budapest that the expulsions showed the new Hungarian government had fallen “captive to ideologically motivated, anti-Russian rhetoric”. He also dismissed Budapest’s assurances that it wanted to preserve dialogue and continue pragmatic cooperation with Moscow.

According to the ambassador, statements by the Hungarian side about maintaining channels of communication with the Kremlin and continuing practical cooperation were now “worth nothing” in light of the decision. Moscow views the move as an “extremely unfriendly step” and an “unprecedented and unjustified escalation”, Stanislavov said, adding that it would receive an appropriate response.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Hungary insists diplomatic relations will continue

Anita Orbán stressed when announcing the expulsions that the measure does not mean Hungary is breaking off diplomatic relations with Moscow. Budapest still intends to maintain the necessary dialogue with them, she said, based on mutual respect and compliance with international rules. The Hungarian government has said the decision was taken to protect the country’s security and sovereignty, while Russian MP’s claim it was only to pledge loyalty to Brussels.

András Rácz, deputy director-general of the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, said that, according to the conventions of diplomatic language, the foreign minister’s statement strongly suggested that the 10 expelled Russian representatives had been working under diplomatic cover while allegedly carrying out intelligence activities.

The Kremlin has already signalled that retaliatory measures could follow. A spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry reportedly promised a “tough and painful” response. Aleksey Chepa, deputy chairman of the State Duma’s International Affairs Committee, told Russian state news agency TASS that Moscow would first respond in kind. He also warned that Hungary’s decision could lead to a reduction in joint economic projects with Moscow.

Stay up-to-date: POLITICO claims Paks II could be delayed until 2035 as Rosatom schedule reveals setback

Opposition parties attack the government’s decision

Hungary’s opposition parties Fidesz and KDNP have also criticised the expulsions, although for different reasons. Fidesz described the move as “nothing more than a distraction”, arguing that the government should instead address issues including the budget deficit, public debt and fuel prices.

The KDNP warned that the decision and the Russian response it may provoke could have “unforeseeable consequences”. The party argued that Russia remained difficult to replace as a source of natural gas and crude oil imports, warning that a hasty diplomatic step could ultimately affect Hungarian households through higher energy bills.

While stressing that every government has a duty to protect national security and sovereignty, the KDNP said the move marked the abandonment of Hungary’s previous “peace policy” and the beginning of a dismantling of the country’s pragmatic relationships outside Europe.

The diplomatic dispute now appears set to deepen, with Moscow promising retaliation while Budapest maintains that it wants to keep communication channels open despite the unprecedented expulsion of 10 Russian embassy employees.

World.title: Danube falls to historic low water levels in Budapest: just 1 centimetre
World.content:
The Danube has fallen to a historic low in Budapest, with water-level gauges showing just 1 centimetre on Tuesday, according to Időkép.

The Danube’s water level is at its lowest ever in Budapest

The reading is significantly lower than the levels recorded during the severe drought conditions earlier in the summer. In July, the Danube had already broken the previous negative record set in 2018, when the water authority measured a level of 27 centimetres at the end of the month, reports Időkép.

The river continued to recede throughout August, falling by almost another 20 centimetres. By Tuesday, the water level had dropped to just 1 centimetre. The exceptionally low level is creating serious difficulties for river navigation and can also pose a direct safety risk to vessels, as obstacles normally hidden beneath the surface become exposed or much easier to encounter.

Some of the consequences of the unusually low water level have already become visible elsewhere along the Danube. Near Baja, a shipwreck emerged from the riverbed to such an extent that it could reportedly be walked around. In Budapest, the remains of the former Ferenc József Bridge, which sank near what is now the Liberty Bridge, also became clearly visible.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

There might be light at the end of the tunnel

Water management experts attribute the extreme conditions to prolonged rainfall shortages and exceptionally dry conditions across the Danube’s catchment area. There could, however, be some relief in sight. A weather front is expected to bring rain to the Danube basin on Wednesday and reach Hungary by the evening. The rainfall could lead to a rise in the river’s water level.

The record low water levels show how Hungary, and all of Europe has become the victim of the all-summer-long dry conditions, with consequences extending beyond the river itself to navigation and water safety.

World.title: Remarkable: Remains of Ice Age animal found in Hungary’s River Tisza
World.content:
An extraordinary prehistoric discovery has been made in River Tisza, in Hungary, where water management workers found what is believed to be the skull of a cave bear that lived during the Ice Age.

Workers first thought they found an old anchor

Staff from the Middle Tisza District Water Directorate (Kötivizig) spotted the object while kayaking between Szolnok and Kisköre. Initially, they thought the object protruding from the riverbed might be an old anchor.

A closer inspection, however, revealed the remains of a large animal. Around three-quarters of the find was buried in the gravel bed, from which the workers were able to recover it thanks to the Tisza’s low water level.

The remains were taken to the Damjanich János Museum in Szolnok, where experts conducted an initial examination. Their preliminary assessment is that the find is probably the skull of an Ice Age cave bear.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

What to know about cave bears?

Cave bears (Ursus spelaeus) lived across much of Europe during the Pleistocene and became extinct thousands of years ago. Their remains are often associated with caves, where the animals sought shelter and hibernated.

The exact age of the newly discovered skull has yet to be established. Museum specialists will carry out further examinations to determine when the animal lived. The discovery demonstrates how falling water levels can expose objects and remains that have been hidden beneath river sediments for centuries or even millennia.

This is how cave bears used to looked like. Illustration. Photo: Sergiodlarosa/Wikimedia Commons

World.title: Russian senator claims Hungary was forced to “prove its loyalty” to Brussels
World.content:
Hungary has expelled 10 Russian diplomats accused of carrying out activities incompatible with diplomatic status, in a move that could mark a significant change in Budapest’s approach to Russian intelligence operations. Moscow has already warned of a “tough and painful” response. The deputy speaker of Russia’s upper house of parliament said that the decision was an unfriendly and confrontational act.

Hungary has ordered 10 Russian diplomatic personnel to leave the country after authorities determined that they had engaged in activities deemed unacceptable under the Vienna Convention.

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced the decision on Tuesday, saying the Foreign Ministry had informed Russia’s ambassador in Budapest that Hungarian authorities had identified activities by 10 members of the Russian diplomatic mission that were incompatible with their diplomatic status.

“The decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty,” Orbán said, while stressing that the move does not amount to a severing of diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary, she added, intends to maintain the necessary dialogue with Moscow based on mutual respect and compliance with international rules.

Expert: The diplomats were Russian intelligence officers

According to Russia expert András Rácz, the wording used by the Hungarian government strongly indicates that the 10 individuals were actually Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover. Rácz, deputy director-general responsible for research and academic affairs at the Hungarian Institute of International Affairs, told MTI that the phrase “activities incompatible with diplomatic status” traditionally refers to espionage.

In practical terms, he said, Hungary has expelled 10 Russian diplomats who were allegedly working as intelligence officers under diplomatic cover in Budapest.

The scale of the move is particularly significant. According to Rácz, more than 600 Russian intelligence officers operating under diplomatic cover have been expelled from EU member states since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Until now, Hungary had been the only EU member state not to carry out such a large-scale expulsion. Rácz therefore described the decision as Hungary effectively joining its EU and NATO allies in efforts to reduce Russia’s intelligence capabilities across the bloc.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Why has Hungary acted now?

The timing of the expulsions is particularly noteworthy given Hungary’s historically close relationship with Moscow under the previous Orbán government.

Rácz said he could not determine precisely why Budapest had chosen this particular moment to act. However, he argued that the decision represents a significant shift in Hungary’s position towards Russian intelligence activities. He also pointed out that, according to official Foreign Ministry figures, 47 Russian diplomats are currently accredited in Hungary, accompanied by 41 spouses.

It is not publicly known how many of the remaining diplomats are connected to Russian intelligence services. However, Rácz noted that a Russian investigative outlet recently identified 15 of the 47 Russian diplomats in Budapest as having links to various Russian intelligence agencies based on publicly available information.

He added that while there had been some “quiet expulsions” of Russian intelligence personnel during the previous Hungarian government, there had never before been a publicly announced expulsion on this scale.

Budapest sends a message to its Western allies

The decision could have implications beyond Hungary’s bilateral relationship with Russia. Rácz argued that Russian intelligence officers based in Hungary can potentially operate elsewhere in the Schengen Area, making their presence a security concern for Hungary’s allies as well. He pointed to Prague as a previous example of how Russian diplomats could use one European capital as a base for intelligence operations in neighbouring countries.

According to the expert, Russian intelligence personnel operating from Budapest have similarly been able to conduct operations elsewhere in the Schengen Area and in Balkan countries outside the zone.

For this reason, Rácz described Hungary’s decision as a long-overdue step towards its EU and NATO partners. He argued that Hungary’s failure to expel such personnel over the previous four and a half years had potentially harmed the security interests of its allies.

Moscow threatens retaliation

Russia has responded angrily to the expulsions. Konstantin Kosachev, deputy speaker of Russia’s upper house of parliament, told the RIA Novosti news agency that the decision was an unfriendly and confrontational act. He argued that the simultaneous expulsion of 10 diplomats was “many times more unfriendly” and amounted to an open challenge to Moscow. Russia, he said, would respond accordingly.

Kosachev also claimed that the decision had been driven by Brussels, arguing that the “post-Orbán” Hungary had been pressured to demonstrate its loyalty to what he described as the anti-Russian policies of the EU and NATO.

Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova likewise warned that Moscow would deliver a “tough and painful response”, referring to what she called the “Russophobic lobby” in Budapest. A reciprocal move is therefore widely expected, with Rácz saying Russia is almost certain to respond proportionally by expelling Hungarian diplomats.

World.title: Hungary waves goodbye to historical county titles, and reintroduces modern forms
World.content:
Hungary’s Parliament has voted to restore the terms “county” and “government commissioner”, reversing the controversial renaming of counties and government commissioners introduced by Viktor Orbán’s Fidesz government in 2022.

Historical titles are gone

The Tisza-majority Parliament approved the legislation on Tuesday with 134 votes in favour and 52 against. Fidesz, the Christian Democrats (KDNP) and Mi Hazánk (Our Homeland) voted against the proposal. Under the changes, Hungary’s vármegyék (literally translated to castle counties) will once again officially be known as megyék, while főispáns (lord lieutenants) will again be referred to as government commissioners.

The 2022 terminology was introduced as part of the 11th amendment to Hungary’s Fundamental Law. The Fidesz government argued at the time that restoring the historical term vármegye would preserve the constitutional traditions of Hungary’s thousand-year statehood, strengthen national unity and reinforce the national character of Hungarian democracy.

Government cites clarity and practicality

The newly adopted legislation takes a different approach, stressing practical and legal considerations. According to the proposal, abandoning the terms vármegye and főispán will make the administrative system more transparent and easier to understand, while promoting consistent application of the law.

The changes are primarily terminological and technical. They do not alter the powers or responsibilities of the affected authorities, nor do they change the substance of administrative, regulatory or local-government relationships. The law will enter into force on the day after its promulgation, while amendments changing the terminology in other legislation will take effect on 1 October.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

From historic tradition to a controversial revival

The term vármegye has deep roots in Hungarian history. It was used for a fundamental administrative unit from the foundation of the Hungarian state until 1949, although the county system developed gradually over several centuries. The system underwent major reforms in the late 19th century, including a significant administrative restructuring between 1876 and 1881.

County boundaries changed repeatedly, including before the Treaty of Trianon. The historical name survived these changes and remained in use after Trianon and during the years following the Second World War. It was officially replaced by megye in 1949, when Hungary adopted a new constitution modelled on the Soviet system.

Stay up-do-date: Hungary orders 10 Russian embassy staff to leave – UPDATE: Russia’s threat

Lázár once opposed the name change

Interestingly, János Lázár, who was a senior minister in Orbán’s fifth government, voted in favour of the 2022 renaming despite having previously criticised the idea. When the change was considered during the drafting of the Fundamental Law in 2011, Lázár argued that the historical term carried negative associations for many Hungarians, particularly those whose families had worked as servants or labourers.

He eventually supported the 2022 change, saying he did so because it formed part of the constitutional amendment before Parliament. The latest vote now reverses that decision, bringing Hungary’s official administrative terminology back to the terms used between 1949 and 2022.

World.title: New documents reveal why Orbán minister Lázár kept his Switzerland trip a secret for 13 years
World.content:
After more than 13 years, new documents have shed light on one of the longest-running mysteries surrounding Hungarian politician János Lázár: what he was doing in Zurich on 22 and 23 March 2013. The details were revealed by investigative outlet Direkt36, which obtained an internal government document from the Tisza government, which took office this spring.

Newly revealed documents show what János Lázár was doing in 2013

According to the document, Lázár, who was then heading the Prime Minister’s Office as a state secretary, met a person identified as “Prof. Mangold” in Zurich to discuss potential cooperation between the Hungarian government and Western European companies.

Direkt36 says the name almost certainly refers to Klaus Mangold, a prominent German businessman with extensive contacts in European and Russian business circles. Mangold established links with the Hungarian government in the early 2010s and later worked as an adviser to Viktor Orbán’s governments. The newly released report was prepared by his consultancy, Mangold Consulting GmbH.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Rothschild, SAP and government communications

The report says Lázár and Mangold discussed three main areas. The first was whether Rothschild could act as an “independent adviser” to the Hungarian government, including assessing the country’s financial risks and advising on the banking sector. A meeting involving then Economy Minister Mihály Varga and newly appointed central bank governor György Matolcsy was reportedly planned, with Orbán himself potentially attending part of the meeting.

The pair also discussed cooperation with business software giant SAP, particularly in financial administration and healthcare. The third topic was the Hungarian government’s marketing strategy. The report mentions German consultancy firms Schuppner and CNC, which Mangold was said to know well and which could advise on responding to critical media. A joint brainstorming session was reportedly proposed.

Rothschild later did work for the Orbán government, including producing a report during the European Union’s investigation into the Paks II nuclear project. The report concluded that the investment could be economically viable under market conditions. Rothschild also later participated in the creation of the partly state-owned MBH Bank.

Stay up-to-date: Hungary orders 10 Russian embassy staff to leave – UPDATE: Russia’s threat

A mystery that began with expensive hotel bills

The Zurich trip had attracted attention because of its unusually high costs. Lázár and his companion spent HUF 189,000 on one night’s accommodation in Zurich. Two other trips also raised questions: HUF 596,000 for one night in Milan and HUF 920,000 for two nights in England.

At the time, Lázár’s office refused to reveal the purpose of the trips, citing national security concerns. Lázár was also responsible for Hungary’s foreign intelligence service. Journalist András Pethő, then working for Origo, sued for access to the information. The case became politically explosive and contributed to pressure on Origo’s editorial team. Editor-in-chief Gergő Sáling was later dismissed, prompting many journalists, including Pethő, to leave the outlet.

Lázár eventually repaid the travel expenses, but the purpose of the Zurich meeting remained secret for years. The former minister declined to comment to Direkt36. Mangold’s consultancy also refused media questions, while SAP said it was unaware of any cooperation linked to the meeting. Rothschild and CNC did not respond.

World.title: Breaking: Hungary orders 10 Russian embassy staff to leave – UPDATE: Russia’s threat
World.content:
Hungary has ordered 10 employees of the Russian Embassy in Budapest to leave the country, saying their activities were incompatible with the conduct expected of diplomats under the Vienna Convention. A spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry said Budapest should expect a “harsh and painful response”.

FM Orbán announces letting go of 10 embassy employees

Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced the decision, describing it as unprecedented in scale. She said the relevant official at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs had informed Russia’s ambassador to Budapest of the decision on her instructions. According to Orbán, the Hungarian authorities assessed that the 10 representatives had engaged in activities that were not acceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention.

“The decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty,” the minister said. She stressed, however, that the move does not mean a break in diplomatic relations with the Kremlin. Hungary intends to maintain the necessary dialogue with Moscow, provided that both sides respect one another and comply with international rules.

UPDATE: Russia’s threat

Russia will respond to Hungary’s expulsion of ten Russian diplomats, according to the Russian state news agency TASS, citing a statement from the Russian Foreign Ministry. Maria Zakharova, spokesperson for the Russian Foreign Ministry, promised a “harsh and painful response.”

“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” she told TASS.

A tougher approach towards Moscow

The expulsions mark a notably tougher public response towards Russian diplomatic activity than previous measures taken by Hungary. Péter Magyar also raised the announcement in Parliament, reading out Orbán’s statement and saying that a Tisza government would protect Hungary’s sovereignty, reports Telex.

Anita Orbán has adopted a more distant diplomatic approach towards Russia than her predecessor, Péter Szijjártó, according to the supplied sources. On 13 May, shortly after taking office, she summoned Russia’s ambassador following a Russian drone attack against Transcarpathia. Szijjártó had last summoned a Russian diplomat in February 2022. The latest move also follows reports of a quieter expulsion of a Russian intelligence officer earlier this year.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

Kremlin intelligence officer reportedly expelled in May

VSquare reported in May that Artur Sushkov, allegedly a Russian intelligence officer operating under diplomatic cover at the Embassy in Budapest, left Hungary on 4 May. According to the report, Hungary’s Constitutional Protection Office had established that Sushkov had spent years collecting information on institutions close to the Hungarian government. VSquare’s government sources claimed that Hungarian intelligence had recommended his expulsion as early as February, but that the previous Orbán government had blocked the proposal.

Stay up-to-date: FM Anita Orbán reports progress on minority rights for Hungarians in Ukraine

2018 Skripal case provides a different precedent

Hungary also expelled a Russian diplomat in 2018 following the poisoning of former Kremlin intelligence officer Sergei Skripal in Britain. However, a subsequent Direkt36 investigation suggested that Budapest deliberately handled the expulsion in a way that would minimise damage to its close relationship with Moscow.

Diplomatic sources reportedly said the expelled Russian was a GRU military intelligence officer whose posting was due to end within months. The latest decision is considerably larger in scale, as the 10 embassy employees have now been ordered to leave Hungary. Despite this, Budapest insists that diplomatic relations with Moscow will continue, with the government presenting the expulsions as a measure to protect Hungary’s security and sovereignty rather than a move towards severing ties with Russia.

World.title: Ratko Mladic’s Lavish Funeral was an Indictment of Serbia’s Govt: Experts
World.content:

Criticism has echoed across Europe over the high-profile funeral of Ratko Mladic on Monday in Belgrade, raising questions about the potential repercussions for Serbia of giving a convicted war criminal a hero’s farewell.

His funeral with military honours was attended by senior officials of Serbia and Bosnia’s mainly Serb entity, Republika Srpska.

World.title: Montenegro Prosecutors Open Case Against Bishop for Praising Mladic
World.content:
Montenegro’s Higher State Prosecutor’s Office in Podgorica has opened a case against a Serbian Orthodox Bishop after he praised the late convicted war criminal Ratko Mladic during a religious service, the Vijesti newspaper reported on Tuesday.

The prosecutor’s office told the newspaper that the bishop was suspected of inciting national, racial and religious hatred. It did not provide further details about the investigation or say whether Bishop Metodije of Budimlje-Niksic Diocese had been questioned.

The bishop praised Mladic during a service at the Piva Monastery in northern Montenegro on August 28, the day after he died, saying people had recognised in Mladic “all those wonderful and holy qualities of Serbian warriors and knights.

“May the most holy Mother of God … raise his soul among all the holy Serbian knights, the famous general Ratko,” Metodije said, according to a recording and transcript published by local media.

The diocese later published a statement on its website saying that, after the liturgy, a memorial service had been held for “the newly departed servant of God, General Ratko Mladic”.

At the same time, Montenegro’s Higher State Prosecutor’s Office in Bijelo Polje has dismissed criminal complaints against Metodije over speeches praising a notorious World War II-era Nazi-alligned commander, Pavle Djurisic, held responsible for mass killings during the war, Vijesti reported on Tuesday.

Mladic, who died on August 27, while serving a life sentence at the UN detention facility in the Hague, commanded Bosnian Serb forces during the 1992-95 war in Bosnia. He was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes by a United Nations tribunal and sentenced to life imprisonment.

The tribunal found him responsible for various crimes including the 1995 massacre of more than 8,000 Bosniaks in Srebrenica – Europe’s worst atrocity since World War II, and the prolonged siege of Sarajevo.

Mladic remains a hero to many Serbs, while victims’ families and survivors regard him as responsible for some of the 1992-95 Bosnian war’s gravest crimes.

Montenegro, a NATO member and candidate for European Union membership, has laws criminalising the incitement of ethnic, racial and religious hatred.

World.title: Turkey’s Ruling Party Seizes Back Control of Important Mayoralty
World.content:
Dundar Ziya Gultekin, candidate of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s Justice and Development Party, AKP, was elected as acting Mayor of Uskudar on Tuesday, defeating Sibel Tan Cetinkaya, the joint candidate of the opposition Republican People’s Party, CHP, and the New Party.

The vote in Uskudar followed the arrest and removal from office of the elected CHP mayor, Sinem Dedetas, in July on alleged corruption charges. Gultekin will serve as acting mayor, as he was elected by the municipal council rather than by popular vote.

The result came after a dramatic shift in the council’s balance. Four councillors elected for the main opposition CHP defected to the AKP days before the vote, while two CHP councillors were detained and so unable to vote.

This left the rival blocs with 21 councillors each. Yet, Gultekin received 23 votes in the secret ballot, indicating that two councillors from the CHP-New Party bloc also backed the AKP candidate. Their identities remain unknown.

“They told people elected from our lists: ‘Either join the AKP or go to prison, either wear the party badge or wear handcuffs,’” Ozgur Celik, Istanbul Provincial Chair of the New Party said after the vote, alleging that some councillors defected because they feared arrest.

The New Party, which cooperated with the CHP in the Uskudar vote, was established earlier this year by Ozgur Ozel and other politicians who broke away from the CHP after a controversial court ruling annulled the 2023 party congress over alleged irregularities, removing Ozel as leader and reinstating his predecessor, Kemal Kilicdaroglu.

Uskudar is a traditional conservative stronghold and was ruled by the AKP and other conservative and Islamist parties for decades. However, the AKP lost the district and major cities and towns in the 2024 local elections.

Uskudar is located on the Asian side of Istanbul and is home to more than half a million people.

Cetinkaya initially won a mayoral election in August, but a court ordered a rerun following an AKP challenge.

Over the last year, dozens of CHP mayors and hundreds of party members have been arrested on corruption and terror charges. Those include the arrest of Istanbul’s Mayor and opposition presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu on March 19, 2025. The prosecutor’s office is demanding a 2,352-year prison sentence for him. Imamoglu denies all the accusations.

Opposition politicians, rights groups and international organisations have said that the government is using the judiciary to crush political rivals in what they describe as an unprecedented crackdown.

World.title: Kosovo Parliament to Reconvene, ‘Chaos’ Looms over Election of President
World.content:
Kosovo’s new parliament reconvenes for its inaugural session on Wednesday, despite continued uncertainty over whether lawmakers will agree on the election of a head-of-state.

The session started on August 6, following elections in June, but was paused after the victorious Vetevendosje party asked for “more time” for negotiations with other parties on the candidate for Kosovo’s next president.

At the end of the month, Vetevendosje leader Albin Kurti and his counterpart from the opposition Democratic League of Kosovo, LDK, Lumir Abdixhiku announced that their parties would both back Judge Bekim Sejdiu as president, only for a third of the LDK’s MPs to cry foul.

Such is the depth of animosity between Vetevendosje and its rivals, constituting parliament and electing a president has become a major challenge, complicated by a rift within the LDK over Abdixhiku’s leadership.

World.title: Albanian Port Bars Alleged Russian-Linked ‘Shadow Fleet’ Oil Tanker
World.content:
The Harbour Master’s Office in the Albanian port of Durres has barred the oil tanker Hanuman from entering the port after Ukraine’s military intelligence identified the vessel as part of Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet”, which Moscow uses to transport oil and petroleum products and evade sanctions.

The Intelligence Directorate at Ukraine’s Ministry of Defence, known as the GUR, welcomed Albania’s move as an example of international cooperation in enforcing sanctions and restricting maritime routes used by Moscow to export oil.

“Albania’s decision not to allow the ‘Hanuman’ to enter its port is an important demonstration of international solidarity in enforcing sanctions,” the GUR said.

“Joint actions by Ukraine and its foreign partners are steadily limiting the Kremlin’s ability to use maritime trade routes to circumvent sanctions, forcing the aggressor state to take responsibility for its actions,” it added.

The Hanuman was flying under the flag of Sierra Leone when it was barred from entering Durres port on August 29.

Data published by the GUR shows that since the start of 2025, the Hanuman has transported at least 452,000 tonnes of fuel out of Russia.

Most of its voyages originated from Novorossiysk, one of Russia’s main Black Sea ports, with destinations including Turkey, Senegal, the United Arab Emirates and a ship-to-ship transfer area near the Italian city of Augusta.

The GUR claims a Russian company, Altoprae Marine, based in Novorossiysk, provided logistical support for these voyages, which it links to a manager from the circle of sanctioned Russian oligarch Gennady Timchenko, a longtime ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The GUR also links Altoprae Marine to the operations of vessels owned by Rosewood Shipping, which Ukrainian authorities claim is controlled by Oksana Marchenko, the wife of pro-Russian Ukrainian politician Viktor Medvedchuk, a longtime ally of Putin.

Russia’s so-called “shadow fleet” consists of a network of tankers it uses to keep its oil exports moving after Western sanctions were imposed over its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

These vessels often operate under the flags of third countries and through ownership structures that are difficult to trace.

The G7 countries and the European Union introduced a price cap on Russian seaborne oil in late 2022, along with restrictions on insurance, financing and other services related to its transport.

Albania, an EU candidate country and NATO member, has aligned itself with the EU’s sanctions against Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Maritime traffic data show that the Hanuman previously visited the Port of Durres in November 2025.

A BIRN investigation published in May 2026 identified the tanker as part of a list of vessels suspected of transporting Russian oil or grain stolen from Ukrainian territories occupied by Russia.

The vessels on the list had visited Albanian ports since 2022, raising questions about the enforcement of sanctions imposed by Albania against Moscow.

World.title: Romanians Flock to Venerate Saint Anne’s Relics in Bucharest
World.content:
“We are particularly happy to welcome the bringing of the relics of St Anne, the grandmother of our Lord Jesus Christ and the mother of the Most Holy Mother of God,” Patriarch Daniel, head of the Romanian Orthodox Church, said after receiving the relics at his patriarchal residence. He described the opportunity to venerate them as “a great blessing”.

In the Orthodox calendar, St Anne is celebrated on September 9. She is traditionally regarded as a protector of families, children and motherhood. The relics will remain at the Bucharest church until September 10, with the church open daily from 7 a.m. until 10 p.m., or longer if pilgrims are still waiting to enter.

World.title: EU Leaders Condemn ‘Shocking’ Glorification of Mladic at Belgrade Funeral
World.content:
This post is also available in this language: Shqip Bos/Hrv/Srp

Senior European Union figures have condemned the military honours and glorification of the convicted Bosnian Serb war criminal Ratko Mladic at his funeral in Belgrade, warning that the scenes undermined Serbia’s European aspirations.

In a joint statement European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa described images from Monday’s funeral as “shocking”, stressing that Mladic died while serving a life sentence for genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity.

“The elements of official support and the presence of some senior Serbian officials at the funeral are deeply regrettable,” Von der Leyen and Costa wrote on X on Tuesday. “They demonstrate a failure to confront a dark chapter in Europe’s recent history and contradict the values underpinning Serbia’s path towards the European Union.”

Several Serbian ministers, including Defence Minister Bratislav Gasic and Justice Minister Nenad Vujic, attended the funeral of Mladic, the former commander of the Bosnian Serb Army, who was buried with military honours in Belgrade.

Officials from Bosnia’s Serb-dominated Republika Srpska entity also attended, as well as an estimated 16,000 mourners, according to the Archive of Public Gatherings, which gauges attendance sizes at large gatherings.

Until his death on August 27 at the UN Detention Unit in the Netherlands, Mladic was serving a life sentence after being convicted of genocide and other wartime crimes.

The EU criticism comes at a politically sensitive moment in Serbia, a candidate for membership of the bloc, where elections are approaching and relations between Brussels and Belgrade have already faced strains over democratic standards.

A group of 118 Serbian professors and researchers wrote on Tuesday in a letter to Von der Leyen ahead of her possible visit to Serbia in October, warning that a meeting with President Aleksandar Vucic during an election campaign could be portrayed by pro-government media as European support for the incumbent authorities.

“We are not asking you to support the student movement, the opposition, or any electoral list. We are asking you to support no one,” the academics said, urging Von der Leyen to consider postponing the visit until after the elections if it could not be protected from political manipulation.

Condemnation also came from US politicians. House of Representatives members Greg Murphy and Marc Veasey said on Monday that Mladic’s funeral was “not an occasion for his glorification”, warning that genocide denial and the glorification of convicted war criminals deepen ethnic divisions and undermine Bosnia and Herzegovina’s stability.

The two US politicians also called for targeted sanctions against individuals who threaten Bosnia’s peace and stability or undermine the 1995 Dayton peace deal framework.

Turkish Foreign Ministry spokesperson Oncu Keceli meanwhile said it was “unacceptable” for the funeral to be exploited in a way that amounted to denying grave crimes and human suffering.

Ankara said rejecting international court judgments or portraying convicted perpetrators as heroes deepens the suffering of victims and their relatives and damages peace and reconciliation in the Balkans.

Turkey said the region needed to learn lessons from the past and build a “peaceful, prosperous and shared future”, while commemorating the victims of the Srebrenica genocide and all innocent people killed during the Bosnian war.

Condemnation has continued to come from neighbouring states as well, with Montenegro’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs expressing concern for Mladic’s victims.

“It is our obligation to preserve the dignity and memory of the victims, to preserve the truth about crimes and individual responsibility for them, and to resolutely oppose any attempt to deny genocide, war crimes and other serious violations of international humanitarian law,” the Montenegrin ministry said in a written statement on Tuesday.

On Monday, Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Foreign Minister Elmedin Konakovic warned that the Serbian leadership is risking “complete isolation in the region”, while Croatia’s Foreign Minister Gordan Grlic Radman said that “glorifying this war criminal is truly incompatible with European values”.

World.title: Falling Profits Cloud Horizons for Turkey’s Booming Tourist Industry
World.content:
Turkey continues to draw millions of holidaymakers to its beaches, resorts and historic sites, but beneath the headline visitor numbers, the country’s tourism industry is showing signs of strain.

After a record year, Turkey entered 2026 with high hopes, having hosted nearly 64 million visitors and generated 65.23 billion US dollars in tourism revenue in 2025, up 2.7 and 6.8 per cent respectively compared to 2024, and ranking fourth globally for international tourist arrivals.

However, official figures show that visitor numbers actually fell 5.1 per cent year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026, while tourism revenue dropped 2.6 per cent to 15.87 billion US dollars.

Meanwhile, industry data cited by Turizm News showed average hotel occupancy falling from 40.17 per cent in the first half of 2025 to 36.80 per cent in the same period this year.

World.title: Former Croatian PM Seeks Suspension of Serbian EU Accession Talks
World.content:
September the 8th, 2026 – Former Croatian PM Jadranka Kosor is seeking total suspension of all Serbian EU accession talks, calling on Ursula von der Leyen to take action.

Former Croatian Prime Minister Jadranka Kosor has called on the European Commission to completely suspend Serbia’s EU accession negotiations following today’s mass farewell for Ratko Mladić in Belgrade, which was held with the highest state and military honours. “After today’s funeral, involving the anti-civilisational bowing of Serbia to a war criminal convicted of genocide, I expect the incompetent European Commission and its incompetent leader Ursula von der Leyen to fully suspend Serbia’s accession negotiations for entry into the EU. That is the minimum,” Kosor wrote on X.

a serbian state funeral for a genocidal maniac

Index reports that thousands of people gathered in Belgrade to bid a final farewell to the former commander of the Army of Republika Srpska. Disgraced Ratko Mladić was buried at Topčider Cemetery with state honours, in the presence of members of the Serbian Army and an honour guard. Numerous Serbian officials, the political leadership of Republika Srpska, and the Russian ambassador to Serbia attended the funeral. Before the burial, his coffin was displayed in the Church of St. Luke, where the service was led by Patriarch Porfirije. On the coffin were his officer’s cap and sabre, and members of the army and veterans of the former Army of Republika Srpska stood beside it. The Serbian Government had previously sent a state aircraft to collect Mladić’s remains from The Hague, and soldiers carried his coffin, covered with the Serbian flag, out of the plane. A commemoration was also held for him on Saturday in an official facility of the Serbian Army.

serbia honours one of the worst monsters of the 20th century

Mladić died on the 27th of August at the age of 84 in The Hague, where he was serving a life sentence. He had suffered several quite serious strokes and his health had been declining rapidly for some time. He was finally convicted of committing genocide in Srebrenica, crimes against humanity, and war crimes during the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina. His forces were responsible, among other things, for the massacre of more than 8,000 innocent Bosniak men and boys in Srebrenica in July 1995, as well as for the multi-year, dreadful siege of Sarajevo.

the eu’s position is clear – no glorification of war crimes and war criminals

The European Union has already very clearly warned Serbia over the glorification of the vile Ratko Mladić. European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos cancelled a planned visit to Serbia after a state aircraft brought his body to Belgrade. The European External Action Service stated that the glorification of war criminals, denial of genocide, and revisionism have no place either in the European Union or in candidate countries. Serbia has otherwise held candidate status for EU membership and has been conducting accession negotiations since 2014.
