World.title: Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018971/Remembering Gyirong: The Bustling Port That Vanished in a Flash
World.content:
Photographer He Xu first passed through the China-Nepal border at Gyirong Port in 2010. He remembers that it was just a row of rustic, clay-colored bungalows.

Over the past 16 years, he has revisited at least 100 times, witnessing the area’s steady growth, with those bungalows eventually replaced by a grand, imposing building.

Yet that progress came to a violent halt on the morning of Aug. 26, when a flash flood caused by a mountain glacier ripped through the port in Shigatse, in China’s southwestern Xizang Autonomous Region. As of Sept. 2, the disaster had killed at least 1,204 in Nepal and 21 in China, according to Xinhua News Agency. Almost 5,000 people remain missing, including 546 in Gyirong.

He, who runs a photo studio in the regional capital, Lhasa, was in Beijing when he heard the news. Over the years, he had gotten to know more than 20 people working at the port, including customs and immigration officials, firefighters, and disease-control workers. He began hurriedly searching through his phone contacts.

“Are you safe? Please reply when you see this. I’m really worried,” he texted them. Most of his messages went unanswered.

Nestled in a deep, winding valley at the foot of the Himalayas, about 100 kilometers from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, China’s Gyirong County is referred to as “the back garden of Mount Qomolangma” — or Mount Everest, as it’s known in the West. The land port there is historically among the largest for trade between China and Nepal. After opening for bilateral customs clearance in 2014, the volume of goods passing through has increased rapidly.

“On one side of the port was a huge parking lot, where vehicles from both countries waited for inspection,” He recalls. “Next to the lot were several white buildings, four or five floors each, where the on-duty staff lived.”

Across from the lot was a police station and a row of small stores including a supermarket run by a middle-aged couple from the neighboring Sichuan province, a souvenir shop run by a Nepalese merchant, and three restaurants.

“Most visitors were tourists who took a quick photo at the border gate and left,” says the 50-year-old photographer. “There wasn’t much demand for a bustling commercial street. But the port staff stayed year-round, and these outlets were their only options for shopping and dining.”

Many of these border officials are among the missing.

With the flash flood destroying about three kilometers of the highway leading to Gyirong, it took two days for the first rescue teams from Xizang and Sichuan to reach the disaster zone. The highway was reportedly reopened on Sept. 2, allowing access to more rescuers, emergency supplies, and heavy machinery.

A warm welcome

The first reply that He received was from a Tibetan friend working at the port’s disease-control station. He had requested the day off on Aug. 26 and gone into town, narrowly escaping the massive torrent of rock, ice, and water that had wiped out his workplace.

The photographer offered to transfer some money so that his friend could purchase food and emergency supplies and bring them to the port, but he declined. “All the roads over there are blocked,” he replied. “The rescue teams are still using bulldozers and excavators to clear a path, moving forward inch by inch.”

After two sleepless nights, He set off from Beijing for Gyirong on the morning of Aug. 28. He had no idea how he would help — he just knew he had to go.

Since the disaster, the Gyirong Entry-Exit Border Inspection Station’s official channel on the WeChat messaging platform has been inundated with messages from well-wishers.

Many staff at the port are in their early 30s and hail from various parts of China. Far from their families, most live quiet, monotonous lives.

He Xu once wandered into the staff dormitories and noted the austerity of the rooms, with just two beds, a desk, and simple storage cabinets. The housing complex had a recreation room with table tennis and other sports facilities, but he’d never seen anyone using them. “The most typical thing I saw staff doing after work was calling their families,” he says.

The workers rarely ventured far, He says, leaving them little opportunity to appreciate the valley scenery — so he decided his lens would be their “eyes.” One person wanted to see a kiang, an indigenous wild ass; another, the splendor of Ngari prefecture, a 15-hour drive west; another, the view from a 4,500-meter platform in the Himalayas just an hour away. Each time, He would capture what they asked for and share the pictures on WeChat.

The customs staff rotated every three or four days. Off-duty workers are accommodated in the county seat, about 90 minutes away by bus, where they can enjoy more variety in terms of meals, shopping, and entertainment.

Those who have passed through Gyirong Port often speak of the “pleasant, helpful” nature of the customs and security personnel there.

Wen Lili from China’s northwestern Shaanxi province visited in early August. She remembers a young police officer who helped suggest the best places to take photos — the checkpoint, boundary marker, and the Friendship Bridge over the border — and where to exchange Chinese renminbi for Nepalese rupees. “It’s such a tiny place, and he told me everything there was to see,” she says.

He Xu says that, one time, his pickup truck was dangerously low on fuel, and a police officer drove more than 40 kilometers to the nearest gas station to bring him a full jerry can.

Two years ago, He joined a customs officer named Dorje and some of his friends for a meal in town. Dorje came from Maizhokunggar County, more than 800 kilometers from Gyirong, and was 10 years from retirement. With a beaming smile, he had talked of his three children, who had all gone to work in major cities.

With the savings he had accumulated, Dorje had planned to return to his hometown, buy some cattle and sheep, and spend his days tending them with his wife. It was his ideal life, he’d said.

Two-way street

Ma Baoxiang, who runs a general store in Gyirong, would often drive the 20 kilometers to the port to shoot videos for his social media channel.

Having made countless trips, he had become familiar with its rhythms: mornings were busiest, as tourists and truck drivers rushed to cross the border before lunch, although crowds could also swell in the afternoon, with vehicles sometimes lining the road. Most were trucks bearing Nepalese license plates, but Ma says that in recent years he has noticed an increase in travelers crossing the border in private cars.

The Bangxing Logistics Park, a 40-minute drive from the port, is the initial destination for most goods arriving from across the border. The facility gets so busy that drivers can be stuck waiting for up to two days to load or unload their cargo.

Nepalese residents near the border with exit-entry permits would also regularly pass through the port to stock up on clothes, daily necessities, and food from the stores in Gyirong.

“You often see Nepalese merchants buying wholesale goods in town,” says Ma, who every few months goes the other way to buy copperware, handicrafts, tea, and other specialty products, which he ships home to sell to tourists.

Trade at Gyirong Port once largely consisted of small businesses run by local residents. In April 2015, when an earthquake in Nepal damaged facilities at the larger Zhangmu Port, Gyirong became the primary China-Nepal border crossing. It was expanded into an international port in 2017.

By 2024, the value of imports and exports passing through Gyirong reached 4.24 billion yuan ($632 million), the highest among all the ports in Xizang.

Ma Qi, the local branch manager of Musa International Logistics, says his company had at least a dozen trucks en route to the port when the disaster struck on Aug. 26. He immediately told the drivers to pull over and wait, and then contacted nearby warehouses to arrange 6,000 square meters of emergency storage for their cargo.

“Gyirong is the best port,” says Ma Qi, who has worked in cross-border export logistics for 13 years. His company exports 400 to 500 cubic meters of goods a day, including clothing, hardware, small household appliances, construction machinery for bridge and tunnel projects, and electric vehicles. He describes the port as a “lifeline.”

The growth in tourists has also helped turn Gyirong into an economic hub, bringing many restaurants and hotels.

“After the mudslide, Gyirong suddenly emptied out,” says Lin Tian, who has owned a store in the county seat selling Nepalese specialty goods for the past five years. “The only people here are residents and the people working or running shops.”

Locals are no strangers to floods, earthquakes, and other natural disasters. It has become an inevitable part of life.

When a mudslide triggered flooding on both sides of the border in July last year, Gyirong Port was closed for nearly six months, forcing logistics companies to shift operations to smaller ports.

“These past few days, the government has been coordinating with us to register and report the cargo stranded at the port. They will arrange for it to be shipped out through the Zhangmu and Lizi ports instead,” says Ma Qi. In the meantime, he is mobilizing resources and coordinating with relief organizations in Lhasa and Shigatse to help transport emergency supplies to the disaster zone.

In late 2024, Gyirong was hit by landslides, leaving many port workers stranded in town with no power for more than a week. The mud in some places was shin-deep.

He Xu recalls asking several port staff whether they feared natural disasters. One simply smiled and replied, “I’m not worried. We’ve always made it through before.”

This time, He wasn’t so sure. In the early hours of Aug. 28, he finally received another message from a contact at the port, this time from a police officer. “I’m in downtown Shigatse. I’m fine,” it said.

Reading it, he felt his anxiety ease a little. Yet many others have remained silent.

(Due to privacy concerns, Wen Lili, Dorje, and Lin Tian are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Yang Shuyuan, Zhang Lingyun, and Wang Qian.

A version of this article originally appeared in Original (Jiefang Daily). It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: Carrie Davies; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

World.title: Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe?
World.content:
The panel discussion starting at 12:30 pm on September 10 brings together stakeholders to identify safety gaps and develop community-led solutions to protect children

MANILA, Philippines – Concerned about your child’s safety and how you can ensure a more secure environment for them?

Watch the live panel discussion as Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH launches “Civic Circles: How can we keep our children and schools safe?” This will be streamed on Rappler’s YouTube channel live from the Rappler Civic Hub in Pasig City on Thursday, September 10.

Organized in partnership with CyberGuardiansPH and Mental Health Youth Hub, this pilot initiative tackles rising school violence and digital risks by turning community discussions into concrete, multisectoral solutions.

Rappler head of community Pia Ranada moderates the conversation with key decision-makers and child protection advocates:

Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte shares local government strategies on community governance, child protection policies, and campus safety.

Police Capt. Wallen Arancillo, spokesperson for the PNP Anti-Cybercrime Group, addresses online grooming, cyberbullying, and digital protection in off-campus hotspots.

Dr. Princess Gairanod, child protection specialist from the Philippine Pediatric Society, discusses student mental health, psychosocial care, and health safeguarding protocols.

After the panel discussion and Q and A, participants joining on-site can take part in a hands-on workshop to collectively develop concrete and actionable responses to threats facing children and schools across four Civic Circles:

Campus security and physical safety

Psychosocial care and mental health

Policy, governance, and accountability

Digital safety and off-campus hotspots

The solutions generated during the session may be featured on Rappler to encourage a broader discussion and possible adaptation by local governments, schools, families, and communities.

Bookmark this page to watch Rappler’s live broadcast.

To join the conversation, download the Rappler App on iOS or Android, tap the Chat tab, and enter the Education chat room while watching the stream. – Rappler.com

World.title: IN CHARTS: Literacy of Filipino students in Grades 1 to 3
World.content:
FIRST DAY. Students of Navarro Elementary School in General Trias City, Cavite, attend the first day of classes on June 8, 2026.

Around half of all students in Grades 1 to 3 still did not have proficient reading skills by the end of SY 2025-2026, the Department of Education's assessment shows

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines faces a daunting challenge to fix the decades-long learning crisis in the country, starting with literacy in children’s early years of schooling.

Rappler checked the Comprehensive Rapid Literacy Assessment (CRLA) results from the Department of Education (DepEd) for school year (SY) 2025-2026 to better understand the reading profiles of Key Stage 1 learners, or students in Grades 1 to 3. The data sets were accessed in early June.

Reflected in the data were literacy rates for mother tongue in Grade 1, Filipino in Grade 2, and English in Grade 3. Under the enhanced K to 10 curriculum, the DepEd offers English and Filipino starting Grade 2.

The DepEd’s curriculum standards also suggest that by the end of Grade 3, students are “becoming literate and increasingly fluent” in the use of English, while using their mother tongue to understand and express “familiar and developmentally appropriate texts” or discuss content in various learning areas.

Here are some data visualizations of the literacy of Grades 1 to 3 pupils in the Philippines:

How many struggling readers are there?

Struggling readers are students assessed to be in low reading profiles. In terms of CRLA results, these are pupils in Grades 1 to 3 who were classified as emerging, broken down into lower or higher emergent.

By the end of SY 2025-2026, there were around 519,000 students from Grades 1 to 3 who struggled with reading. That’s 10% of all assessed students in Key Stage 1.

But the CRLA results also revealed that around half of all students in Grades 1 to 3 still cannot read “at grade level” or at the standard expected for their current grade.

By 2028, the Philippines is targeting 75% of Key Stage 1 learners to be reading at grade level, according to the National Education Plan 2026-2035, which was introduced by the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) in January. (READ: [ANALYSIS] What does ‘at least nearly proficient’ mean in Philippine education?)

Where are the struggling readers?

Among the regions, the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) has the highest percentage of struggling readers.

Focusing at the end of Key Stage 1, over 22% of Grade 3 pupils in BARMM remain at low proficiency in literacy.

In its January report, EDCOM 2 stressed that children should be literate by the end of Grade 3 so they do not fall behind in later stages of schooling.

Senior technical officials of BARMM and various national government agencies are already preparing for the first meeting of the newly formed Bangsamoro Education Coordination Forum (BECF).

The BECF, a coordinating mechanism between the national and Bangsamoro governments, will attempt to address issues in early childhood care and development, curriculum and learning, learner support, governance and finance, teacher education, and higher and technical-vocational education in the autonomous region.

You can also check the percentage of struggling Grade 3 readers per schools division office in the table below.

Did Key Stage 1 learners show improvement in reading?

There are improvements seen in the reading profiles of Grades 1 to 3 pupils, as data showed decreases in the share of struggling readers by the end of SY 2025-2026.

Still, half of the students remain below the proficient level.

That trend is seen throughout the Philippine basic education system.

In its analysis, EDCOM 2 found that while the results show “consistent improvement” within SY 2025-2026, around 18% or 3 million out of 16.5 million students remain in non-proficient reading levels. (READ: Most Grade 11 students struggle with reading. What now?)

The assessment was done after the first full year of implementation of the DepEd’s Academic Recovery and Accessible Learning (ARAL) Program.

The DepEd was given P8.9 billion for the initiative in 2026. However, for next year, the Department of Budget and Management did not include an allocation for the ARAL Program in the proposed budget.

The ball is with Congress as Education Secretary Sonny Angara appealed for an additional budget to fund the ARAL Program, as well as beef up various aspects of the sector.

Funding for basic education reached P1 trillion in 2026. Will the government push to at least keep the education budget at this level to address the country’s learning crisis? – Rappler.com

World.title: Philippines’ reading, math, science scores improve in 2025 PISA
World.content:
BACK TO SCHOOL. Students of Carmona National High School in Carmona City, Cavite, attend the opening of academic year 2024-2025 on July 29, 2024.

The Department of Education says the Philippines’ ‘strongest PISA performance’ to date ‘should be seen as a starting point,’ with much more to be done

MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines’ performance in the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) improved in 2025, with the country climbing out of the bottom 10 in the subjects covered.

The Philippines ranked 72nd out of 90 countries in reading, 74th out of 90 countries in mathematics, and 77th out of 91 countries in science, according to the 2025 PISA results released on Tuesday, September 8.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which conducts the test, found that Filipino students had average scores of 373 in science (up by 17 points from the previous PISA edition), 371 in mathematics (up by 16 points), and 367 in reading (up by 20 points).

The Department of Education (DepEd) noted that this is the Philippines’ “strongest PISA performance” to date since the country first joined the global assessment in 2018 and again in 2022, where it saw dismal results both times.

Although an improvement, it “should be seen as a starting point” and “highlights the work that remains,” added the DepEd.

“This is a significant achievement for our learners and for the entire Philippine education system. But more than the numbers, we are seeing evidence that our learners are capable of making real and meaningful progress,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said in a press release.

“We should be proud of how far our learners and teachers have come, but we should be even more determined about how much farther we can go.”

The Second Congressional Commission on Education said the task now is to sustain the momentum, stressing that education reforms require “consistency of purpose, continuity in implementation, and the commitment of the entire country.”

In 2018, the Philippines was ranked lowest in reading, and second to the last in science and mathematics. Four years after that, the Philippines was still among the bottom 10.

Play Video

The average scores among OECD countries for 2025 were 482 in science, 463 in mathematics, and 461 in reading.

“PISA 2025 recorded the lowest OECD-average performance observed so far in science, reading, and mathematics,” the international group said. “Reading has declined after peaking around 2012, while science has declined more gradually over the past decade, and mathematics has fallen especially sharply after 2018.”

Globally, the Chinese jurisdictions of Beijing, Shanghai, Jiangsu, and Zhejiang, along with Singapore, were the highest performers across science, mathematics, and reading in 2025.

Also among the top 10 performing education systems in all three subjects were Estonia, Japan, Korea, Macau (China), Chinese Taipei, and the United Kingdom.

According to the DepEd, around 8,000 15-year-old students from 208 schools in the Philippines took part in PISA 2025 through a computer-based assessment. Most of the participating schools were regular public schools, but there were also public science-oriented schools and private schools. – Rappler.com

World.title: As peso lingers at record-low P62, what does it mean for Filipinos?
World.content:
The Philippine peso has never been this weak. Here's how that could affect everything from fuel prices to remittances.

The Philippine peso has pushed deeper into territory it had never entered before.

For the first time in history, the currency sank past P62 to the US dollar on August 28, closing at a then-record low of P62.265. The peso then touched an unprecedented P62.775 intraday on Monday, September 7, before closing slightly stronger at P62.586.

On Tuesday, September 8, it weakened again to a fresh record-low closing rate of P62.625 to $1.

The peso’s slide began in March 2026, when it sank to an all-time low of P60 to the dollar. A month later, it sank to an all-time low again, breaking past P61. Now, it has sunk to an all-time low yet again, this time beyond P62.

So what does a peso sinking deeper into record-low territory actually mean for the economy?

A weaker peso can make its way to fuel pump prices and grocery checkouts, raise costs for businesses, complicate the central bank’s fight against inflation, and weigh on the Philippines’ economic growth.

For OFW families, a weaker peso might provide some relief since they get more pesos for every dollar sent home. But that gain is partly eroded if the same currency weakness pushes up the cost of fuel, food, transport, and other everyday expenses anyway.

Currency depreciation hits the Philippines particularly hard because it is a country of imports – bringing in large amounts of fuel, food, machinery, raw materials, and other goods all priced and paid for in dollars.

As the peso weakens, Philippine importers have to spend more pesos to pay for exactly the same dollar-priced shipment. Companies can absorb some of that increase through lower profit margins, but they’re more likely to pass the cost on to consumers.

More expensive fuel

Fuel is one of the clearest examples of how quickly the exchange rate can ripple through the economy.

At the Department of Energy’s September 7 briefing, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin said the peso’s depreciation was adding pressure to domestic pump prices because petroleum products are bought in dollars.

DOE officials said the peso weakened by around 68 centavos during the latest pricing period, compounding an increase of roughly $9 to $10 per barrel in petroleum import costs caused by renewed Middle East tensions.

In other words, Filipinos are being hit twice because global oil prices are rising at the same time as the peso is falling. The fuel itself becomes more expensive in dollars, while each dollar needed to buy it also costs more pesos.

The impact goes beyond just motorists having to pay more for their trips. Diesel powers trucks moving food and merchandise around the country too, while businesses depend on imported machinery, fertilizers, ingredients, and other inputs. As those costs rise, companies may eventually pass on at least some of them through higher prices.

Inflation, and the BSP’s reserves

BPI lead economist Emilio Neri Jr. warned that the recent peso depreciation could fuel further inflation through higher import costs, with headline inflation in August already at a worrying 6.1%. That’s why peso weakness is also becoming a headache for the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) as it tries to bring inflation back within its 2% to 4% target range.

The BSP will not, however, defend the currency at a particular level. At an August 27 Senate budget hearing, BSP Governor Eli Remolona Jr. said the central bank can smooth out sharp movements in, but trying to fix the peso at a particular rate would burn through the country’s dollar reserves.

Nevertheless, BSP data show that ammunition remains substantial.

Photo from the BSP.

The country’s gross international reserves rose to $104.8 billion at end-August, from $103.3 billion in July, largely because higher gold prices boosted the value of the BSP’s holdings and because of income from its overseas investments. The increase was partly offset by government withdrawals of foreign currency to service external debt.

Still, the buffer has thinned from $110.8 billion at the end of 2025. At its August level, reserves could cover about 6.8 months of imports and around 3.7 times the country’s short-term external debt.

“These provide sufficient foreign currency to meet the country’s import needs, service its external debt obligations, and serve as a buffer against external economic shocks,” the BSP said in a statement on Monday.

If depreciation keeps inflation elevated, the BSP may instead have to keep interest rates high for longer or tighten further. Higher borrowing costs can then weigh on household spending, business expansion, housing, and investment, creating another drag on an economy already struggling with slower growth. – Rappler.com

World.title: LIVE UPDATES: First BARMM parliamentary elections
World.content:
WHAT YOU NEED TO KNOW

The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao is holding its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026, after being postponed at least four times: first in May 2022, then in May 2025, October 2025, and again in March 2026.

The historic polls are seen as a pivotal moment in the decades-long peace process in a region that was mired in conflict and socioeconomic and political challenges. The upcoming elections are also a test for the Bangsamoro transition and the institutions and systems established in the last seven years.

World.title: Prevent outside influence in Bangsamoro polls, groups urge Marcos
World.content:
SPEECH. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers his fifth State of the Nation Address at the House of Representatives on July 27, 2026.

Civil society also urges the Moro Islamic Liberation Front 'not to fan the flames of division'

MANILA, Philippines – Civil society groups urged President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Tuesday, September 8, to prevent external actors from attempting to influence the outcome of the Bangsamoro parliamentary polls and undermine the autonomy the region fought hard for.

Duyog Bangsamoro, a coalition comprised of regional and national civic organizations, urged the national government to continue supporting the peace process “regardless of which parties win the elections.”

“They have to make sure that this election turns out to be peaceful and credible,” Josua Mata, secretary general of labor group Sentro ng mga Nagkakaisa at Progresibong Manggagawa, said in a press briefing Tuesday.

Duyog Bangsamoro said there is a “persistent perception” in the region that Malacañang has been meddling with the affairs of the regional government.

This started when Malacañang made “irregular appointments” to the transition government, the group said, which deepened cracks within the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF).

“We call on the AFP and PNP personnel assigned to the region to observe the highest level of professionalism and reject influence from any actor that would deprive the Bangsamoro people of a genuine exercise of their autonomy,” their statement read.

The historic election is a milestone in the peace process between the Philippine government and the MILF.

But other things have yet to be done, such as decommissioning former combatants and the implementation of transitional justice. (READ: Transitional justice for Bangsamoro should be a ‘national project,’ say peace advocates)

MILF’s prerogative

The call for peaceful and credible elections followed MILF’s recent move to dismiss a number of its commanders and strip Abdulraof Macacua of his position as the organization’s military chief.

Macacua is the Bangsamoro interim chief minister, running in the 3rd parliamentary district of Maguindanao del Norte. Macacua has refused to run under the banner of United Bangsamoro Justice Party, the MILF’s official regional parliamentary political party.

This move manifested a long-running conflict inside the MILF. However this affects the election outcome, Amina Rasul, president of the Philippine Center for Islam and Democracy, said that MILF’s decision is their prerogative.

“It’s within their right,” Rasul said on Tuesday. “In truth, we don’t know the rationale for that. We have to accept the decision and just make sure that everything is going to proceed as peacefully as possible.”

To the MILF, the coalition said: Don’t fan the flames of division, continue to engage in debates, and instruct the Bangsamoro Islamic Armed Forces to “stand down.”

Over 2.3 million voters are expected to participate in the September 14 parliamentary elections. The Bangsamoro region is electing political party and district representatives. The elected parliament will eventually choose one member to become the chief minister. – Rappler.com

Quotes translated to English for brevity.

World.content:

MANILA, Philippines – The intense rivalry between these parties can be both good and bad for the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM).

With 13 regional parliament political parties and a total of nearly 700 candidates seeking just 80 seats, political participation in the region could broaden and offer BARMM voters a wider range of choices, according to the Asian Network for Free Elections (ANFREL).

World.content:
Marinduque map. INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Two suspects were arrested and around P3.54 million worth of petroleum products and transport equipment were seized in a joint police operation in Gasan, Marinduque, on Tuesday (Sept. 8).

The suspects were arrested in Barangay Bachao Ibaba after they were caught distributing and dispensing petroleum products using a tanker allegedly without the required Department of Energy (DOE) authority and permit, according to the Criminal Investigation and Detection Group (CIDG) and the MIMAROPA police.

READ: 3 men arrested for fuel theft in Cavite

Article continues after this 

Seized during the operation were about 19,800 liters of petroleum products valued at P1.734 million, consisting of 12,000 liters of premium gasoline, 6,000 liters of diesel and 1,800 liters of unleaded gasoline.

Police also confiscated a blue-and-white 10-wheeler tank lorry valued at about P1.805 million, a black suction hose, the vehicle’s official receipt and certificate of registration, and a delivery receipt.

The total estimated value of the seized petroleum products and equipment was placed at P3.538 million.

The suspects would.be charged for violating Section 2 (a), in relation to Section 3 (h), of Batas Pambansa Blg. 33, as amended by Presidential Decree No. 1865, which penalizes unlawful acts involving petroleum products. /jpv

World.title: PNP reports P3.4-M haul from La Union drug busts in a week
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

SAN FERNANDO CITY, La Union – The Ilocos Regional Police’s campaign against illegal drugs led to the confiscation of P3.4 million worth of suspected shabu and marijuana plants, during crime suppression operations conducted from September 1-7.

A police report showed that it conducted 25 operations during which they arrested 24 suspects in possession of 411.48 grams of suspected shabu, 2,740 fully grown marijuana plants, 1,400 marijuana seedlings, and 30 grams of dried marijuana leaves.

READ: Chinese national, 5 others nabbed; P2.72B ‘shabu’ seized in Pangasinan, La Union

Article continues after this 

The intensified manhunt operations also secured the arrest of 56 fugitives, including seven most wanted persons (MWPs) and 49 other wanted suspects, the report said.

The police’s 20 operations against illegal gambling also led to the arrest of 20 suspects and the confiscation of bet money amounting to P33,457.00.

The drive against loose firearms likewise accounted for nine weapons, consisting of six surrendered and three deposited firearms.

“Our weekly accomplishments reflect the police’s commitment to responsive and effective law enforcement. We will remain relentless in our operations and steadfast in safeguarding the peace, safety, and security of communities across the Ilocos Region,” said Brig. Gen. Crisaleo Tolentino, Ilocos police director, in a statement.

The Ilocos Region is composed of the provinces of Ilocos Norte, Ilocos Sur, La Union and Pangasinan. /jpv

World.title: Mindoro missionary, teacher Fr. Edgar Javier dies at 77
World.content:
INQUIRER FILE PHOTO

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro – Divine Word missionary and scholar Fr. Edgar Javier, SVD, who served the Church for five decades, mostly in Mindoro, had passed away on Tuesday (Sept. 8). He was 77.

Javier died at around 10 a.m., according to the Catholic Bishops’ Conference of the Philippines (CBCP) News.

READ: Diocese of Calapan formally established amid rain, earthquake

Article continues after this 

The Society of the Divine Word (SVD) did not disclose the cause of his death. “We entrust him to God’s loving embrace and give thanks for his life of service, compassion, and missionary zeal,” the SVD said.

Javier’s missionary journey took him from Mindoro to the Pacific and later to the Philippines’ seminaries and theological institutions, where he helped form priests, religious and missionaries.

For Catholic communities in Mindoro, he is particularly remembered for his early missionary service in Occidental Mindoro and ministry among the Mangyan communities.

Born on May 5, 1949 in Guimba town, Nueva Ecija, Javier entered the Christ the King Mission Seminary in 1968 and was ordained a priest on Sept. 5, 1975.

He began his missionary ministry in Mindoro, serving at St. Augustine Parish and the St. Joseph Parish Mangyan Mission in San Jose town, Occidental Mindoro, from 1976 to 1979.

Article continues after this 

He later served as chancellor of the Apostolic Vicariate of Calapan, which is now the Diocese of Calapan.

Javier pursued advanced studies in missiology at the Pontifical Gregorian University in Rome, earning a licentiate in 1982 and a doctorate in 1985.

Article continues after this 

He served as a missionary in Samoa from 1985 to 1995 and Fiji from 1995 to 1999 before returning to the Philippines, where he focused on priestly formation, missiological education and research.

He taught at Christ the King Mission Seminary and headed the Mission Institute in Tagaytay before becoming director of the Divine Word Institute of Mission Studies (DWIMS). He also taught at several theological institutions in the Philippines and served as a visiting professor in Vietnam and Macau.

For his former co-faculty at DWIMS, Fr. Andy Peter Lubi, Javier was more than an academic.

“Fr. Egay Javier is an intimately engaging person and a deeply passionate mentor, one who challenges and brings out the best in his students,” Lubi said.

Fr. Renz Hernandez, one of Javier’s students in missiology, said Javier encouraged him to pursue a master’s degree in the field and volunteered to become his thesis adviser.

“As a professor, his way of teaching is engaging and his missiological ideas are profound yet practical. As an adviser, he’s very encouraging and supportive. He reads, checks, and corrects my paper thoroughly,” Hernandez said.

“I will never forget his writing techniques which he imparted to us—the SJA Method (See, Judge, Act) and the RRR Method (Reality, Reflection, Response),” he added.

World.title: Impeach court revisiting ‘2/3’ conviction rule
World.content:
On its 23rd day of proceedings at the Senate in Pasay City on Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, the impeachment court continued its evaluation of Article I, which focuses on allegations surrounding Vice President Sara Duterte’s misuse of confidential funds. —Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — The Senate impeachment court will revisit the voting threshold required to convict Vice President Sara Duterte, with legal experts set to weigh in on the matter on Sept. 16 before the prosecution and defense present their arguments on Sept. 23.

The court’s presiding officer, Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero, ruled to have it taken up after Senator-judge Erwin Tulfo on Tuesday formally asked the body to reconsider Escudero’s July 6 pronouncement that a vote by two-thirds of all 24 senators—or 16 votes—is needed for a conviction.

Article XI, Section 3(6) of the 1987 Constitution provides that an impeached official cannot be convicted “without the concurrence of two-thirds of all the members of the Senate.”

Article continues after this 

The dispute centers on whether “all members” should mean all 24 senators regardless of their ability to participate, or only those legally able to take part in the impeachment proceedings and final vote.

READ: Highlights: Day 23 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 8, 2026

Four senators are currently unable to attend the trial: Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa, who is in hiding because he faces an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court; Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta, who are detained on the nonbailable charge of plunder before the Sandiganbayan; and Loren Legarda, who is abroad on an extended medical leave.

Escudero said the court would not immediately resolve Tulfo’s appeal through the usual ayes-and-nays voting because of the “sensitive and serious nature” of the issue.

Instead, the court will hear from amici curiae, or “friends of the court,” on Sept. 16. The prosecution and Duterte’s defense will each be given 15 minutes to present their positions during oral arguments on Sept. 23, after which the Senate will vote on the threshold question.

Article continues after this 

Escudero said the legal experts could provide independent expertise and perspectives on the constitutional issue. Their names have yet to be announced as the court is still confirming their availability.

Legal experts split

Senator-judge Francis “Kiko” Pangilinan said the amici could include eminent legal experts, retired chief justices or Supreme Court justices, and constitutional law specialists.

Article continues after this 

The question has already drawn differing views from retired Supreme Court justices and a former president of the Integrated Bar of the Philippines (IBP).

Former Supreme Court Associate Justice Adolfo Azcuna, in an ANC interview on June 19, said he believed the 16-vote requirement should remain because the Constitution refers to the membership of the Senate, not merely those physically present.

“My view is that the voting threshold is based on the number of members of the Senate whether or not those members are present or able to actively participate,” Azcuna said.

“As long as they remain members of the Senate they should be counted in computing the two-thirds,” he added, maintaining that the threshold remained 16 because the four senators unable to participate were still members of the chamber.

Azcuna, however, raised a possible exception involving Dela Rosa, saying that if the senator is legally considered a fugitive, his status could potentially amount to a constructive resignation because he had placed himself outside the legal system.

Retired Supreme Court Senior Associate Justice Antonio Carpio took a different position.

In a June 21 post on his website, Carpio argued that the two-thirds computation should be based on senators who are legally qualified to participate in the proceedings.

“If you cannot hold office, you cannot vote,” Carpio said.

Carpio nevertheless noted that Dela Rosa remained a qualified senator because he had neither been suspended nor removed from office.

Former IBP president Domingo Cayosa, meanwhile, said in an interview with the Inquirer on July 11 that the 16-vote threshold could be lowered to reflect the senators actually able to participate in the impeachment trial.

Cayosa described this as a “fair and practical” reading of the Constitution, saying it was consistent with the Charter’s spirit, which he characterized as “not restrictive.”

The operative phrase, he said, was “two-thirds” of all members of the Senate.

Estrada, Dela Rosa and Marcoleta “are all alive and are not yet unseated by any of the constitutionally allowed modes of removal, so they are still senators,” Cayosa said. “Except when they transform themselves into an impeachment court, they all become judges.”

That distinction, he said, creates a constitutional nuance: “because how can you be a judge when you were not there, [and] you did not observe and participate.”

But Cayosa acknowledged that a “simple and strictly literal” reading of the Constitution, particularly from the defense’s perspective, would keep the threshold at 16.

Tulfo seeks clarification

Tulfo raised the issue on Tuesday, asking whether senators who are unable to attend the trial should nevertheless be allowed to vote.

“When we refer to all members, who exactly are we counting?” Tulfo asked.

He questioned whether the absent senators’ votes would be accepted despite their nonparticipation, or whether their absence would effectively count as a vote against conviction.

Tulfo warned that retaining a fixed 24-member voting base could result in an “acquittal by default” if enough senators were unable to cast votes.

He cited Avelino v. Cuenco, which he said considers members within the Senate’s coercive jurisdiction in determining the voting base and quorum.

Senator-judge Pia Cayetano disputed the argument, saying it was inaccurate to suggest that the Senate had adopted the Supreme Court ruling as its governing rule.

Escudero clarified that Tulfo’s appeal seeks a determination of what constitutes “all members” under the Constitution. He also pointed out that changing the voting base would affect not only the two-thirds requirement for conviction but also the one-third threshold for acquittal.

Tulfo said the matter should be resolved quickly because the trial calendar has been expedited, with the prosecution dropping several witnesses and Duterte’s defense indicating it might not present its own case.

“These developments … could bring the court to the final question sooner than expected,” Tulfo said.

He stressed that he was not seeking to make conviction easier, but to settle how the constitutional requirement should operate under the Senate’s present circumstances.

“What we should ask ourselves this time … should the constitutional design of making impeachment difficult, override equally important constitutional demand for accountability?” he said.

Escudero said the court would take the matter under advisement, hear the amici and the parties, and then decide. —With a report from Inquirer Research

World.title: Prosecutors opt to drop 15 witnesses, want to grill VP instead
World.content:
Inquirer photo/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — House prosecutors on Tuesday dropped their remaining 15 witnesses on the alleged misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds and instead, manifested their intention to call Vice President Sara Duterte to testify in her own impeachment trial, drawing an immediate objection from the defense.

Private prosecutor Lorna Kapunan said the prosecution had originally listed 27 witnesses for Article 1, which concerns the alleged misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds under the Office of the Vice President (OVP) and the Department of Education (DepEd).

So far, 10 had been presented, while the parties had stipulated on the testimonies of two others. Three of the 15 remaining witnesses were scheduled to testify on Tuesday, Day 23 of the trial.

Article continues after this 

“In lieu of presenting 15 other witnesses, we will be presenting the Vice President herself as regards use, misuse, misappropriation of confidential funds,” Kapunan told the court.

READ: Highlights: Day 23 of Sara Duterte impeachment trial | Sept. 8, 2026

She said the evidence already presented pointed to Duterte as the person accountable for the alleged irregularities.

VP ‘queen’ of confidential funds

“In the game chess, we have what we call pawns. There are bishops, there’s a castle, there are horses. And, the most important piece, more important than the king, and I speak this because not of my gender, but the queen is more important than the king, because the queen can move in many directions and we have seen that,” Kapunan said, using a chessboard analogy.

“We have seen that in the evidence presented, the pawns… the witnesses presented here. From the Landbank, we have been able to show that withdrawal, that there were confidential funds and these were withdrawn from two witnesses,” she added.

Article continues after this 

“All of these pawns and castles and horses and bishops point to only one person and that accountable person is the Vice President,” Kapunan declared.

But the prosecution did not seek a subpoena for Duterte yet, saying they intended to call her after presenting evidence on all four articles of impeachment.

Article continues after this 

Kapunan said Duterte’s testimony would be material to all four allegations—grave threats, misuse and misappropriation of confidential funds, unexplained wealth and bribery.

“Not at this time, your Honor,” Kapunan said when asked about a subpoena. “The testimony of the Vice President will be material to all four articles.”

The prosecution has completed its presentation on Article 4, which accuses Duterte of culpable violation of the Constitution and betrayal of public trust over alleged threats against President Marcos, first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former Speaker Martin Romualdez.

The articles on unexplained wealth and bribery remain to be presented.

Defense objection

The defense immediately objected to the prospect of Duterte being compelled to testify.

Lead defense counsel Sheila Sison said there was an “innate problem” with having Duterte testify in her own trial, citing the constitutional protection against testimonial compulsion.

Sison invoked Article III, Section 17 of the 1987 Constitution, which provides that no person shall be compelled to be a witness against himself or herself.

“This is a fundamental right,” she said, stressing that the protection emanates from the Constitution.Sison also said Duterte was already participating in the proceedings through her lawyers.

“It is clear that the respondent is here through her counsel. If the respondent is not interested in this trial, she would not have even sent her lawyers to defend her in this case,” she pointed out.

The defense reserved the right to file a formal comment if the prosecution later seeks a subpoena.

House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro defended the move, saying it was consistent with the Constitution’s principles of transparency and accountability.

“It is important that the impeachment court, including the viewing public, witness how the respondent Vice President answer all these allegations,” Luistro said.

“The Filipino people have the right to hear the answer of the respondent Vice President to all these four allegations,” she added.

Court keeps Article 1 open

Presiding officer Francis Escudero directed both sides not to formally rest on Article 1 pending the court’s decision on whether to call witnesses on its own initiative.

Several senator-judges have sought testimony from former Vice Presidential Security and Protection Group commander Col. Raymund Dante Lachica and his DepEd counterpart, Col. Dennis Nolasco, particularly on who authorized and executed liquidation documents involving the confidential funds.

Escudero reminded the parties that the impeachment court may summon witnesses on its own initiative. Both sides would then be allowed to cross-examine them and present rebuttal and surrebuttal evidence.

Lachica was identified as the recipient of P500 million in OVP confidential funds from former special disbursing officer Gina Acosta, who testified that Duterte ordered the transfer.

Nolasco was also implicated in the handling of DepEd’s P112.5-million confidential funds. Duterte’s counsel and former Education Undersecretary Michael Poa previously testified that former DepEd special disbursing officer Edward Fajarda released confidential funds to Nolasco upon Duterte’s orders.

New trial calendar

The Senate has adopted a revised schedule for the impeachment trial and budget proceedings for September and October.

The September calendar is:• Sept. 7-9: Impeachment in the morning; budget hearings and legislative sessions in the afternoon.• Sept. 10-11: Budget hearings whole day.• Sept. 14-16: Impeachment in the morning; budget hearings and legislative sessions in the afternoon.• Sept. 17-18: Budget hearings whole day.• Sept. 21-23: Impeachment in the morning; budget hearings and legislative sessions in the afternoon.• Sept. 24-25: Budget hearings whole day.• Sept. 30: Session suspended.

World.title: Remullas flying to France to seek help in finding Co
World.content:
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla (left) and Ombudsman Jesus Crispin “Boying” Remulla

MANILA, Philippines — Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla will also fly to France to follow up with the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) the Philippine government’s request for a red notice against resigned lawmaker and fugitive Zaldy Co.

Remulla disclosed this at a press briefing on Tuesday, after his brother, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla, said on Monday that he would travel to France to work with authorities there to find Co, who is believed to be seeking asylum in that country.

READ: Remulla to visit France amid Zaldy Co and Loren Legarda’s stay

Article continues after this 

“We will again file a request for a red notice against Zaldy Co. Coincidentally, I am going to Lyon, France, to follow up [Co’s] red notice at the Interpol,” said the chief of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG).

Locate and arrest

An Interpol red notice is a request for law enforcement agencies worldwide to “locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action.”

“I will work with the Interpol. He (Ombudsman Remulla) will work with the diplomatic efforts [to get] Zaldy Co,” said the younger Remulla.

The Interpol’s headquarters are in Lyon, the city east of France that is widely acknowledged as the country’s culinary capital.

Co, who was charged in November last year in connection with a flood control project in Occidental Mindoro, was again the subject of an arrest warrant issued on Monday by the Sandiganbayan.

Article continues after this 

Apart from the resigned Ako Bicol party list lawmaker, the antigraft court also ordered the arrest of former Speaker and Leyte Rep. Martin Romualdez for plunder. The pair is accused of receiving around P7.44 billion in kickbacks from government projects between 2022 and 2025.

The amount, according to the information filed by the Office of the Ombudsman before the Sandiganbayan, allegedly came from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects that were funded under the General Appropriations Act for fiscal years 2022 to 2025.

Article continues after this 

Romualdez, who is confined at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City for a “cardiovascular event,” has asked the court to allow him to remain at the hospital after his arrest.

In their motion for continued hospital confinement, his lawyers cited his “documented cardiac history,” diabetes and primary hypothyroidism, among other ailments. /cb

World.title: PH improves rank in int’l education assessment
World.content:
DepEd Sec. Sonny Angara

MANILA, Philippines — Three years after ranking near the bottom of international learning assessments in 2022, the Philippines expanded its reach in 2025, surpassing 18 education systems in reading, 16 in mathematics, and 14 in science.

Based on the latest Programme for International Student Assessment (Pisa) results, the Philippines, when ranked from the bottom, placed 15th in science, 17th in mathematics, and 19th in reading.

In the 2022 PISA results, the Philippines ranked sixth from the bottom in reading and mathematics and third from the bottom in science, out of 81 participating countries.

Article continues after this 

READ: Marcos vows to sustain PH education push after Pisa gains

In response to the 2022 performance, the advocacy group Philippine Business for Education warned that the country’s education system was in its “worst state”.

This year, the Philippines obtained a mean score of 373 in science, 371 in mathematics, and 367 in reading, representing increases of 17, 16, and 20 points, respectively, from the country’s 2022 Pisa results.

Data from OECD also showed that the Philippines is among the countries showing big changes between 2022 and 2025, with Georgia, Cambodia, Jordan, Montenegro, United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Thailand, and Turkiye on top of the list.

The assessment, conducted by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), aims to evaluate the academic performance of more than 760,000 students aged 15 across partner countries every three years.

Article continues after this 

Highest score since joining

Education Secretary Sonny Angara on Tuesday announced the marked improvement in the Philippines’ performance, with Filipino students achieving their highest Pisa scores to date in reading, mathematics, and science.

Angara presented the results during the national launch at Caloocan City Science High School, highlighting gains across all three subject areas as he cited the Marcos administration’s continuing efforts to improve the country’s learning outcomes.

Article continues after this 

“This is a significant achievement for our learners and for the entire Philippine education system,” Angara said.

“But more than the numbers, we are seeing evidence that our learners are capable of making real and meaningful progress,” he added. “We should be proud of how far our learners and teachers have come, but we should be even more determined about how much farther we can go.”

Andreas Schleicher, OECD Director for Education and Skills, congratulated Filipino teachers and school leaders for the results, saying “what you have achieved in this latest round of OECD’s Pisa assessment is not just good news for the Philippines, it’s a story that deserves to be noticed far beyond your borders.”

The latest results show that the share of Filipino learners attaining Level 2 or higher, which is the baseline proficiency level under Pisa, has increased.

In science, the proportion rose from 23 percent to 32 percent; in mathematics, from 16 percent to 21 percent; and in reading, from 24 percent to 31 percent.

Bullying scores

However, Angara also noted that the Philippines recorded an increase in verbal and cyber bullying in schools compared to the 2022 Pisa results.

Based on the 2025 data, 33 percent of students claimed that other students made fun of them compared to the 22 percent reported in 2022.

Reports on the spread of rumors across students also increased from 15 percent to 19 percent in the latest assessment.

Reported experiences of physical bullying among Filipino students reflected only a one-percentage-point decrease from last year’s results, changing from 16 percent to 15 percent.

Meanwhile, reported threats between students remained at 19 percent in both the 2022 and 2025 Pisa results.

‘On the right track’

In a statement, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (Edcom 2) hailed the latest Pisa results and said the country’s educational reforms were “on the right track” and “gaining momentum.”

“This progress belongs to the entire country,” the commission said, noting that “over the past three years, teachers, parents, civil society organizations, volunteers, legislators, local government units, and communities have come together to confront the learning crisis and support every Filipino child.”

World.title: DILG chief: ‘We won’t allow’ Romualdez to stay at private hospital
World.content:
Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla addresses members of the media regarding the arrest of former House Speaker Martin Romualdez during a press briefing at Camp Crame in Quezon City on Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026. —Inquirer photo/Grig C. Montegrande

MANILA, Philippines — Secretary Jonvic Remulla of the Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) said the agency would ask the Sandiganbayan to have former Speaker Martin Romualdez transferred, as a person under arrest, from a private hospital to the police medical facility inside Camp Crame.

Remulla announced the plan as the antigraft court ordered Romualdez to appear on Thursday regarding his motion seeking continued hospital confinement following his arrest for plunder on Monday night.

The Leyte congressman, a cousin of President Marcos, was served an arrest warrant and underwent police booking procedures at Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City, where he had been admitted for anxiety attacks and what Remulla called a “cardiovascular event” hours before the warrant came out.

Article continues after this 

READ: Romualdez ordered to appear in Sandiganbayan on Sept. 10

A motion to have the lawmaker moved to the Philippine National Police General Hospital at Camp Crame, Quezon City, will be filed on Wednesday “just to show you that we won’t allow him to stay at Cardinal Santos,’’ Remulla said.

“We can monitor his condition at Crame, but it’s up to the discretion of the court if he’ll be allowed to be moved to Crame,” he added. “We will give his doctors visitation and practicing rights so they can go to Camp Crame.”

Romualdez, former Ako Bicol Rep. Elizaldy Co and two others were charged with plunder, a nonbailable offense, before the Sandiganbayan over allegations they received more than P7 billion in kickbacks from government projects between 2022 and 2025.

Based on charges prepared by the Office of the Ombudsman, Romualdez and Co were accused of “repeatedly receiving, directly or indirectly, on at least fifteen (15) occasions, commissions, shares, percentages, kickbacks, ‘commitments’ and/or other pecuniary benefits” worth at least P7.44 billion.

Article continues after this 

The amount allegedly came from contractors, persons and entities with interests in flood control, infrastructure and/or other government projects that were funded under the General Appropriations Acts for fiscal years 2022 to 2025.

The P7.44 billion, according to the case, was “specifically traced and laundered [by] setting up and/or using shell or dummy corporations and conduits.”

Article continues after this 

Respecting legal process

Aside from Romualdez and Co, also named in the charge sheet were a member of the former Speaker’s staff, Jocelyn Sereño, and a certain Felicito Guevarra, the president of a money changer corporation.

In a statement on Monday, Romualdez’s lawyer and spokesperson Ade Fajardo said his client respects the courts and legal process and will face the charges.

“We recognize the public interest surrounding this case. But ultimately, criminal liability must be determined by the evidence presented in court, under the rules and safeguards of our justice system,” Fajardo said.

He said Romualdez was not asking for special treatment but “asks only for the same due process and fair hearing guaranteed to every Filipino.”

Custody

The Sandiganbayan Third Division, in its order on Tuesday, stressed that the court now has custody of Romualdez.

“If there are concerns regarding the accused’s medical condition, it is only this court that can determine whether such condition affects the implementation of the warrant, the confinement of the accused at a hospital, or his commitment to a jail facility,” the court said.

It also issued a subpoena to Romualdez’s doctors Rody Sy, Rogelio Libarres, Kurt Allen Sibayan and Rosalio Torres, ordering their appearance on Thursday.

According to his motion requesting continued hospital stay, Romualdez is suffering from Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, primary hypothyroidism and other illnesses.

According to Remulla, Romualdez suffered a stroke and a transient ischemic attack, or the temporary blockage of blood to a part of the brain, in July.

“It wasn’t that serious. From what I saw, he had no deficiency, but he suffered a cerebrovascular event,” he said.

Regarding security arrangements, Remulla said “We have two armed guards stationed outside his room 24/7. We also have armed guards in the lobby, and a mobile patrol unit waiting outside the hospital.”

Remulla described Romualdez as a “flight risk,” noting that he has “two private jets… three helicopters … and three yachts.”

The DILG on Tuesday also released Romualdez’s official mug shot taken during the booking procedure.

The photo, flashed on screen during a press briefing in Camp Crame, shows Romualdez in a hospital bed with an orange PNP detainee shirt placed on top of his medical gown.

No instruction

The PNP earlier explained that Romualdez could not be made to stand up for the photo or wear the orange shirt due to the medical implements attached to his body.

Remulla maintained he had not received any instruction from President Marcos on how to treat the former House leader.

“The President has no male sibling, so Romualdez is his closest cousin. If you think this was easy for him, it wasn’t,” Remulla said. “If you’re asking whether there were instructions on how to treat him, there was none. Zero.”

Remulla also told reporters that he and Romualdez briefly spoke during the serving of the warrant, noting that they were fraternity brothers at the University of the Philippines.

“He had no requests… I told him, ‘Brother, I hope you understand why I am doing this. It’s nothing personal.’ And he said, ‘It’s okay, I understand.’ That was the entire length of our conversation,” he said.

Reacting to criticism over Romualdez happening to be at a hospital just hours before the warrant was released, the interior secretary said: “That’s the hard part. We do not have the right to intercept (an accused) before the warrant of arrest is issued by the court.”

World.title: Kazakhstan Expands Air Links to Southeast Asia with New Singapore Route
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan is continuing to broaden its aviation network across Asia, with SCAT Airlines set to launch flights from Shymkent to Singapore via China’s Sanya on Oct. 20. The new service comes amid a wider expansion of routes by Kazakh carriers to China and other Asian destinations.

Via Sanya

The Shymkent-Sanya flight will take around 6.5 hours, followed by an approximately two-hour transit in Sanya. Passengers will remain in the airport’s sterile transit zone and continue their journey without passing through Chinese passport control.

The Sanya-Singapore segment will take nearly three hours, the airline reported on Sept. 7.

The new route comes as Kazakhstan’s airlines continue to expand connectivity with China and other Asian destinations.

Growing Asian Connectivity

The Air Astana Group reported an 81% increase in capacity to China during the 2026 summer season, reaching 49 flights per week across seven destinations.

The group launched new services from Almaty to Shanghai and Xi’an, from Astana to Guangzhou and from Aktau to Urumqi. FlyArystan is also scheduled to launch twice-weekly flights between Almaty and Chongqing on Sept. 23.

Across the wider network, the group increased services to Central Asia, the Caucasus, Europe, Türkiye and Asia during the summer season.

Passenger Advisory

FlyArystan has advised passengers traveling to or from China to arrive at the airport at least three hours before departure following updated entry and exit procedures that will take effect on Sept. 15.

The airline said immigration checks may take longer and advised passengers to check passport validity and current entry requirements in advance.

The visa-free regime between Kazakhstan and China remains in effect, allowing Kazakh citizens to stay in China for up to 30 calendar days per trip.

World.title: Expert: Kazakhstan Residents See Infrastructure Gains, Demand Further Development
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan residents are largely positive about improvements in their towns and villages, but their expectations are shifting toward further development of everyday infrastructure and services, according to a nationwide survey presented on Sept. 7.

National Analytical Center expert Roza Tleukhan said the findings show that people continue to expect the development course to move forward.

“The survey clearly shows that people retain a strong demand for further development – they notice the changes, value them and expect this course to continue,” Tleukhan said.

Conducted in July-August among 1,000 adult residents through telephone interviews, the survey found that 68% believe conditions in their settlements have improved over the past three years. 82% are satisfied with their current living conditions, while 68% expect further improvement over the next three years.

Visible improvements shape expectations

Residents most often notice improvements in areas they encounter in daily life. Roads were identified by 32% of respondents, followed by landscaping and public amenities (29%), parks and greenery (22%), schools and kindergartens (18%), and new housing (15%).

The results show that public perceptions of infrastructure development are shaped not only by the scale of investment, but also by how visible and usable its results are. The survey reflects residents’ perceptions rather than the actual volume of completed work.

A clear urban-rural distinction also emerged. City residents were more likely to notice improvements in parks, greenery, new housing and public transport, while rural residents more often pointed to roads and utilities.

The next demand is broader

Future priorities indicate where expectations remain high. Roads and landscaping ranked joint first at 26% each, followed by hospitals and clinics (21%), internet and mobile connectivity (20%), schools and kindergartens (19%), utilities (17%), and parks and greenery (16%).

Roads and landscaping rank highly both among recent improvements and future priorities, suggesting that progress has not reduced demand for continued investment.

Meanwhile, healthcare, connectivity and utilities feature more prominently among future priorities than among areas where residents have noticed major improvements. This indicates that public expectations are increasingly focused on service quality and accessibility.

Expectations will test implementation

Confidence in further progress remains relatively strong, with 70% of urban residents and 63% of rural residents expecting conditions to improve over the next three years. Among respondents aged 18-35, the share rises to 76%.

The findings suggest that infrastructure policy will increasingly be judged not only by new construction, but by whether projects improve access to healthcare, connectivity, utilities and other essential services.

For policymakers, the key measure will be whether visible infrastructure gains translate into improvements in the areas where demand remains highest.

The survey therefore points to a positive public assessment while setting a higher benchmark for the next three years: development is expected to remain continuous, visible and relevant to everyday life.

World.title: EDB: Kazakhstan Maintains Growth, Strengthens Position Amid Tighter Global Financing Conditions
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s resilient economic growth, moderate public debt and strong external buffers are strengthening its ability to access global capital markets despite tighter borrowing conditions worldwide, according to the Eurasian Development Bank (EDB) September Macroeconomic Outlook.

The EDB experts said the economy continued to expand this year, with GDP growing 4.1% year-on-year in January-July, while the non-oil sector increased by 5.4%. Construction rose 15.3%, manufacturing 9%, transport and warehousing 7.4%, and trade 5.9%.

“The key factor behind economic growth was the increase in output in the non-resource sector by 5.4% year-on-year,” the report said.

Investment activity also remained strong. Fixed capital investment increased 7.7% year-on-year to 11.5 trillion tenge (US$25.3 billion), supported by state-backed manufacturing projects and growing investment in electricity, information and communications.

At the same time, oil production fell 8.9% to 53.2 million tons in January-July, underscoring the need for continued economic diversification.

Annual inflation slowed to 9.8% in August from a peak of 12.9% in September 2025. The EDB expects inflation to moderate to 9.7% by the end of 2026, while the National Bank’s base rate stood at 16.25% in September.

“The strengthening of the tenge against the dollar by 8.5% since the beginning of the year reduces imported price pressure, while tight monetary conditions limit domestic demand,” the report said.

The report noted that Kazakhstan’s fiscal deficit widened to 1.7% of GDP in January-July, reflecting higher government spending and continued fiscal support for economic activity.

Kazakhstan’s external position remains a key strength. Gross international reserves stood at $63.3 billion as of Aug. 1, while National Fund foreign assets reached $66 billion.

The EDB also highlighted Kazakhstan’s improved sovereign credit standing. On Aug. 21, S&P Global Ratings upgraded Kazakhstan’s sovereign rating from BBB- to BBB with a stable outlook, citing the country’s economic resilience, substantial foreign exchange reserves and expectations of a declining non-oil deficit.

According to the EDB, Kazakhstan’s average public debt stood at 24% of GDP in 2023-2025, significantly below the average for selected A-rated economies. The bank projects the country’s gross public debt to rise moderately to 32% of GDP by 2031.

“Maintaining sustainable economic growth in a complex and rapidly changing external economic environment is another pillar of Kazakhstan’s investment attractiveness,” the report said.

According to the EDB experts, Kazakhstan retains the possibility of regularly accessing global capital markets “in the medium term on comfortable terms.” It added that the transition to the “A” category will depend on “the success of ongoing institutional reforms and the pace of economic diversification.”

The EDB’s regional outlook showed that the economies in its region of operations grew 1.5% year-on-year in the first half of this year, while Central Asian economies expanded by 6%. Domestic demand, investment activity and infrastructure projects remain key drivers of growth.

World.title: Kazakhstan Takes Lead as Central Asia Expands Space Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA — Kazakhstan is positioning itself as a Central Asian space hub as the nation expands its satellite and spacecraft capabilities and deepens regional cooperation, including discussions on a proposed Central Asia Space Agency.

The ambitions were highlighted at Space Days Kazakhstan 2026, an international forum taking place in Astana on Sept. 7–9. The event brings together government representatives, space agencies, international organizations, scientists, technology companies and investors to discuss satellite communications, Earth observation, artificial intelligence and new space technologies.

Speaking at the opening, Deputy Prime Minister – Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said Kazakhstan’s priority is to strengthen its space industry while making greater use of the country’s space infrastructure.

“Our task is to use the unique legacy of Baikonur to develop a modern and competitive space industry,” Madiyev said.

Kazakhstan is currently modernizing its satellite infrastructure and expanding its capabilities in Earth observation and spacecraft manufacturing.

By 2030, the nation plans to create an international Earth remote sensing satellite constellation comprising nine spacecraft. It will include six satellites from Kazakhstan, as well as spacecraft from Mongolia, the Republic of the Congo and Nigeria. Madiyev said Kazakhstan is open to cooperation with new partners and sees potential to expand the constellation to 14 satellites.

The country is also working to replace KazSat-3 with a new KazSat-3R spacecraft to maintain the stability of Kazakhstan’s national satellite communications system and meet modern technological requirements.

In July, the government allocated 10.4 billion tenge ($22.8 million) from its reserve fund for the creation of KazSat-3R. The new spacecraft is intended to enter service as KazSat-3’s expected service life ends in 2029.

At the same time, Kazakhstan is expanding its domestic space capabilities. A spacecraft assembly and testing center in Astana allows the country to build and test satellites, train engineers and participate in international space projects.

Kairzhan Kozhayev, chairman of Kazakhstan Gharysh Sapary, Kazakhstan’s national operator for Earth remote sensing and high-precision satellite navigation systems, said the country is building the capabilities needed to strengthen its role in the regional space industry.

“We are gradually positioning ourselves as a kind of Central Asian space hub,” Kozhayev told The Astana Times.

Kozhayev also highlighted Kazakhstan’s spacecraft assembly, integration and testing center in Astana and the growing pool of young engineers as important advantages for the country’s space industry. The Astana Times visited the facility in December 2025 to see how Kazakhstan’s spacecraft are assembled and tested.

“We have a lot of brave, smart and unique minds, new generations of engineers growing up so fast,” he said, emphasizing the importance of involving younger specialists in major space projects.

Regional cooperation gains momentum

The forum also highlighted efforts to build an integrated Central Asian and Turkic space ecosystem.

Uzbekistan is exploring closer cooperation with Kazakhstan in Earth observation and space-based monitoring, particularly for water management, agriculture, land use and environmental protection.

Shukhrat Kadirov, director of the Space Research and Technology Agency under Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Digital Technologies, said the two countries were also discussing an initiative to establish a Central Asia Space Agency.

“I believe Central Asia has significant potential to become an active regional hub for the space industry, connecting East and West, and creating new opportunities for innovation, business, international cooperation, and investment,” Kadirov said.

He noted that common regional challenges, including water scarcity, climate change, land degradation and desertification, require solutions that extend beyond national borders.

Deputy Secretary General of the Organization of Turkic States Merey Mukazhan said space cooperation was becoming an important part of the organization’s broader technological agenda.

The OTS has held five meetings of the heads of space agencies, alongside technical consultations and working groups. One of the most concrete outcomes is the joint OTS-SAT satellite project, which will support Earth observation, technology demonstrations in orbit and the development of joint space capabilities.

Mukazhan said the project shows how regional countries can combine expertise and resources to develop capabilities that would be difficult to build independently.

“We are determined to ensure that the Turkic world is not merely a consumer of new technologies but an active contributor to their development,” he said.

From satellites to practical applications

For Kazakhstan, the development of the space sector is increasingly tied to practical applications on Earth.

Madiyev stressed that satellites and launches should not be viewed as an end in themselves. Satellite data are used in Kazakhstan for emergency response and monitoring climate and environmental changes.

The next step, he said, is to move from individual satellite images toward integrated data analysis and practical digital services.

“Artificial intelligence allows us to process space data faster, detect changes earlier, and improve the accuracy of forecasting,” Madiyev said.

This approach is particularly relevant to water management, agriculture and environmental monitoring, areas where Kazakhstan and other Central Asian countries face common challenges.

The European Union is also supporting the development of satellite ground infrastructure and digital connectivity in Central Asia. Ambassador of the European Union to Kazakhstan Aleška Simkić highlighted the EU’s cooperation with Kazakhstan in satellite infrastructure and Earth observation.

She noted that satellite data can increasingly support farmers and improve water management across the region.

“This is space technology working best for farmers, for water management, and for us,” Simkić said.

Madiyev said Kazakhstan’s space strategy would continue to combine infrastructure development with international partnerships. Baikonur Cosmodrome, a major space launch facility in southern Kazakhstan, is expected to remain an active launch site while also developing as an international center for space technology, science, education and tourism.

He identified three priorities for the development of Kazakhstan’s space industry: data, technology and people.

These include improving analytical products based on satellite data, expanding the use of AI, integrating space data into government and sectoral digital platforms, attracting investment and commercializing technologies, as well as strengthening education and international training programmes.

For Kazakhstan, Space Days Kazakhstan is intended to become part of that longer-term effort.

“This forum is only the beginning of this journey,” Madiyev said, adding that Kazakhstan expects concrete agreements and joint projects to emerge from the event and plans to make Space Days Kazakhstan a regular international forum.

World.title: Caspian Sea’s Decline Raises Water Security Concerns As Kazakhstan Strengthens Management
World.content:
ALMATY – The rapid decline of the Caspian Sea is emerging as one of Kazakhstan’s most complex water and environmental challenges, with falling water levels threatening ecosystems, fisheries, coastal infrastructure and communities. As the country strengthens its broader water management system, the changing Caspian is adding urgency to efforts to improve how Kazakhstan monitors and uses its water resources.

The scale of the challenge is becoming visible along Kazakhstan’s Caspian coast. A newly emerged island, already referred to locally as Rybachy, has become a visible sign of the sea’s retreat, while scientists have warned of potentially significant ecological consequences.
