World.title: Years of waiting for diagnosis causing mental distress for women
World.content:
It took almost two decades for Samantha Banton to receive an endometriosis diagnosis, after years of pain that began as a teenager.

"The few days leading up to my period were really awful, lots of cramping, lots of pain, headaches," she said.

"Then when my period would actually start it would be excruciatingly painful."

Samantha Banton's pain began when she was a teenager living in Geraldton. (Supplied: Samantha Banton)

Visits to multiple GPs in Geraldton, 400 kilometres north of Perth where she grew up, did not give Ms Banton any answers.

"I was always told that I was being dramatic and that it was normal because my cycle was 28 days," she said.

" I was told that it was pretty much life, and just to get on with it and find a way to deal with it. "

After difficulties falling pregnant, a laparoscopy finally provided Ms Banton with a severe endometriosis diagnosis.

But the years of uncertainty around her physical struggles took a significant toll on her mental health.

Samantha Banton underwent surgery to treat her endometriosis. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

"The amount of searching up symptoms and also gaslighting yourself," she said.

"You do start to fall into rabbit holes where you just re-evaluate your entire life and try to work out what you're not doing enough of because you still have these symptoms."

Link between mind and body

A recently released study by Women's Mental Health Australia has found Ms Banton is not alone.

The Beyond the Surface report showed women living with female-specific physical conditions like endometriosis experience greater psychological distress than women with conditions impacting both sexes.

Bronwyn Graham believes physical and mental health support should be more integrated. (Supplied: University of New South Wales)

Neuroscientist and report co-author Bronwyn Graham said there were different factors at play when explaining the connection.

"I think the biggest issue is that these conditions are under-diagnosed … so women are spending many years with undiagnosed discomfort, pain, other symptoms," Professor Graham said.

" The symptoms themselves are going to be causing mental health distress, but then the way that they are received within the health system causes secondary distress … which elevates those symptoms. "

Professor Graham believed one of the biggest barriers to women seeking mental health support was service availability, particularly in regional and remote areas.

Regional women face added challenges

The report found women living outside metro areas had significantly higher rates of mental health issues, including depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Isolation, limited service providers, and long appointment waiting times are just some of the challenges regional women face.

Samantha Banton's experience of now living more than 1,000km from Perth meant the cost of medical treatment was an added burden.

"You don't like to count costs, but sometimes you keep a running total in your head about what you have spent in order to get answers," she said.

A desire to fight the sense of isolation inspired Dee Van Beek to start Karratha Women's Place.

The not-for-profit organisation provides free health programs and activities, with Ms Van Beek's daughter, Fern, a provisional psychologist at the centre.

Dee and Fern Van Beek provide health and social support for women in Karratha. (ABC Pilbara: Amy Rossbach)

Fern Van Beek said getting help to deal with physical health conditions could add to mental health strain for women living in the regions.

“Being away from family and friends, support networks, you also have that social isolation," she said.

"Then the lack of services and options for support here … also creates additional stress and anxiety."

More integrated health care

The report's recommendations include a call for improved "wrap-around" care, with mental health support integrated into more routine healthcare.

Professor Graham said fragmented service delivery failed to reflect the complex requirements of modern healthcare.

"People may be going to get their symptoms of pelvic pain treated," she said.

"But actually the thing that's most bothering them is the mental health side effects of that, and there aren't clear referral pathways."

She also urged women to advocate for their own healthcare and treatment needs.

" You know your body, you know when something is not normal. "

Samantha Banton says she had mixed emotions after her endometriosis diagnosis. (Supplied: Samantha Banton)

For Ms Banton, after years of pain and treatments, she experienced joy with the birth of her two children.

Looking back, she still remembered how it felt when she was finally diagnosed with endometriosis.

"Euphoric and really saddening because it was nice to have an answer, but it was sad at the same time," Ms Banton said.

"It meant that it hadn’t all been in my head for many years; there was actually a reason."

World.title: Live: Invite-only grant scheme 'pork-barrelling by design': Haines
World.content:
Infrastructure Minister Catherine King called in to ABC Radio Newcastle this morning, presumably keen to talk about a local extension of the M1 motorway.

Instead, she spent most of the interview defending a grant scheme which awarded the Marrickville Golf Club $6 million in Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's seat of Grayndler.

Albanese held an honorary membership at the club, which he has not declared on his register of interests, and the fund more generally heavily favoured Labor seats.

But King insisted the PM had no obligation to declare an interest in the club, because she was the decision-maker for the program.

"The prime minister is not the decision-maker of this program, I am the decision-maker of the program," she says.

Asked repeatedly if she was aware of the honorary membership, she insisted it was not relevant.

World.title: Sabalenka stays alive at US Open by telling herself 'the match is over'
World.content:
World number one Aryna Sabalenka has survived her toughest test of the tournament to beat Wimbledon champion Linda ​Noskova 7-6(7/1), 3-6, 7-6(10/7) and reach the US Open semifinals for a sixth consecutive year.

Two-time defending champion Sabalenka had not dropped a set before facing the Czech sixth seed, who fired ​18 aces and saved ‌seven of nine break points but faltered when leading by a break at 2-4 in the final set.

Sabalenka, chasing a third straight title at Flushing Meadows, next plays the winner of ‌an all-American clash between Jessica Pegula and Emma Navarro.

"What a battle. What ⁠an incredible player she is. I'm speechless right now because ‌I was pushing myself to ​the limit this match," ‌said Sabalenka, who has now won 21 of her past 22 matches at the year-end grand slam.

"In the third set I honestly thought, 'That's it, the match is over.' Probably that's what helped me to kind of feel loose and just go after my shots. Super happy to get this win."

By reaching the final four for a sixth straight time, Sabalenka matched the 2011-2016 run of Serena Williams, during which she won three of her six US Open crowns.

The Belarusian broke in the second game, whipping a forehand into the corner that Noskova did not even attempt to chase down, but the Czech broke back with a pair of powerful groundstrokes from the baseline in ​the ‌ninth.

Sabalenka, who reached a record 21 consecutive tiebreak wins at the slams earlier this year, was completely in her element in the opening-set breaker, ⁠where she sprinted through the first ‌six points.

But her firepower deserted ‌her in the second set and she struggled to contain Noskova's serve before handing the ‌Czech a 4-2 lead with a double fault.

After levelling the contest at one set all, Noskova set about pressing home her ‌advantage.

Sabalenka ​screamed in frustration when ⁠a pair of double faults midway through the third set helped her opponent secure another break.

Noskova seemed to be heading for an upset win before Sabalenka recovered her poise to level the contest in the ⁠eighth game.

And the Belarusian was right at home again in the decisive tiebreak, clinching it with an ace ‌before giving ‌credit to the fans for helping to propel her to ​the win.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Prince George arrives at Eton College for first day at new school
World.content:
Prince George has started his first day at Eton College, following in the footsteps of his father, Prince William, by attending the 600-year-old school.

Prince William and his wife, Catherine, the Princess of Wales, were with King Charles's grandson when he arrived at his new school, with footage showing them smiling and relaxed as Eton's head teacher, Simon Henderson, greeted them.

The future king's uncle, Prince Harry, also attended Eton, which is close to the monarch's Windsor Castle, west of London, and where William and Catherine and their other two children, Charlotte and Louis, also have a home.

Fees for the all-boys boarding school, which was founded by King Henry VI in 1440, are about £65,000 ($121,000) a year.

The royal family meet head teacher Simon Henderson and provost Nicholas Coleridge. (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

Thirteen-year-old Prince George, who is the second in line to the throne, previously attended the private Lambrook School, also near Windsor, with his sister and younger brother.

Prince George's younger cousins, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, the children of Prince Harry and Megan, are also due to start new schools in the UK this month, but it is not clear which schools they will attend.

Prince George is the second in line to the throne. (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

The Prince and Princess of Wales shared pictures on X of Prince George, who will be boarding, wearing his new uniform.

Prince William was the first member of the royal family to attend Eton. Charles went to Gordonstoun, the same private school ‌on the north coast of Scotland that his father, Prince Philip, attended.

It was all smiles for Prince George's first day. (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

Eton has long been the alma mater for many of the ⁠country's political leaders. Twenty British prime ministers, including Boris Johnson and David Cameron, went to the school, as did actors Hugh Laurie, Damian ⁠Lewis and Tom Hiddleston.

It retains many traditions. Pupils wear tailcoats, waistcoats and gowns, and teachers are referred to as "beaks".

Eton College has educated many of Britain's political leaders. (Reuters: Adrian Dennis/Pool)

Prince George's first day also coincided with the fourth anniversary of the death of his great-grandmother, Queen Elizabeth II.

World.title: Rural towns finding the right medicine to end doctor drought
World.content:
In his early days as a solo general practitioner in rural Queensland, Ewen McPhee remembers them as both exhilarating and exhausting.

"I have evidence I worked for three days without getting any sleep at all," he said.

Despite the long nights and mounting pressure, Dr McPhee ended up staying for decades in the central Queensland town of Emerald.

He said the turning point came with the arrival of the community-owned "super-clinic" in 2012.

Ewen McPhee says the workload of GPs has increased over the decades. (Supplied: Ewen McPhee)

"The growth in the number of clinicians required is very much related to the complexity of general practice," he said.

"It's no longer coughs, colds and runny noses; it's chronic disease management."

Dr McPhee said the community model had a specific focus on the education of young career doctors.

"We're also allowing Central Highlands residents and nurses to have opportunities to train," he said.

" This is a first for rural Queensland. "

Ewen McPhee says a community-owned model makes it easier to bring trainee doctors in. (Supplied: Ewen McPhee)

'Patchy' coverage

The peak body for GPs said there had been further federal investment in regional health care, but it was still up to local doctors to make use of it.

Royal Australian College of General Practitioners (RACGP) rural chair Michael Clements said a local practice's success came down to how well the three levels of government managed practice rents, hospital staff-sharing and Medicare exemptions.

"Generally, when a state government provides a health service, it's supposed to achieve that funding through national health reform agreements; they're not supposed to be tapping into Medicare," Dr Clements said.

"In rural and remote communities, there are exceptions."

Michael Clements says general practice has become more attractive for graduates. (Supplied: RACGP)

Dr Clements has seen the changes himself.

His practice in Cloncurry in north-west Queensland was previously run by a single doctor stretched between hospital and general care.

When rebuilding the practice, Dr Clements said he secured agreements with Queensland Health and other health bodies to ensure trainees would be allowed to work in the remote town.

Cloncurry's new general practice has focused on balancing hospital and primary care responsibilities. (Supplied: Clements Medical)

"The doctors are all salaried via Queensland Health with all of those entitlements yet still able to work from a community, privately owned general practice."

Dr Clements said the money made from those GP appointments from Medicare then went back to Queensland Health.

He said the Cloncurry council also helped guarantee accommodation and access to health care for staff, which gave the practice its best chance to succeed.

Cloncurry is home to more than 3,000 residents. (Supplied: Cloncurry Shire Council)

GP shortage easing

The latest figures from the RACGP and its counterpart the Australian College of Rural and Remote Medicine (ACRRM) show nearly 33 per cent of medical graduates were training to become either GPs or rural generalists.

That was music to the ears of John Burnett from community group Clermont4Doctors, who had advocated for more sustainable health care in his central Queensland hometown for close to a decade.

He said as far back as 1886, it was the Clermont community and not health authorities who made the town enticing for doctors, offering the modern equivalent of $150,000.

"The town raised 500 pounds to bring doctors out, which would have been a lot of money," he said.

John Burnett says better healthcare in Clermont is vital to attracting young families and keeping older residents. (ABC Tropical North: Liam O'Connell)

More recently, the town was left without a permanent GP in January, leaving not just Clermont but the broader agricultural region and drive-in-drive-out mine workers in limbo.

Mr Burnett said people were driving 200 kilometres for treatment, only to be told the doctor was busy.

"They go, 'Actually, I won't come back tomorrow, I'll just treat myself with a bit of aspirin and maybe a bit of sheep dip,'" he said.

The Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS) has stepped into the breach, opening a Primary Health Care Clinic in the town of 3,000 which will run until next year.

RFDS chief operating officer for clinical services Dom Tait said the organisation was "excited" to run a clinic from within the Clermont Hospital.

"We know how important it is to have continuity of care from your GP," he said.

The RFDS will provide GP services in Clermont until early next year. (Supplied: RFDS)

"Our GPs will be fly-in and fly-out, but really importantly is those GPs are the same GPs on a rotation every four weeks.

"So, the community will get to know the GPs from the RFDS because it'll be the same GPs."

Finding the 'right recipe'

Dr Clements said the number of medical graduates taking on general practice was exciting, and he was optimistic more local practices could rebuild their training pipeline.

"It's actually competitive to get into GP training now," Dr Clements said.

"If you're a rural community and you've got the right recipe of a good, functioning practice with a good reputation for training, you can have a solution."

World.title: Former SA teacher Narelle Zanker crowned Rural Woman of the Year
World.content:
When South Australian dairy farmer Narelle Zanker sees the recognition in a child's face when they realise that milk comes from cows and not a bottle in the fridge, she's reminded of the difference she's making.

Growing up on the family dairy farm on the banks of the Murray River near Mannum, just over an hour's drive east of Adelaide, Ms Zanker always wanted to be a teacher.

But four years into her new career, she experienced a "light bulb moment" when she realised she could merge her love for teaching with her love for farming. And so, with the support of her husband and family, Dairy Adventures was born in 2024.

"[Dairy Adventures] is a fun, educational, interactive experience for families and school groups to come onto the farm and bottle-feed the calves, milk the cows, tour the farm and learn about where their food comes from, from paddock to plate," Ms Zanker said.

Winner takes home a $20k grant

Celebrating rural women Australia's Rural Woman of the Year will be announced in Canberra on Tuesday, September 8.

The only agritourism venture of its kind in South Australia, Ms Zanker said Dairy Adventures addressed a massive gap between farmer and consumer.

"People don't know where their food comes from, they don't know where milk comes from, they think it comes from the fridge in their house or from the shops," she said.

Now the former teacher has been recognised as Australia's AgriFutures Rural Woman of the Year at Canberra's Parliament House last night and will receive a $20,000 grant to develop Dairy Adventures further and take it nationwide through virtual classrooms.

"Having a love for education and farming is what makes it work," she said.

The AgriFutures Rural Women's Award National Runner-Up was Northern Territory pilot and innovator Kelly Shotton, founder of Stationly, a digital platform that helps remote stations monitor tanks, bores and other water infrastructure across vast properties.

The Rural Women's Award, originally established by ABC Rural in 1994 and now in its 26th year as an AgriFutures initiative, recognises women who are shaping the future of rural and regional Australia through innovation, enterprise and leadership.

World.title: Inside the new police powers to target Sydney's criminal underworld
World.content:
NSW Police are set to get extraordinary powers to tackle underworld violence, but whether the move will be effective remains to be seen.

Prompted by two mistaken identity gangland murders within 48 hours last week, the beefed-up serious crime prevention orders (SCPO) will be a valuable tool for crime fighters.

The deaths of Marco Tapia and Joshua Macdonald tragically marked the sixth and seventh murders of innocent people attributed to underworld hostilities in the space of a year.

Joshua Macdonald (left) and Marco Tapia were both killed in separate shootings in Sydney last week. (Supplied)

What is a serious crime prevention order?

Though rarely used, the orders are broad powers restricting the activities of those who police suspect are involved in organised crime conflict.

Currently, police have to bring an application before the Supreme Court before one is made.

An SCPO can restrain who a gangster talks to, where they live, what bank accounts they use and force them to hand over passwords to email and social media accounts.

They restrict what they are allowed to wear, what phones they can use and what car they can drive.

The extraordinary nature of the orders is that those on the receiving end do not have to be charged with committing a crime to effectively be on conditions akin to house arrest.

Ghassan Amoun, Bassam Hamzy's brother, was jailed when he breached an SCPO. (Supplied)

Those who breach the orders can face jail, as Hamzy crime family member Ghassan Amoun found out in 2021, months before he was shot dead.

He was given a 12-month jail term for breaching his SCPO and was gunned down in South Wentworthville just days after being released from serving his sentence.

What is changing?

The catch has always been that NSW Police have to wait for Supreme Court approval for an SCPO, which could take weeks if not months.

And time is vital when underworld violence spirals out of control.

In 2022, one Sydney-based head of a bikie gang subject to an SCPO was only handed it six months after the acts of violence that sparked the order's necessity.

Fugitive Rafat Alameddine, previously subjected to an SCPO, now remains overseas. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Premier Chris Minns's announcement on Monday of an "interim" SCPO that does not require a court's approval essentially bypasses this hurdle for police.

While the legislative changes make the battle to stem the bloodshed easier for the state's crime fighters, NSW Police face another roadblock.

Unlike previous eras of tit-for-tat violence, police suspect most of the criminals orchestrating the recent attacks are not in NSW.

Their utility in stopping overseas-based crime figures organising kidnappings, assaults and murders this time around will be the first challenge for police.

Detectives believe the heads of the self-proclaimed "Coconut Cartel" and the Alameddine crime family remain scattered across Asia, eastern Europe and Lebanon.

Globe-trotting gangster's social media taunts while on the run A wanted Sydney underworld figure may have unwittingly helped police after posting social media messages mocking his underworld adversaries from overseas.

The Coconut Cartel consists of Pacific Islander Australians from the city's western suburbs and takes its name from a historical slur against Pasifika people.

The two groups, police believe, are at the centre of a surge in attacks, kidnappings and assassinations that culminated in last week's tragedies.

With key figures remaining offshore, those likely to be on the receiving end of SCPOs this time around are possibly their Sydney-based underlings and the fledgling teenage crime-for-hire groups they contract.

Great powers, great responsibility

Those involved in the current conflicts plaguing Sydney's streets will be familiar with the acronym SCPO.

The orders were credited in police circles with stemming a wave of gangland violence between the Hamzy and Alameddine crime families in 2020.

Alleged crime figures Rafat Alameddine, Masood Zakaria, Ibrahem Hamze and others in the rival clans were subject to them for 12 months as police worked to calm tensions.

Similarly, that conflict also saw two innocent people killed in the crossfire: Toufik Hamze and Mustapha Naaman.

Police believe Mustapha Naaman was mistaken for a member of the Hamze family when he was shot dead in January 2021. (Supplied)

The orders granted police some of the broadest powers in NSW legislation, though the main complaint from crime bosses at the time was that it made them "sitting ducks" for their adversaries.

Sydney's era of 'disorganised crime' One of the state's top police officers has promised feuding gangs bringing terror to Sydney's streets will not exist "by the time we finish" as police stare down a new era of disorganised crime.

When the conflict spread to the Comanchero bikie gang and the Ahmad family in 2022, the upper hand police had on underworld violence found its limits.

The oppressive nature of the SCPO saw the gang's sergeant-at-arms Tarek Zahed and national president Allan Meehan move to Victoria and Queensland respectively to escape the scrutiny.

This is where the orders met their match.

World.title: Cameron Smith among superstars owed millions as LIV Golf files for bankruptcy
World.content:
Breaking SportLIV Golf Series Cameron Smith among superstars owed millions as LIV Golf files for bankruptcy Reshmi Basu and Soma Biswas Updated September 9, 2026 — 8:38am ,first published 8:06am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Australia’s Cameron Smith is among a group of players who are owed millions of dollars after LIV Golf filed for bankruptcy protection on Wednesday (AEST) – a dramatic fall for the Saudi-backed league that had big ambitions to challenge the supremacy of the PGA Tour. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, its main benefactor that earlier this year pulled its financing, has agreed to provide $US49.6 million ($68.7 million) in debtor-in-possession financing. The league said in a press release it remains in “advanced discussions” with players to take control of the business, while BC Partners Credit and other investors are expected to provide exit financing when the reorganised company exits Chapter 11. Australia’s Cameron Smith is among 30 players who are owed money by LIV Golf. Getty Images LIV said in its bankruptcy filing it owes millions of dollars to golfers: Jon Rahm, more than $US7.4 million ($10.2 million); Bryson DeChambeau, roughly $US5.7 million ($7.8 million); and Dustin Johnson, $US5.4 million ($7.4 million) and Cameron Smith, $US4.8 million ($6.6 million). The league valued its assets between $US100 million and $US500 million ($138 million-$690 million) and its liabilities between $500 million and $1 billion ($690 million-$1.3 billion). Australian Lucas Herbert is also owed about $US1 million ($1.3 million).



LIV burst onto the golf scene in 2022, shaking up the sport by signing top professional players to giant contracts and offering faster tournament play with more theatrics. It was all made possible by the Saudis, part of their big push into sports investing that also includes football and tennis. But earlier this year, the Saudis decided to stop funding LIV amid a broader shift in strategy toward investments with better returns. PIF had invested an estimated $US5 billion ($6.9 billion) over four years in the league. Bryson DeChambeau is also owed money by the breakaway league. AP The question remains how sustainable this version of LIV will be without the Saudis’ deep pockets. The pull-back by the Saudis was reported in April and in the following months LIV couldn’t secure another funding source to avoid bankruptcy. Maintaining players will be crucial and some of the top golfers the league lured away have returned to the PGA Tour and been financially penalised to do so.



But others haven’t gone back to the PGA Tour, and LIV is trying to persuade players to stay with settlements on what they were owed on their previous contracts and then offering ownership in the league. The 2026 LIV season ended earlier than planned after the cancellation of the team championship in Detroit. LIV confirmed it was “scaling back operations”, and some employees were laid off at the start of this month. Other high-profile Australians to have played with LIV Golf include Marc Leishman, Elvis Smylie and Matt Jones. Speaking in the build-up to the Irish Open, before news of the Chapter 11 petition broke, LIV’s biggest star, Rahm, was asked if he knew what the future held.



“Yes and no, it hasn’t really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis a few weeks ago,” the two-time major winner said. “And there’s just a lot of things in place, right? There’s a lot of things that could happen, and it’s one of those things where time’s gonna tell. To be fair for us people that joined LIV, I’m pretty good at dealing with turbulence.” Bloomberg, AAP News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘Electric knife or saw’: How burglars got away with valuable Renoirs in three-minute art heist
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeCrime ‘Electric knife or saw’: How burglars got away with valuable Renoirs in three-minute art heist Angela Charlton Updated September 9, 2026 — 8:27am ,first published 6:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paris: Two thieves sliced through a fence, climbed through a window and stole four valuable Renoir paintings from a small museum on the French Riviera, but abandoned two of the artworks as they fled, authorities said. Investigators have launched a national search for the perpetrators. The Renoir Museum, in Cagnes-sur-Mer, France. AP Photo/Philippe Magoni The whole operation took less than three minutes and targeted the most valuable works in the Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer, the regional prosecutor’s office said. The theft conjured up painful memories of the spectacular heist of crown jewels at the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and revived calls for better security and better funding for the many cultural sites large and small that dot France’s landscape.



Cagnes-sur-Mer Mayor Bryan Masson estimated the value of the combined Renoir works stolen at €9 million ($14.5 million), but art-theft experts warned they will be extremely hard to sell. The Renoir Museum is housed in the last home of painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, where he lived before his death in 1919. It’s the most famous attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, situated between Cannes and Nice on the Mediterranean coast. Renoir’s Young Girl at the Well is one of the paintings still missing. The “well-equipped” and “well-informed” thieves entered the Renoir Museum via the garden, Masson told reporters at the scene. They sliced through a fence with an electric knife or saw, entered the museum through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames, Masson said in remarks carried by local broadcaster Ici Azur.



The museum’s alarm system went off at 5.48am on Tuesday (French time), and police arrived five minutes later, the mayor said. Their swift arrival “forced the burglars to flee in haste and helped limit the scale of the theft”, the mayor said. Two of the stolen works were found dropped in the museum garden – Portrait of Madame Pichon, painted about 1895, and Coco Reading, a painting of Renoir’s daughter from about 1905 – the prosecutor’s office said in a statement. This painting, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano, also remains unaccounted for. The two still missing are Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano, painted about 1910, and Young Woman at the Well, an oil painting from about 1886. At least two of the works targeted had a troubled history.



Young Woman at the Well is believed to have been looted by the Nazis during World War II, and was recovered in Bavaria in 1949 and brought back to France, according to the French Culture Ministry database of spoliated art. A German officer in Paris gave Coco Reading to a German soldier at the end of the war under orders to take it to Germany, according to the database. The soldier later gave it to a German priest, who handed it over to a Berlin museum in 1972. Germany’s government returned it to France in 1994. Coco Reading, a painting of Renoir’s daughter, was found abandoned in the museum garden. A police car is parked in front of the Renoir Museum on Tuesday. AP Photo/Philippe Magoni The Cagnes-sur-Mer museum had 12 works by Renoir in total, the mayor said. The museum was closed on Tuesday while the investigation unfolded.



The Marseille prosecutor opened an investigation into theft by an organised gang. The French national office for traffic in cultural goods is joining the investigation. “This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums,” said Masson, the mayor. Art theft expert James Ratcliffe of the Art Loss Register said that underfunding is the main problem facing museums everywhere, not just in France. And smaller museums are especially exposed because of their limited finances. “The theft of the Louvre has demonstrated to everybody with criminal intent that museums are potentially soft targets,” he said. “People are looking at museums differently.”



Related Article Crime Gone in 180 seconds: Smash-and-grab gang nicks Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse paintings Unlike the Louvre heist or other recent museum thefts targeting gold or jewels that can be melted down or recut, the Renoir theft leaves the thieves in a predicament. “Although the [paintings] are valuable, and will have probably seven figures attached to them in terms of the financial value, trying to find a buyer who will pay that is going to be almost impossible for them,” Ratcliffe said. “Unless they have a plan for that in advance, they’re not going to be able to just go to an art dealer and say, ‘Look, I’ve got these two nice Renoirs, would you like to buy them?’” AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Former Bluesfest music festival site in northern NSW hits the market
World.content:
NationalQueenslandMusic festivals Former Bluesfest music festival site in northern NSW hits the market Dominique Tassell September 9, 2026 — 7:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The former site of Bluesfest in Byron Bay has hit the market, five months after the music event was cancelled. The festival entered liquidation and organisers axed the event in March, weeks ahead of its scheduled opening, blaming the cancellation on rising costs. The former festival site, at 30 Tanner Lane in Tyagarah, NSW, is open to expressions of interest. An aerial view of Bluesfest in Byron Bay in 2024. The 118-hectare site was valued at $7.14 million in July 2025. “The property was formerly leased to the operators of the Byron Bay Bluesfest, with the site having a long-standing association with one of Australia’s most recognised and iconic music festivals,” the listing description said.



The 118-hectare property comprises six separate titles. Three residential dwellings on the property are each on their own title. The property also has extensive commercial infrastructure, established office accommodation, an entertainment facility and existing income-producing tenancies. The holding includes dedicated offices, staff amenities and extensive site infrastructure including roads, car parking, site sheds, box-office facilities, bridges, fencing, lighting, drainage, on-site sewerage and irrigation systems, fibre and electrical infrastructure and a dam. This year’s five-day festival was planned to be held from April 2, headlined by Split Enz, Earth, Wind and Fire, Sublime, 19-Twenty, the Wailers and Erykah Badu.



It was axed on March 13, just three weeks before opening. Organisers confirmed the event’s cancellation in a statement on the festival’s website, saying ticket holders would be contacted by liquidators about how to get a refund. The NSW government, which had provided funding for the event since 2009, described the cancellation as “deeply disappointing”. “After 36 years as Australia’s most awarded music festival, Byron Bay Bluesfest has made the difficult decision not to proceed with the 2026 event,” festival organisers said. “We are deeply saddened by this outcome and the impact it will have on our artists, staff, partners, vendors and the many loyal Bluesfest fans who have been part of the festival’s journey for more than three decades. “Rising production, logistics, insurance and touring costs, together with a more challenging environment for major live events, mean it is not possible to deliver the festival to the standard audiences, artists and partners expect.”



Since its inception in 1990, Bluesfest has hosted artists including Bob Dylan, Jimmy Barnes, Santana, Midnight Oil and Kendrick Lamar. Its numbers swelled near capacity to about 100,000 in 2025 – compared with about 70,000 in 2024 – following Bluesfest’s announcement that year that it would be its last show. Major Collision Investigation Unit detectives are investigating a single vehicle fatal rollover in Parwan on Tuesday. Nine News

World.title: ‘Electric knife or saw’: How burglars got away with valuable Renoirs in three-minute art heist
World.content:
Updated WorldEuropeCrime ‘Electric knife or saw’: How burglars got away with valuable Renoirs in three-minute art heist Angela Charlton Updated September 9, 2026 — 8:27am ,first published 6:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Paris: Two thieves sliced through a fence, climbed through a window and stole four valuable Renoir paintings from a small museum on the French Riviera, but abandoned two of the artworks as they fled, authorities said. Investigators have launched a national search for the perpetrators. The Renoir Museum, in Cagnes-sur-Mer, France. AP Photo/Philippe Magoni The whole operation took less than three minutes and targeted the most valuable works in the Renoir Museum in the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer, the regional prosecutor’s office said. The theft conjured up painful memories of the spectacular heist of crown jewels at the Louvre Museum in Paris last year and revived calls for better security and better funding for the many cultural sites large and small that dot France’s landscape.



Cagnes-sur-Mer Mayor Bryan Masson estimated the value of the combined Renoir works stolen at €9 million ($14.5 million), but art-theft experts warned they will be extremely hard to sell. The Renoir Museum is housed in the last home of painter Pierre-Auguste Renoir, where he lived before his death in 1919. It’s the most famous attraction in Cagnes-sur-Mer, situated between Cannes and Nice on the Mediterranean coast. Renoir’s Young Girl at the Well is one of the paintings still missing. The “well-equipped” and “well-informed” thieves entered the Renoir Museum via the garden, Masson told reporters at the scene. They sliced through a fence with an electric knife or saw, entered the museum through the ground floor, and then cut the clips securing the artwork frames, Masson said in remarks carried by local broadcaster Ici Azur.



The museum’s alarm system went off at 5.48am on Tuesday (French time), and police arrived five minutes later, the mayor said. Their swift arrival “forced the burglars to flee in haste and helped limit the scale of the theft”, the mayor said. Two of the stolen works were found dropped in the museum garden – Portrait of Madame Pichon, painted about 1895, and Coco Reading, a painting of Renoir’s daughter from about 1905 – the prosecutor’s office said in a statement. This painting, Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano, also remains unaccounted for. The two still missing are Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano, painted about 1910, and Young Woman at the Well, an oil painting from about 1886. At least two of the works targeted had a troubled history.



Young Woman at the Well is believed to have been looted by the Nazis during World War II, and was recovered in Bavaria in 1949 and brought back to France, according to the French Culture Ministry database of spoliated art. A German officer in Paris gave Coco Reading to a German soldier at the end of the war under orders to take it to Germany, according to the database. The soldier later gave it to a German priest, who handed it over to a Berlin museum in 1972. Germany’s government returned it to France in 1994. Coco Reading, a painting of Renoir’s daughter, was found abandoned in the museum garden. A police car is parked in front of the Renoir Museum on Tuesday. AP Photo/Philippe Magoni The Cagnes-sur-Mer museum had 12 works by Renoir in total, the mayor said. The museum was closed on Tuesday while the investigation unfolded.



The Marseille prosecutor opened an investigation into theft by an organised gang. The French national office for traffic in cultural goods is joining the investigation. “This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums,” said Masson, the mayor. Art theft expert James Ratcliffe of the Art Loss Register said that underfunding is the main problem facing museums everywhere, not just in France. And smaller museums are especially exposed because of their limited finances. “The theft of the Louvre has demonstrated to everybody with criminal intent that museums are potentially soft targets,” he said. “People are looking at museums differently.”



Related Article Crime Gone in 180 seconds: Smash-and-grab gang nicks Renoir, Cézanne and Matisse paintings Unlike the Louvre heist or other recent museum thefts targeting gold or jewels that can be melted down or recut, the Renoir theft leaves the thieves in a predicament. “Although the [paintings] are valuable, and will have probably seven figures attached to them in terms of the financial value, trying to find a buyer who will pay that is going to be almost impossible for them,” Ratcliffe said. “Unless they have a plan for that in advance, they’re not going to be able to just go to an art dealer and say, ‘Look, I’ve got these two nice Renoirs, would you like to buy them?’” AP Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Former Bluesfest music festival site in northern NSW hits the market
World.content:
NationalQueenslandMusic festivals Former Bluesfest music festival site in northern NSW hits the market Dominique Tassell September 9, 2026 — 7:53am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The former site of Bluesfest in Byron Bay has hit the market, five months after the music event was cancelled. The festival entered liquidation and organisers axed the event in March, weeks ahead of its scheduled opening, blaming the cancellation on rising costs. The former festival site, at 30 Tanner Lane in Tyagarah, NSW, is open to expressions of interest. An aerial view of Bluesfest in Byron Bay in 2024. The 118-hectare site was valued at $7.14 million in July 2025. “The property was formerly leased to the operators of the Byron Bay Bluesfest, with the site having a long-standing association with one of Australia’s most recognised and iconic music festivals,” the listing description said.



The 118-hectare property comprises six separate titles. Three residential dwellings on the property are each on their own title. The property also has extensive commercial infrastructure, established office accommodation, an entertainment facility and existing income-producing tenancies. The holding includes dedicated offices, staff amenities and extensive site infrastructure including roads, car parking, site sheds, box-office facilities, bridges, fencing, lighting, drainage, on-site sewerage and irrigation systems, fibre and electrical infrastructure and a dam. This year’s five-day festival was planned to be held from April 2, headlined by Split Enz, Earth, Wind and Fire, Sublime, 19-Twenty, the Wailers and Erykah Badu.



It was axed on March 13, just three weeks before opening. Organisers confirmed the event’s cancellation in a statement on the festival’s website, saying ticket holders would be contacted by liquidators about how to get a refund. The NSW government, which had provided funding for the event since 2009, described the cancellation as “deeply disappointing”. “After 36 years as Australia’s most awarded music festival, Byron Bay Bluesfest has made the difficult decision not to proceed with the 2026 event,” festival organisers said. “We are deeply saddened by this outcome and the impact it will have on our artists, staff, partners, vendors and the many loyal Bluesfest fans who have been part of the festival’s journey for more than three decades. “Rising production, logistics, insurance and touring costs, together with a more challenging environment for major live events, mean it is not possible to deliver the festival to the standard audiences, artists and partners expect.”



Since its inception in 1990, Bluesfest has hosted artists including Bob Dylan, Jimmy Barnes, Santana, Midnight Oil and Kendrick Lamar. Its numbers swelled near capacity to about 100,000 in 2025 – compared with about 70,000 in 2024 – following Bluesfest’s announcement that year that it would be its last show. World.title: How safe are digital driver's licences?
World.content:
How will digital drivers licenses work - consultation closed Nine To Noon Download MP3 14m

The technology behind upcoming digital driver's licences is close to military grade in a bid to foil hackers, an expert who has been part of the process says.

The legislation paving the way for digital driver's licences passed in May and public consultation on how it would work closed last month.

Christopher Goh is an Australian-based digital identity consultant who has worked with the Department of Internal Affairs on the framework.

He told Nine to Noon a digital licence would be just the same as a physical one - confirm a person's identity and from a police perspective, confirm the owner was qualified to drive.

In Australia cybersecurity has gone through about 15 years of development, meaning it was now close to military grade, Goh said.

Data was stored in a separate location and encrypted within the phone, similar to the process within credit cards, he said.

The cryptography used was endorsed by NATO, European Commission and US Homeland Security and has been tested by experts in several countries.

"So it's passport grade. ...It's a constant evolution, and we know these threats are always evolving but it's gone through very sound cyber security checking."

Smart phones not mandatory

Generally speaking, people would need smart phones; the alternative would be smart chips in physical cards.

It would be accessed via an app with some level of security such as a thumbprint or face.

In the New Zealand legislation there was also a data minimisation clause while facial tattoos for Māori have also been addressed and will not disrupt the ability to get a digital licence.

While 80 percent of New Zealanders possess smart phones, the remaining 20 percent of motorists would be accommodated - unlike some countries where digital licences have been made mandatory.

"What we hope is, as New Zealand builds trust in this capability and brings more credentials in this format, it will also ease the greatest barrier meeting those eligibility requirements or streamlining those eligibility requirements ... The driver's licence is the start but hopefully with the rest of those credentials [eg birth certificate] in there as an ecosystem it brings a pathway to streameline service for the New Zealand government and for general services for Aotearoa."

For people on the margins, such as the homeless, who couldn't supply addresses, it would still be possible to have a digital licence. He was pleased the government was accommodating them, he said.

In the states in Australia where it was being used, the digital licences were being used for other things beside police checks. It can be proof of age for the likes of pubs and clubs, doing away with the need to hand over other personal information.

For online shopping it can verify a person's identity.

World.title: We have a minimum wage – but should we have a maximum?
World.content:
When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

The idea of a maximum wage is something that has been discussed in recent weeks after Xero chief executive Sukhinder Singh Cassidy received a pay rise to NZ$30.9 million.

It came after a review found her pay was below that of other comparable positions.

While Xero has headquarters in Wellington, Singh Cassidy is based in the United States.

Gentrack chief executive Gary Miles has been reported as New Zealand's highest-paid chief executive, making more than $17 million last year.

The minimum wage works out at about $50,000 a year on full-time hours.

Researcher Max Rashbrooke said he did not see a lot of merit in the idea of capping pay because it would be difficult for the Government to decide what the right amount was for people to earn.

But he said what was more plausible was the idea of pay ratios, so that a chief executive should not earn more than a certain number of times the pay of their average or worst-paid employee.

"That connects top and bottom, ensures that if one person is doing well then everyone else is, and allows for pay variations depending on firm size, etc. It's more flexible and a reasonable fit with most people's intuitions."

It has been reported that typical Xero pay is about NZ$100,000. Xero would not confirm this.

Rashbrooke said in previous years, Mondragon Cooperatives in Spain had a maximum pay ratio of eight-to-one. At one point icecream firm Ben & Jerry's had a five-to-one ratio.

NZ Initiative chief economist Eric Crampton said whether a company's chief executive was being paid the right amount was a question for its board and shareholders.

"Paying too much means shareholders miss out on dividends they could otherwise receive. Paying too little means they could easily miss out on expertise necessary for improving company performance.

"The market for talent is global. Top executive pay in New Zealand is very low by US standards, but American companies tend to be much larger than those based here. The best executives have more opportunity to use their skills in larger companies, and small differences in performance can turn into large differences for the company's fortunes.

"Policies like maximum wages would mean that globally-focused businesses based in New Zealand would struggle to attract the talent necessary to compete in global markets. They would most likely reincorporate elsewhere. A company's board has very good reason to monitor executive pay and performance. There is no good reason for governments to interfere in those decisions."

A report earlier in the year found global real worker pay fell 12 percent between 2019 and 2026, while real chief executive pay increased 54 percent.

In this country, real worker pay declined by 1.3 percent in real terms from 2024 to 2025, while the top CEOs increased their pay by 45 percent.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said what was reasonable income was subjective.

"If there's always a maximum cap no one's going to strive to innovate to that degree because why would you, there's not as much benefit.

"The other practical bit is, is it the New Zealand government doing this, in which case everyone will just go and have their businesses headquartered wherever there isn't a maximum so they can continue to have that sort of option to pay higher … what's the issue we are trying to solve? If it's income inequality or workers' rights or something like that I'd suggest there are better ways."

He pointed to Fletcher Building executives missing out on their performance pay because their safety record was not strong enough.

"New Zealand does have a fairly high minimum wage we also know that income inequality is always challenging, there's always work to try and improve those outcomes in … it depends on who we're comparing ourselves to there's always relative improvements we can make our income inequality and equality levels are generally much better than a lot of other countries at least in absolute terms."

World.title: Is a bigger solar system always better?
World.content:
When can I stop giving money to my kids? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 12m

Homeowners installing solar power systems may get a better return from a slightly bigger system.

Kristy Hoare, managing director of My Solar Quotes, says she analysed 279 residential solar quotes provided to New Zealand homeowners this year and found the median payback for a system without a battery was 6.9 years.

But systems under 5kW performed much more poorly, with a payback period of 11.1 years. Depending on the output, this could be about a dozen panels.

Solar buyers urged to look beyond the cheapest quote Morning Report Download MP3 2m

She said smaller systems had a median price of $11,490.

But slightly bigger systems, with a median cost of $12,148 and delivering up to 7kW, had a payback time of 6.6 years.

Hoare calculated that all systems between 7kW and 20 kW would have payback periods between 6.8 and 7.7 years.

"A huge part of the system cost is actually in the labour," she said. "You get someone out to your house and you have to put scaffolding on… just that cost alone makes the smaller systems not as good for payback."

More than half of solar quotes included a battery, she said.

That would increase the median payback for all systems to nine years because it would roughly double the price of the system. She said about 30 percent of people went on to install batteries.

"The value isn't only in the payback with batteries, it's the energy resilience side. Being able to power your home during a power outage is incredibly valuable."

A spokesperson for Rewiring NZ said it would always recommend people opted for a bigger system if they could, because many households would increase their power use once solar was installed.

"We've heard from a lot of installers - more at the high end - that 9kw systems are the norm in New Zealand now. This is quite a long way above what EECA says is the average and about what the average has been in Australia in recent years. In Australia, this is actually increasing, in part because of the battery subsidy and EV adoption, solar system size is also growing.

"We know people love a payback period, but we do like to point out that it's better to look at ROI or yearly net savings in comparison to doing nothing."

Rewiring calculated that solar should deliver $1000 a year in savings on top of the cost of paying off the system.

Gareth Williams, chief operating officer of the Sustainable Energy Association of New Zealand, agreed the incremental cost of adding more panels to a system was relatively low.

"A 7 kW system may cost $14,000. The cost of another kW - roughly two panels more - would add only about $1000. The effective cost of energy that the extra panels generate is only around 5c/kWh - which is therefore worthwhile based just on export value. Furthermore, in winter or on overcast days the extra generation will have higher value in offsetting homeload.

"In terms of balcony solar the payback period is similar to larger rooftop solar systems; however, the long-term savings are significantly lower."

Powerswitch general manager Paul Fuge said one of the most important factors affecting solar payback was whether people were with the right retailer and on the right plan.

"Solar buy-back rates, which determine how much you're paid for excess electricity exported to the grid, can vary significantly between retailers, from around 8 cents per kWh to more than 20 cents per kWh in some cases.

"Batteries can also play an important role. On some electricity plans, households can effectively arbitrage electricity prices by storing energy when prices are low and exporting it, when prices are high.

"However, being able to do so is contingent on being on the right electricity plan. At present, only a relatively small number of plans offer pricing structures that make this worthwhile, although we expect more retailers to introduce these types of products as solar and battery uptake grows."

He said it was difficult to draw broad conclusions about how long a system would take to pay for itself based only on its size.

"While larger systems can often be more economical on a cost-per-watt basis because installation costs don't increase proportionately with system size, it would be wrong to assume that a larger system will always deliver a faster payback for every household. Payback is highly household-specific and depends on a range of factors that can vary from one home to the next.

"A key consideration is how much of the electricity generated by the solar system is consumed within the home. Self-consumed solar power is generally worth more to the household than exported electricity because it offsets power that would otherwise be purchased from the grid at higher retail rates. By contrast, electricity exported to the grid is usually paid out at a lower rate than the price consumers pay for grid-supplied electricity. Simply put, retailers buy electricity from you for less than they sell it back to you.

"This means system sizing can be critical for payback. A small household installing a large solar system will export a significant proportion of its generation, extending the payback period. Conversely, a larger household with higher electricity use may be able to utilise more of the energy generated and achieve a faster return on investment."

He said it was important to choose a reputable installer that did not have incentives to sell larger systems than a household needed.

Power retailer Octopus said solar generation had increased 56 percent last year and it was seeing more customers install bigger systems. "We expect this change in market prices to continue to become more pronounced, we've seen in countries around the world that as solar penetration grows those day time energy prices fall."

It said that it had led it to launch a new pricing plan that gave free power between 11am and 2pm everyday.

World.title: Labour policy on breaking up supermarket duopoly to come, Vanushi Walters says
World.content:
Weekly Political Panel: Nicola Willis and Vanushi Walters Morning Report Download MP3 16m

Labour's yet to rule out the Green Party's plan to establish a publicly-owned supermarket chain, saying it has its own policy on breaking up the duopoly in New Zealand.

It comes as both Labour and National defend their records on failing to bring down grocery prices, with all food groups recording price increases between May 2025 and May 2026.

Speaking on Morning Report's political panel, co-host Ingrid Hipkiss asked Labour's Vanushi Walters what the party would do to even up competition in supermarkets.

Walters responded only to say "New Zealanders really can't afford three more years of this government".

"They've done not a thing to fix the increasing prices at the supermarket.

"Nicola's been talking a big game about a third supermarket competitor for probably more than 18 months now ... but the duopoly still controls more than 80 percent of the market for grocery prices."

Walters said when Labour was in government it banned restrictive land covenants, enforced mandatory wholesale access and introduced a grocery commissioner as well.

"So we didn't just talk about change, we actually legislated for it."

National's Nicola Willis. RNZ/Nick Monro

Hipkiss suggested those changes weren't effective in bringing prices down.

Walters said the duopoly needed to be addressed, and Labour would release policy on that soon.

National's Nicola Willis was quick to attack, saying she was astounded Walters didn't rule out the "Soviet-style nationalisation that Chlöe Swarbrick promoted at the weekend".

Willis was referring to the Green Party policy that would aim to break up the duopoly and drive down food prices by establishing the publicly-owned chain, KiwiMart, that would be mandated to prioritise affordability.

Foodstuffs and Woolworths would be forced to sell 120 stores and two distribution centres into public ownership which would require new legislation, Swarbrick said, at a cost of about $2.8 billion.

Swarbrick referenced the likes of Consumer New Zealand as identifying "it does make sense to have a publicly-owned supermarket as a third competitor", during the announcement.

Willis said on Wednesday the Greens wanted to "force supermarket owners to sell their supermarkets to the government".

"And then she wants you to put her faith in her and Chris Hipkins to run a government-run supermarket line.

Greens co-leaders Marama Davidson and Chlöe Swarbrick introduce the party's Affordable Kai policy, September 2026. RNZ

"Now, last time I heard something this grandiose, it was called Kiwi Build, and it didn't work out well. Vanushi should just rule it out."

Morning Report co-host Hipkiss asked Willis whether she'd given up on getting a third player to enter the market.

In early 2025, the government had promised "meaningful change" in order to bring down food prices.

Willis said at the time "all options" were on the table, and if competition failed to improve, ministers said they were even prepared to consider the "nuclear option" - forcibly breaking up the companies that dominate New Zealand's grocery sector.

She promised to "pull out all the stops" for shoppers paying some of the highest food prices in the developed world.

On Wednesday, Willis told Hipkiss she hadn't given up, and pointed to legislating fast-track capability for people to establish new supermarkets easier, "there are signs that we will make progress there".

"However, we have continued to look at the structure of the supermarket sector because in the absence of a significant national player entering the scene, there is a question about how do you get the existing supermarkets to compete harder with each other."

She said one proposal that had been discussed and looked at "carefully" was having Pak'n Save competing as a separate cooperative against Four Square and New World.

"That would effectively mean you'd have three main players in New Zealand."

Walters countered this by accusing the government of removing the role of the grocery commissioner.

"By removing that referee, by removing that single point of accountability, you slow down any potential changes that can be made in this area. So effectively, they're taking us backwards."

Willis said the powers of the commissioner would remain with the Grocery Commission, but admitted the role would no longer have a title.
